He wrote New Delhi Times in 1986, in which Kapoor plays a newspaper editor pursuing a political murder through a system that gradually closes around him, and which won him the National Film Award for Best Actor; he wrote Baseraa in 1981, turning on a wife's mental illness and the sister who takes her place in the household; and he wrote and directed Ijaazat in 1987, a three-hander on a marriage reconstructed in a railway waiting room, adapted from a Subodh Ghosh story and scored by R. D. Burman. In all three the romantic material is retrospective and unresolved rather than courtship-driven, which makes them unusual within the patterns this workbook measures. Born Sampooran Singh Kalra in 1934, Gulzar entered films as a lyricist for S. D. Burman on Bandini and became the most decorated literary figure in Indian cinema, holding five National Film Awards, twenty-two Filmfare Awards, an Academy Award, a Grammy, the Padma Bhushan, the Dadasaheb Phalke Award and the Jnanpith.

name: K. A. Narayan
career_background: Also credited as K A Narayan and simply as Narayan. An Indian screenwriter active from 1957 until about 1985. His article is a stub and gives no dates of birth or death.
debut: Screenwriting from 1957.
major_works: With Kapoor: Insaaniyat (1974), Chori Mera Kaam (1975), Neeyat (1980). Elsewhere: Ek Musafir Ek Hasina (1962), Geet Gaya Patharon Ne (1964), Jewel Thief (1967), Johny Mera Naam (1970) and Victoria No. 203 (1972).
recurring_themes: Caper and crime plots, concealed identity and the comic thriller.
creative_style: A plot constructor working in the caper idiom; his best-known films turn on disguise, theft and revelation.
historical_importance: The writer of Jewel Thief, Johny Mera Naam and Victoria No. 203, three of the most successful Hindi crime entertainments of their period.
relationship_with_actor: Three writing credits between 1974 and 1980: Insaaniyat, Chori Mera Kaam and Neeyat. Chori Mera Kaam, a caper directed by Brij Sadanah, is the most characteristic of his manner and the most successful of the three. His article lists his major films but does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Chori Mera Kaam (1975)
biography: K. A. Narayan wrote three Shashi Kapoor films between 1974 and 1980 — Insaaniyat, Chori Mera Kaam and Neeyat — of which the middle one, a caper comedy directed by Brij Sadanah, best represents what he was known for. His larger reputation rests on films outside this filmography: Jewel Thief in 1967, Johny Mera Naam in 1970 and Victoria No. 203 in 1972, three of the most successful Hindi crime entertainments of their period, all built on the mechanics of disguise and theft that recur in his Kapoor scripts. His Wikipedia article is a stub: it dates his career from 1957 to about 1985 and lists his principal films, but records no birth or death date and nothing of his life. It does not mention Kapoor, and the entry is graded Medium.

name: Manoj Kumar
career_background: Born Harikrishan Giri Goswami on 24 July 1937; died 4 April 2025. An actor, director, screenwriter, lyricist and editor who worked in some fifty-five films over four decades and became identified above all with patriotic subjects.
debut: Acting from 1957; his turn to direction followed Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri's request, after the 1965 war, for a film built on the slogan Jai Jawan Jai Kisan.
major_works: With Kapoor: Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974), Kranti (1981), Clerk (1989) — on all three he is director, producer and writer.
recurring_themes: Nation, duty and sacrifice; the honest citizen against institutional corruption; the patriotic historical epic.
creative_style: Declamatory and emblematic, organising large casts around a national argument rather than individual psychology.
major_awards: The Padma Shri in 1992 and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 2015; a National Film Award and seven Filmfare Awards.
historical_importance: The filmmaker who made patriotic cinema a mass commercial genre in the 1960s and 1970s.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, on each of which Kumar is simultaneously director, producer and writer, so the collaboration is unusually concentrated in one person's control. Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974) is the significant one: it took one of the top two box-office places of its year and, with Chor Machaye Shor, made Kapoor one of the most saleable stars of the decade. Kranti (1981) is the large patriotic epic that followed, and Clerk (1989) a late and poorly received reunion. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974)
biography: Manoj Kumar directed, produced and wrote all three of his films with Shashi Kapoor, so the collaboration is unusually concentrated in one man's control. The first of them changed Kapoor's commercial standing: Roti Kapda Aur Makaan in 1974 was among the top two Hindi releases of its year and, together with Chor Machaye Shor released the same year, made him one of the most bankable stars of the decade. Kranti followed in 1981, a large patriotic epic with an ensemble cast, and Clerk in 1989 closed the association to little effect. Born Harikrishan Giri Goswami in 1937, Kumar built his career on films of national duty and sacrifice — a genre he effectively made commercial after Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri asked him, following the 1965 war, for a film on the slogan Jai Jawan Jai Kisan — and worked as actor, director, writer, lyricist and editor across some fifty-five films. He received the Padma Shri in 1992 and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 2015, and died in April 2025. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: R. K. Studios
career_background: The studio at Chembur, Mumbai, established by Raj Kapoor (PERSON-036) in 1948 alongside his production company R. K. Films (PERSON-078). It has no Wikipedia article of its own; the source used here is the article on R. K. Films, which covers both. The studio was sold in 2019 after a fire.
debut: Founded in 1948, the year after independence; the company's first film, Aag, did not perform well.
major_works: With Kapoor, as facility or banner: Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974), Mukti (1977), Satyam Shivam Sundaram (1978).
recurring_themes: The article notes that most R. K. productions share a theme of social criticism and of love across social divides.
creative_style: Not applicable; a studio rather than an individual.
historical_importance: The home of the Kapoor family's filmmaking and one of the most recognisable production houses in Indian cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, and the nature of the credit differs between them. Satyam Shivam Sundaram (1978) is a genuine R. K. production, directed by Raj Kapoor with his youngest brother as the male lead. On Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974) and Mukti (1977) the credit is for the studio facility, those films having been made by other producers. The distinction matters: only one of the three implies the family company's creative involvement. The separate R. K. Films entry (PERSON-078) covers the two earliest films, Aag and Awaara.
most_important_collaboration: Satyam Shivam Sundaram (1978)
biography: R. K. Studios appears on three Shashi Kapoor films, but only one of them is an R. K. picture in the full sense. Satyam Shivam Sundaram in 1978 was directed by Raj Kapoor and starred his youngest brother, the one occasion on which Shashi took an adult lead in a film made by the family company. On Roti Kapda Aur Makaan and Mukti the credit records the Chembur facility where the films were shot, not creative participation by the Kapoors, and the two kinds of credit are kept distinct here to avoid overstating the collaboration. The studio was established in 1948 alongside R. K. Films and became the most recognisable production address in Indian cinema before being sold in 2019 after a fire. It has no article of its own; the source is the R. K. Films article, which covers the studio as well.

name: Rahi Masoom Reza
industry: Hindi cinema, television and Urdu literature
career_background: Born 1 September 1927; died 15 March 1992. An Urdu and Hindi poet, novelist and screenwriter who also wrote film lyrics. The name is also spelled Rahi Masoom Raza.
debut: Writing from 1945, initially as a poet and novelist.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zameen Aasmaan (1984), Ilzaam (1986), Commando (1988). Elsewhere: Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki (1979), Tawaif (1985), Lamhe (1991) and the television Mahabharat.
recurring_themes: The moral argument conducted in dialogue; Urdu literary diction inside commercial forms.
creative_style: A poet and novelist writing dialogue of unusual literary weight for otherwise conventional commercial pictures.
major_awards: The Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue three times, for Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki (1979), Tawaif (1985) and Lamhe (1991).
historical_importance: Best known for the screenplay and dialogue of the television Mahabharat, one of the most watched Indian television productions ever made, and a significant Urdu novelist in his own right.
relationship_with_actor: Three writing credits in the 1980s — Zameen Aasmaan (1984), Ilzaam (1986) and Commando (1988) — all in Kapoor's supporting and character phase. They are ordinary commercial pictures carrying dialogue by a writer of serious literary standing, which was Reza's characteristic position in the industry. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Ilzaam (1986)
biography: Rahi Masoom Reza wrote dialogue for three Shashi Kapoor films in the 1980s: Zameen Aasmaan, Ilzaam and Commando. All three are mainstream commercial pictures from the period in which Kapoor had moved into supporting and senior roles, and all three carry the work of a writer whose standing lay well outside such films. Born in 1927, Reza was a significant Urdu and Hindi poet and novelist who came to cinema in middle age and won the Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue three times, for Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki, Tawaif and Lamhe. His largest audience came from television: he wrote the screenplay and dialogue for Mahabharat, among the most widely watched Indian productions ever made. He died in 1992. His article does not mention Kapoor, and this entry rests on the credits together with his biography.

name: Raj Kapoor
career_background: Born Ranbir Raj Kapoor on 14 December 1924 in Peshawar; died 2 June 1988. The eldest son of Prithviraj Kapoor and therefore Shashi Kapoor's eldest brother, he founded R. K. Films (PERSON-078) and R. K. Studios (PERSON-034) in 1948 and has been called the greatest showman of Indian cinema.
debut: Acting from 1935; Aag (1948) was his first film as director.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aag (1948), Awaara (1951), Satyam Shivam Sundaram (1978). Elsewhere: Shree 420 (1955) and Mera Naam Joker (1970).
recurring_themes: Social criticism and love across class divides; the tramp figure adapted from Chaplin; spectacle used to carry moral argument.
creative_style: A showman's cinema of large emotion, music and image, with a persistent socialist sympathy beneath the spectacle.
major_awards: Three National Film Awards and eleven Filmfare Awards; his performance in Awaara was ranked among the top ten greatest performances of all time in a list his article cites.
historical_importance: One of the most influential actors and filmmakers in the history of Indian cinema, and the figure through whom his youngest brother entered films.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, and they bracket the career at both ends. In Aag (1948) and Awaara (1951) the child Shashi plays the younger version of Raj's own character — the literal origin of his screen life, and the reason he was billed as Shashiraj. Twenty-seven years later Raj directed him as an adult lead in Satyam Shivam Sundaram (1978), a film built on the disfigured face and beautiful voice of Rupa, played by Zeenat Aman. It is the only time the brothers worked together as director and adult star.
most_important_collaboration: Satyam Shivam Sundaram (1978)
biography: Raj Kapoor gave his youngest brother both his first screen appearance and, three decades later, one of his most discussed adult roles. In Aag in 1948, Raj Kapoor's debut as a director and the founding production of R. K. Films, the nine-year-old Shashi plays the child version of his brother's character; Awaara in 1951 repeats the arrangement, and those two performances are where this filmography begins, the reason he was billed Shashiraj. Twenty-seven years then pass before they work together again. Satyam Shivam Sundaram in 1978 cast the adult Shashi as the male lead of an R. K. production opposite Zeenat Aman, in a film about a disfigured face and a beautiful voice that drew large audiences and heavy criticism in roughly equal measure. Raj Kapoor, born in Peshawar in 1924 as the eldest son of Prithviraj Kapoor, founded R. K. Films in 1948 and became the most famous showman of Indian cinema, drawing on Chaplin for his tramp persona and pairing spectacle with social criticism; he won three National Film Awards and eleven Filmfare Awards, and died in 1988.

name: Ram Kelkar
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credits of the three films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shankar Dada (1976), Hira Aur Patthar (1977), Ilzaam (1986).
recurring_themes: On the evidence of these credits, mainstream action and crime melodrama.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: Three writing credits: Shankar Dada (1976) and Ilzaam (1986), both directed by Shibu Mitra (PERSON-024), and Hira Aur Patthar (1977). The link with Mitra is the only discernible pattern — two of the three are that director's films, a decade apart.
most_important_collaboration: Ilzaam (1986)
biography: Ram Kelkar has three writing credits in this filmography: Shankar Dada in 1976, Hira Aur Patthar in 1977 and Ilzaam in 1986. Two of the three are films of Shibu Mitra, who appears separately in this sheet, and that association a decade apart is the only pattern the credits reveal. No Wikipedia article exists for him under this name or any variant attempted in research, and no other biographical source was found, so nothing can responsibly be said about his career beyond these films. Ilzaam is the most consequential of the three, a commercial success that launched Govinda and in which Kapoor plays the senior supporting figure. The entry is graded Low and rests entirely on the film credits.

name: Ramesh Sippy
career_background: Born Ramesh Sipahimalani, son of the producer G. P. Sippy (PERSON-059). An Indian film director, producer and actor in Hindi cinema; his article gives no birth date. In 2017 he founded the Ramesh Sippy Academy of Cinema & Entertainment in Mumbai.
debut: Directing in the early 1970s; Sholay (1975) made his reputation.
major_works: With Kapoor: Trishna (1978) as producer, Shaan (1980) and Akayla (1991) as director. Elsewhere: Sholay (1975), often described as one of the most influential Indian films ever made.
recurring_themes: The large-scale action ensemble; friendship and vengeance; the widescreen commercial spectacle.
creative_style: A director of scale and pace, working with big casts, elaborate action and a strong sense of screen geography.
major_awards: The Padma Shri in 2013.
historical_importance: The director of Sholay, the defining Hindi blockbuster, whose success set the template for the multi-starrer form in which Kapoor spent his peak years.
relationship_with_actor: Three films across thirteen years. He produced Trishna (1978) and directed Shaan (1980) and Akayla (1991). Shaan is the significant one: made in the wake of Sholay, it is a large-scale caper in which Kapoor and Amitabh Bachchan play brothers, and it belongs to the run of ensemble films that dominates Kapoor's late-1970s and early-1980s work. Akayla, eleven years later, is a Bachchan vehicle in which Kapoor's part is much smaller. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Shaan (1980)
biography: Ramesh Sippy directed two Shashi Kapoor films and produced a third. Shaan in 1980 is the one that matters: made immediately after Sholay, the film that had made Sippy's name and reshaped Hindi commercial cinema, it is a large-scale caper in which Kapoor and Amitabh Bachchan play brothers, and it sits squarely inside the multi-starrer cycle that defines Kapoor's peak. He had produced Trishna two years earlier, an Anil Ganguly melodrama pairing Kapoor with Raakhee at the quieter end of his output, and returned in 1991 with Akayla, by which time Kapoor's role was supporting in a Bachchan vehicle written by Salim Khan alone. Sippy is the son of the producer G. P. Sippy, who also appears in this sheet and produced two of these three films, so the association is really with a family company. Born Ramesh Sipahimalani, he received the Padma Shri in 2013 and founded a film academy in Mumbai in 2017. His article is brief, gives no birth date and does not mention Kapoor.

name: Ramesh Talwar
career_background: Born Ramesh Attarchand Talwar. A film, theatre and television director, co-producer and actor, and the nephew of the writer Sagar Sarhadi (PERSON-020). He began as a child artist in Dhool Ka Phool (1959), Love in Simla (1960) and Phool Aur Kaliyan (1960).
debut: Assistant director to Yash Chopra (PERSON-005) from 1969 to 1979; directing in his own right from 1977 with Doosra Aadmi.
major_works: With Kapoor: Doosra Aadmi (1977), Baseraa (1981), Sawaal (1982). He has also directed extensively in the theatre.
recurring_themes: Domestic and romantic drama in the Yash Chopra manner: second attachments, marriages under strain and the pull of the past.
creative_style: A director formed inside the Chopra house style, working with its writers, its banner and its preference for interior emotional conflict.
major_awards: A Filmfare Best Director nomination for Baseraa (1981).
historical_importance: Principally as the closest inheritor of the Yash Chopra idiom in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, all of them Yash Chopra productions and all with Kapoor in the lead: Doosra Aadmi (1977), Baseraa (1981) and Sawaal (1982). Two were written by his uncle Sagar Sarhadi and one by Gulzar (PERSON-031). These are among the most romantically substantial films of Kapoor's later career — Doosra Aadmi turns on a younger woman's attachment to a married man, Baseraa on a wife's illness and a sister's substitution — and they supply several of the more ambivalent rows in the Romances sheet.
most_important_collaboration: Baseraa (1981)
biography: Ramesh Talwar directed three Shashi Kapoor films, all produced by Yash Chopra and all giving Kapoor the lead at a point when he was more often one name among many in a large ensemble. Doosra Aadmi in 1977, written by his uncle Sagar Sarhadi, turns on a young woman's attachment to an older married man; Baseraa in 1981, written by Gulzar, on a wife's mental illness and her sister's place in the household; Sawaal followed in 1982, again with Sarhadi writing and Khayyam composing. These are among the most romantically substantial films of his later career, and they supply several of the more ambivalent rows in this workbook's Romances sheet. Talwar had been Chopra's assistant director from 1969 to 1979 and absorbed the house idiom thoroughly — interior conflict, belated attachment, the past pressing on the present — and Baseraa brought him a Filmfare Best Director nomination. Born Ramesh Attarchand Talwar, he began as a child artist in Dhool Ka Phool and Love in Simla and has directed extensively in the theatre. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: S. D. Burman
career_background: Born Sachin Dev Burman on 1 October 1906 into the Tripura royal family; died 31 October 1975. He began in Bengali films in 1937 and became one of the most influential Hindi film composers, scoring more than a hundred films. He was the father of R. D. Burman (PERSON-003).
debut: Composing from 1932; his Hindi career began in the 1940s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Benazir (1964), Sharmeelee (1971), Deewaangee (1976). Elsewhere: Chalti Ka Naam Gaadi (1958) and Sujata.
recurring_themes: Folk music of East Bengal, Hindustani classical material and light semi-classical song, absorbed into film melody.
creative_style: A composer who drew on folk idiom and everyday sound, and who sang himself in a distinctive unpolished voice.
major_awards: The Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for his compositions in Sujata — his article notes he remains the only music director to have won it.
historical_importance: One of the small group of composers who defined the sound of Hindi cinema's golden age, and the founder of a two-generation musical dynasty.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, all song credits, across twelve years: Benazir (1964), Sharmeelee (1971) and Deewaangee, released in 1976 after his death in October 1975. Sharmeelee is the important one — a major success of Kapoor's star period opposite Raakhee, with a soundtrack that remains among the best known of his films. His son R. D. Burman worked with Kapoor eleven times, so between them the Burmans scored fourteen of these films.
most_important_collaboration: Sharmeelee (1971)
biography: Sachin Dev Burman scored three Shashi Kapoor films, the most important of them Sharmeelee in 1971, a major success of the actor's star period whose songs are among the best remembered of his career, with Raakhee in a double role as twin sisters. Benazir came in 1964, made under Bimal Roy's banner during the uncertain years before Kapoor's stardom, and Deewaangee in 1976, released after the composer's death in October 1975 and sharing its song credit with Ravindra Jain. Born in 1906 into the Tripura royal family, Burman began in Bengali cinema in 1937 and became one of the defining composers of the Hindi golden age, scoring more than a hundred films and drawing openly on the folk music of East Bengal and on Hindustani classical material; he sang as well, in an unmistakable unpolished voice, and remains the only music director to have received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, for Sujata. His son R. D. Burman scored eleven Kapoor films, so father and son together account for fourteen. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: S. K. Kapur
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credits of the three films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shankar Dada (1976), Apna Khoon (1978), Maan Gaye Ustaad (1981).
recurring_themes: Commercial action melodrama of the late 1970s and early 1980s.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: Three producing credits in five years — Shankar Dada (1976), Apna Khoon (1978) and Maan Gaye Ustaad (1981) — all Kapoor star vehicles of the action register, and all three sharing their composer, the duo Sonik Omi (PERSON-044), which suggests a small recurring production unit rather than three unrelated engagements.
most_important_collaboration: Shankar Dada (1976)
biography: S. K. Kapur produced three Shashi Kapoor films between 1976 and 1981: Shankar Dada, Apna Khoon and Maan Gaye Ustaad. The three hang together as a unit — all action vehicles with Kapoor in the lead, and all scored by the composing duo Sonik Omi, who likewise worked on no other film in this filmography — which suggests a single small production outfit returning to the same star and the same collaborators rather than three separate arrangements. Nothing further can be established: no Wikipedia article exists under this name or any variant tried during research, and no other biographical source was located. The entry is graded Low and rests entirely on the credits of the three films.

name: Salil Chowdhury
career_background: Born 19 November 1925; died 5 September 1995. A music director, songwriter, lyricist, writer and poet who composed for films in thirteen languages, including more than seventy-five Hindi, forty-one Bengali and twenty-seven Malayalam films. His article's short description gives his birth year as 1922, which conflicts with the 1925 date in its own opening sentence; the discrepancy is unresolved.
debut: Paribortan (1949) in Bengali; he moved to Bombay in 1953.
major_works: With Kapoor: Prem Patra (1962), Kaala Patthar (1979), Swami Vivekananda (1998). His last Bengali score was Mahabharati (1994).
recurring_themes: Bengali folk and Western classical material fused with film melody; a political sensibility formed in the left cultural movement.
creative_style: An accomplished composer and arranger, proficient on flute, piano and esraj, known for choral and orchestral writing unusual in Indian film music; he also wrote poetry and screen stories.
major_awards: The article records wide recognition across three film industries rather than a single dominant award.
historical_importance: One of the most musically sophisticated composers to work in Indian cinema, and among the very few to hold major careers in Bengali, Hindi and Malayalam film simultaneously.
relationship_with_actor: Three films spread across thirty-six years, and each involves a different function. On Prem Patra (1962), Bimal Roy's film and one of Kapoor's early successes, he is both song composer and a credited writer. On Kaala Patthar (1979) he provides the background score while the songs are by Rajesh Roshan (PERSON-017). On Swami Vivekananda (1998), one of Kapoor's last films, he is again song composer, the credit appearing three years after his death.
most_important_collaboration: Prem Patra (1962)
biography: Salil Chowdhury worked on three Shashi Kapoor films in three different capacities across thirty-six years. On Bimal Roy's Prem Patra in 1962 he composed the songs and took a writing credit, in one of the earliest and most distinguished productions of Kapoor's adult career, made when Dharmputra had failed and his future as a leading man was still unsettled. On Kaala Patthar in 1979 he wrote only the background score, the songs going to Rajesh Roshan. And on Swami Vivekananda, released in 1998, he is credited with songs three years after his death. Born in Bengal in 1925 — his article's short description says 1922, contradicting its own opening sentence, and the discrepancy is unresolved — Chowdhury composed for films in thirteen languages, including more than seventy-five Hindi, forty-one Bengali and twenty-seven Malayalam titles, holding simultaneous careers in three industries. He was an accomplished arranger proficient on flute, piano and esraj, with a command of choral and orchestral writing rare in the industry, and published poetry in Bengali besides. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Shyam Sunder Shivdasani
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him under this spelling or the variant Shyamsunder Shivdasani. Everything here rests on the credits of the three films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Paap Aur Punya (1974), Chor Sipahee (1977), Gautam Govinda (1979).
recurring_themes: Commercial action and crime pictures of the 1970s.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: Three producing credits between 1974 and 1979. Two of the three — Paap Aur Punya (1974) and Chor Sipahee (1977) — were directed by Prayag Raj (PERSON-009), who likewise has no Wikipedia article, so this small recurring unit of producer and director is entirely undocumented outside the films themselves. All three are Kapoor vehicles of his peak commercial period.
most_important_collaboration: Chor Sipahee (1977)
biography: Shyam Sunder Shivdasani produced three Shashi Kapoor films in the actor's busiest commercial years: Paap Aur Punya in 1974, Chor Sipahee in 1977 and Gautam Govinda in 1979. Two of them were directed by Prayag Raj, and the pairing of this producer with that director forms a small recurring unit in the filmography — one for which no biographical record survives on either side, since neither man has a Wikipedia article. No source was found under this spelling or under Shyamsunder Shivdasani. What can be said is limited to the credits: three mainstream vehicles, made within five years, with Kapoor in the lead and a consistent creative team behind them. The entry is graded Low.

name: Sonik Omi
career_background: No Wikipedia article was found for this composing duo under the credited spelling or under the variants Sonik-Omi and Sonik–Omi. Everything here rests on the credits of the three films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Shankar Dada (1976), Apna Khoon (1978), Maan Gaye Ustaad (1981).
recurring_themes: Songs for commercial action melodrama of the late 1970s.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: Three song credits, and they coincide exactly with the three films produced by S. K. Kapur (PERSON-041) — Shankar Dada (1976), Apna Khoon (1978) and Maan Gaye Ustaad (1981). The duo appears nowhere else in this filmography, which confirms that the association is with that producer's unit rather than with the actor.
most_important_collaboration: Shankar Dada (1976)
biography: Sonik Omi composed the songs for three Shashi Kapoor films — Shankar Dada in 1976, Apna Khoon in 1978 and Maan Gaye Ustaad in 1981 — and for no others in this filmography. The three are precisely the films produced by S. K. Kapur, so the duo's presence follows that producer rather than the star: a small, self-contained unit working repeatedly with the same lead. No Wikipedia article was located for them under the credited spelling or under the hyphenated and en-dashed variants attempted in research, so nothing can be said of their wider output, their membership or their dates. The entry is graded Low and rests on the film credits alone.

name: Subodh Mukherjee
career_background: Born 14 April 1921; died 21 May 2005, aged 84. A producer and director of Hindi-language films, and the brother of the leading producer-director Sashadhar Mukherjee. The surname is also spelled Mukerji. His article is short.
debut: Filmmaking from 1953.
major_works: With Kapoor: Abhinetri (1970), Sharmeelee (1971), Deewaangee (1976).
recurring_themes: Romantic and domestic comedy-drama; on the evidence of these films, plots turning on doubling and on temperamental opposites.
creative_style: Not assessed in the article; the films themselves are mainstream romantic entertainments of high commercial polish.
historical_importance: A member of the Mukherjee filmmaking family, one of the most powerful production dynasties of mid-century Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Three films in seven years. He directed, produced and wrote Abhinetri (1970), and produced Sharmeelee (1971) and Deewaangee (1976), both directed by Samir Ganguly (PERSON-021). Sharmeelee is the significant one — a major romantic success with Raakhee as twin sisters — and this producer-director pairing accounts for two of Kapoor's most characteristic star-period vehicles.
most_important_collaboration: Sharmeelee (1971)
biography: Subodh Mukherjee produced three Shashi Kapoor films and directed one of them. Abhinetri in 1970 he directed, produced and wrote himself, with a script shared among five credited writers; Sharmeelee in 1971 and Deewaangee in 1976 he produced for the director Samir Ganguly. Sharmeelee is much the most important of the three, a romantic hit in which Raakhee plays twin sisters of opposite temperament opposite Kapoor, scored by S. D. Burman, and it belongs to the core of his star period; Deewaangee closed the association with songs credited to both Ravindra Jain and S. D. Burman, the latter posthumously. Born in 1921 and active from 1953 to 1986, Mukherjee was a brother of the producer-director Sashadhar Mukherjee and part of one of the most powerful filmmaking families of mid-century Bombay, a family whose reach extended across several studios and decades. His Wikipedia article is brief — little more than dates, the description 'filmmaker, producer and director', and that family connection — and does not mention Kapoor, so this entry rests largely on the credits. It is graded Medium.

name: Suraj Prakash
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him. The title 'Suraj Prakash' holds an article about an 1843 Sikh text by Kavi Santokh Singh, a different subject entirely, and no biographical article was found under any variant. Everything here rests on the credits of the three films.
major_works: With Kapoor, as director: Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965) and Raja Saab (1969). As director and producer: Aamne Samne (1967).
recurring_themes: Romantic drama built on class difference — the boatman and the heiress of Jab Jab Phool Khile is the clearest instance.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established from any available source, which is a striking gap given that he directed the single most important film of Kapoor's early stardom.
relationship_with_actor: Three films in five years, and the first is among the most consequential in the whole filmography. Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965) made Kapoor a star, won him the BFJA Best Actor award, and fixed the gentle, courteous romantic persona that this workbook's scoring is largely built to measure; its Kashmiri boatman opposite Nanda's wealthy visitor is the template for much that follows. Aamne Samne (1967) and Raja Saab (1969) continued the association through the rest of the decade.
most_important_collaboration: Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965)
biography: Suraj Prakash directed the film that made Shashi Kapoor a star, and no biographical record of him survives. Jab Jab Phool Khile in 1965 cast Kapoor as a Kashmiri boatman opposite Nanda's wealthy visitor, won him the BFJA Best Actor award, and established the courteous, unthreatening romantic persona that defines the pattern this workbook measures across the rest of his career. He directed and produced Aamne Samne in 1967 and directed Raja Saab in 1969, both again with Kapoor. Beyond these credits nothing could be established: the Wikipedia title bearing his name holds an article on an 1843 Sikh text, and no biography was found under any variant spelling attempted during research. That the director of so pivotal a film is undocumented is among the more notable gaps in this filmography. The entry is graded Low.

name: Usha Khanna
career_background: Born 7 October 1941. A music director in Hindi cinema and, after Jaddan Bai and Saraswati Devi, the third woman to work as one — and among the most commercially successful, in what her article describes as a male-dominated field. She remained active for more than three decades and has continued to compose occasionally since.
debut: Dil Deke Dekho (1959).
major_works: With Kapoor: Gehri Chot - Urf: Durdesh (1983), Pyar Ki Jeet (1987), Ghar Bazar (1998). Elsewhere: Shabnam, Hum Hindustani, Souten (1983) and Aap To Aise Na The.
recurring_themes: Melodic romantic songs in the mainstream idiom, sustained across three decades of changing fashion.
creative_style: A melodist working in the conventional playback form, whose best-known songs are built on simple, durable tunes.
major_awards: A Filmfare Award nomination for the songs of Souten (1983).
historical_importance: The most enduring woman composer in Hindi film music, and for most of her career the only one working regularly at the commercial centre.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, all late, and the last of them closes the filmography: Ghar Bazar, long delayed and released in 1998, is the final film of Kapoor's acting career. Gehri Chot - Urf: Durdesh (1983) and Pyar Ki Jeet (1987) precede it. She was married to Sawan Kumar Tak (PERSON-304), who directed and produced one further Kapoor film, and her article notes the couple separated. Her article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Ghar Bazar (1998), the last film of his career
biography: Usha Khanna composed for three Shashi Kapoor films, all in his final phase, and the last of them is the last film he made: Ghar Bazar, completed years earlier and released in 1998, the year he stopped acting, directed by D. S. Azad. Gehri Chot - Urf: Durdesh in 1983 and Pyar Ki Jeet in 1987 came before it, the latter directed and produced by Saawan Kumar Tak, to whom she was married and from whom her article records she later separated. Born in 1941 and composing since Dil Deke Dekho in 1959, Khanna was the third woman to work as a music director in Hindi cinema, after Jaddan Bai and Saraswati Devi, and by some distance the most commercially durable, sustaining a career of more than thirty years in a field that had almost no other women in it and continuing to write for films and television long afterwards. Her best-known songs come from Shabnam, Hum Hindustani and Souten, the last bringing a Filmfare nomination in 1983. Her article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Vanraj Bhatia
industry: Indian parallel cinema and Western classical music
career_background: Born 31 May 1927; died 7 May 2021 in Mumbai. A composer best known for his work in Indian New Wave cinema and also one of the leading composers of Western classical music in India.
debut: His article states that his first feature film score was Ankur (1974), Shyam Benegal's debut — which sits oddly beside his credit on The Householder in 1963, eleven years earlier; the discrepancy is unresolved here and the entry is graded accordingly.
major_works: With Kapoor: The Householder (1963), Junoon (1979), Kalyug (1981). Elsewhere: Ankur (1974) and almost all of Benegal's subsequent films, and the television film Tamas (1988).
recurring_themes: Scores for the parallel cinema: restrained, often chamber-scaled, and rooted in both Indian classical and Western art-music traditions.
creative_style: A composer of unusual technical formation for Indian film — trained in Western classical composition, and willing to write sparely where the commercial cinema demanded songs.
major_awards: The National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Tamas (1988); the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for Creative and Experimental Music (1989); and the Padma Shri (2012).
historical_importance: The house composer of the Indian New Wave, and the musical signature of the Benegal school.
relationship_with_actor: Three films, and all three sit outside the commercial mainstream. He wrote the background score for The Householder (1963), Kapoor's first English-language film, and the songs for Junoon (1979) and Kalyug (1981), both directed by Shyam Benegal (PERSON-083) and both produced by Kapoor himself. The collaboration is therefore almost a definition of Kapoor's non-commercial career: one Merchant Ivory film and two of his own Film-Valas productions.
most_important_collaboration: Junoon (1979)
biography: Vanraj Bhatia scored three Shashi Kapoor films and every one of them lies outside commercial Hindi cinema. He wrote the background score for The Householder in 1963, the first Merchant Ivory production and Kapoor's first English-language role, and the songs for Junoon in 1979 and Kalyug in 1981, both directed by Shyam Benegal and both financed by Kapoor himself through Film-Valas. The three credits are almost a definition of his non-commercial career. Born in 1927, Bhatia was trained in Western classical composition — he was also among the leading composers of Western art music in India — and became the defining musical voice of the Indian New Wave, scoring Ankur and most of Benegal's subsequent work. He won the National Film Award for Best Music Direction for the television film Tamas in 1988, the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award for Creative and Experimental Music in 1989 and the Padma Shri in 2012, and died in 2021. One inconsistency is worth recording: his article names Ankur in 1974 as his first feature score, which cannot be reconciled with the 1963 Householder credit.

name: A. K. Nadiadwala
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under the variant A.K. Nadiadwala or under the family name Nadiadwala. Everything here rests on the credits of the two films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aa Gale Lag Jaa (1973), Amar Shakti (1978).
recurring_themes: Mainstream commercial production of the 1970s.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established, though the Nadiadwala name is among the long-established producing families of Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two producing credits five years apart, both squarely in Kapoor's commercial peak: Aa Gale Lag Jaa (1973), directed by Manmohan Desai (PERSON-072), and Amar Shakti (1978), directed by Harmesh Malhotra (PERSON-063).
most_important_collaboration: Aa Gale Lag Jaa (1973)
biography: A. K. Nadiadwala produced two Shashi Kapoor films: Aa Gale Lag Jaa in 1973, a Manmohan Desai picture that was among the actor's substantial successes of the early 1970s, and Amar Shakti in 1978, directed by Harmesh Malhotra. No Wikipedia article exists for him under this name or the variants tried in research, and no other biographical source was located, so nothing can responsibly be added about his wider output — though the Nadiadwala name belongs to one of the long-established producing families of Hindi cinema. The entry is graded Low and rests on the two films' credits.

name: A. Krishnamurthy
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him under this name or the variant A. Krishnamoorthy. Everything here rests on the credits of the two films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Ek Mandir (1984), Sindoor (1987).
recurring_themes: Family melodrama of the mid-1980s.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: Two producing credits, Ghar Ek Mandir (1984) and Sindoor (1987), which share their writer Gyandev Agnihotri (PERSON-062) and their composer Laxmikant–Pyarelal (PERSON-001). Sindoor was the last commercial success of Kapoor's career, so this small unit is responsible for the final hit in the filmography.
most_important_collaboration: Sindoor (1987)
biography: A. Krishnamurthy produced two Shashi Kapoor films, Ghar Ek Mandir in 1984 and Sindoor in 1987, and the second of them was the last commercial success of the actor's career. The two share more than a producer: Gyandev Agnihotri wrote both and Laxmikant–Pyarelal scored both, so they represent a single recurring production unit working in the family-melodrama register that suited Kapoor's senior roles of the mid-1980s. No Wikipedia article exists for him under this spelling or the variant Krishnamoorthy, and no other biographical source was found. The entry is graded Low and rests entirely on the film credits.

name: Akhtar-Ul-Iman
career_background: Born 12 November 1915; died 9 March 1996. A major Urdu poet with a lasting influence on the modern Urdu nazm, who also worked as a screenwriter in Hindi cinema. His article's short description gives his dates as 1915–1966, which contradicts the 1996 death date in its own opening sentence; the later date is consistent with his 1966 award and is used here.
debut: Established as a poet before his screen work; his film writing belongs mainly to the 1960s and 1970s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Dharmputra (1961) and Waqt (1965) — and he won the Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue for both. Elsewhere: the poetry collection Yadein.
recurring_themes: Communal division and its human cost, the family split by history, and the moral weight carried in spoken Urdu.
creative_style: A poet's dialogue — compressed, formal and written in literary Urdu, unusually weighty for commercial cinema.
major_awards: The Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue in 1963 for Dharmputra and again in 1966 for Waqt; the Sahitya Akademi Award in Urdu in 1962 for his poetry collection Yadein.
historical_importance: One of the most important modern Urdu poets, and among the few of that standing to write regularly for the commercial screen.
relationship_with_actor: Only two films, but they are the two that open Kapoor's adult career, and both won their writer the Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue. Dharmputra (1961) is Kapoor's first adult leading role, a partition drama that failed commercially; Waqt (1965) is the multi-star hit that, with Jab Jab Phool Khile the same year, made him a star. Both were directed by Yash Chopra (PERSON-005) and produced by B. R. Chopra (PERSON-055).
most_important_collaboration: Waqt (1965)
biography: Akhtar-ul-Iman wrote only two Shashi Kapoor films, but they are the two that begin his adult career and both brought their writer the Filmfare Award for Best Dialogue. Dharmputra in 1961 gave Kapoor his first adult lead, a partition drama about a Hindu nationalist who learns he was born Muslim; Waqt in 1965 was the multi-star family melodrama that helped make him a star. Both were Yash Chopra films produced by B. R. Chopra. Away from the screen Akhtar-ul-Iman was a major Urdu poet whose work reshaped the modern nazm, and he won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1962 for the collection Yadein. One caution: his article's short description dates him 1915–1966, contradicting the 1996 death date given in its own text, and the later date is used here as consistent with his 1966 award.

name: Anil Ganguly
career_background: Born 26 January 1933; died 15 January 2016. A film director and screenwriter who worked in Hindi cinema from the 1970s to 2001 and also made films in Bengali.
debut: Active from 1962; his reputation was made with Kora Kagaz (1974).
major_works: With Kapoor: Trishna (1978), Neeyat (1980). Elsewhere: Kora Kagaz (1974) and Tapasya (1975), both of which won the National Film Award for Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment, and Aanchal, Saaheb (1985) and the Bengali Balidan (1990).
recurring_themes: Domestic melodrama centred on a woman's endurance; a sustained working relationship with the actress Raakhee.
creative_style: A director of restrained middle-class melodrama, working against the spectacle of the period.
major_awards: Two of his films, Kora Kagaz and Tapasya, won the National Film Award for Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment.
historical_importance: A leading exponent of the sober domestic drama that ran alongside the masala cinema of the 1970s.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, Trishna (1978) and Neeyat (1980). Trishna is the more substantial and fits his pattern exactly: it pairs Kapoor with Raakhee, the actress around whom Ganguly built much of his best work. Both films sit at the quieter end of Kapoor's late-1970s output, away from the multi-starrers that dominate those years. His article names Trishna among his Raakhee films but does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Trishna (1978)
biography: Anil Ganguly directed two Shashi Kapoor films, Trishna in 1978 and Neeyat in 1980, and the first belongs squarely to the line of work for which he is remembered. Ganguly built his reputation on sober domestic melodramas about women under pressure — Kora Kagaz in 1974 and Tapasya in 1975, both of which won the National Film Award for Best Popular Film Providing Wholesome Entertainment — and on a long association with the actress Raakhee, who plays opposite Kapoor in Trishna. These are quiet films, made in years when Kapoor's other work was dominated by large ensembles and action, and they show him continuing to accept chamber-scale romantic drama. Trishna was produced under the Sippy banner and written by Sachin Bhowmick with M. G. Hashmat, the lyricist of Ganguly's own Kora Kagaz. Born in 1933 and working from 1962 until 2001, Ganguly also directed in Bengali, where his Balidan became a substantial commercial success in 1990. He died in 2016. His article names Trishna but says nothing of Kapoor.

name: Anu Malik
career_background: Born Anwar Sardar Malik on 2 November 1960, the son of the composer Sardar Malik, who was active from the 1950s to the 1970s. A composer, singer, arranger and score composer for the Hindi film industry.
debut: Composing from 1974; his prominence dates from the late 1980s and the 1990s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naam O Nishan (1987), Meri Zabaan (1989). Elsewhere: Baazigar, Baadshah, Refugee, Yaadein and Main Hoon Na.
recurring_themes: Mainstream film songs across disco, pop and rock registers, with a noted use of the tabla inside otherwise modern arrangements.
creative_style: A prolific commercial composer working in whatever idiom the decade demanded; his article notes melodious and classical-based writing alongside the dance material.
major_awards: A National Film Award and three Filmfare Awards.
historical_importance: One of the dominant composers of 1990s Hindi film music, arriving at the tail end of Kapoor's career.
relationship_with_actor: Two films at the very end of Kapoor's working life as a regular screen presence, Naam O Nishan (1987) and Meri Zabaan (1989), both action pictures in which he is a senior supporting figure rather than the lead. The collaboration is chronological accident rather than partnership: Malik's major period began after Kapoor had effectively stopped. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Meri Zabaan (1989)
biography: Anu Malik scored two late Shashi Kapoor films, Naam O Nishan in 1987 and Meri Zabaan in 1989, both action pictures in which the actor appears in a senior supporting capacity rather than as a lead. The overlap between the two careers is slight and essentially chronological: Malik, born Anwar Sardar Malik on 2 November 1960 and composing since 1974, did not reach his dominant period until the 1990s, by which time Kapoor had largely stopped working. He is the son of Sardar Malik, a composer active from the 1950s to the 1970s, and his article notes a melodious, classical-based streak alongside the dance material, with a characteristic use of the tabla inside otherwise modern arrangements — 'Woh Ladki Jo' and 'Hum Toh Deewane' from Baadshah, 'Baazigar O Baazigar', 'Mere Humsafar' from Refugee, 'Tumhe Jo Maine Dekha' from Main Hoon Na. He holds a National Film Award and three Filmfare Awards. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Asit Sen
career_background: Born in Dhaka on 24 September 1922; died 25 August 2001. A director, cinematographer, documentary filmmaker and screenwriter who worked in both Bengali and Hindi cinema and made seventeen features. He is a different person from the comic actor of the same name.
debut: Directing from 1948; his Bengali reputation was made with Deep Jweley Jai (1959).
major_works: With Kapoor: Anari (1975), Vakil Babu (1982). Elsewhere: Deep Jweley Jai (1959) and Uttar Falguni (1963) in Bengali; Mamta, Khamoshi (1969) and Safar (1970) in Hindi.
recurring_themes: Illness, sacrifice and unspoken devotion; the woman who gives up her own life for another's.
creative_style: A restrained melodramatist who worked in soft focus and long emotional silences, and who often remade his own Bengali films in Hindi.
major_awards: The Filmfare Best Director Award for Safar (1971), with an earlier nomination for Mamta; his Uttar Falguni won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Bengali in 1963.
historical_importance: One of the significant bilingual directors of the period, and the maker of Khamoshi, among the most admired Hindi films about psychiatric care.
relationship_with_actor: Two films late in Sen's career, Anari (1975) and Vakil Babu (1982), neither of them among his best-known work. The pairing is nonetheless notable: a director formed in the Bengali art-melodrama tradition working with Kapoor in years otherwise dominated by the masala ensemble. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Anari (1975)
biography: Asit Sen directed two Shashi Kapoor films, Anari in 1975 and Vakil Babu in 1982, both late in a career that had begun in Bengali cinema almost thirty years earlier, and neither among his best-known work. The pairing is nonetheless of interest: a director formed in the Bengali art-melodrama tradition working with Kapoor during years otherwise dominated by the masala ensemble, which is useful evidence that he continued to take chamber-scale drama when it was offered. Sen — not to be confused with the comic actor of the same name, a distinction this sheet preserves — was born in Dhaka in 1922 and directed seventeen features in Hindi and Bengali. He made his reputation with Deep Jweley Jai and Uttar Falguni in Bengali, the latter winning the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Bengali in 1963, and then with Mamta, Khamoshi and Safar in Hindi, a body of restrained, illness-haunted melodrama. Safar brought him the Filmfare Best Director Award in 1971, after an earlier nomination for Mamta. He died in 2001.

name: B. R. Chopra
career_background: Born Baldev Raj Chopra on 22 April 1914; died 5 November 2008. A prolific director and producer and the elder brother of Yash Chopra (PERSON-005), who began his career as B. R.'s assistant. He founded B. R. Films (PERSON-056).
debut: Working from 1944; his directing career includes Afsana and Ek Hi Raasta.
major_works: With Kapoor: Dharmputra (1961), Waqt (1965) — both as producer. Elsewhere, as director: Sadhna, Kanoon, Gumrah, Hamraaz, Dhund, Pati Patni Aur Woh and Nikaah; as producer: Dhool Ka Phool, Ittefaq, The Burning Train, Baghban and the television Mahabharat.
recurring_themes: The social-issue melodrama — divorce, remarriage, communal identity and the law — argued through a domestic situation.
creative_style: A producer-director of issue pictures made to reach a mass audience, and an early user of the multi-star format.
major_awards: The Dadasaheb Phalke Award for 1998 and the Padma Bhushan in 2001.
historical_importance: One of the major studio-builders of post-independence Hindi cinema and the producer of Mahabharat, among the most watched television productions ever made in India.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and they are the two that launched Kapoor's adult career: he produced Dharmputra (1961), the actor's first adult lead, and Waqt (1965), the multi-star hit that made him. Both were directed by his younger brother Yash Chopra and written by Akhtar-ul-Iman (PERSON-051). The B. R. Films banner credit on the same two films is recorded separately at PERSON-056.
most_important_collaboration: Waqt (1965)
biography: B. R. Chopra produced the two films that begin Shashi Kapoor's adult career. Dharmputra in 1961, directed by his younger brother Yash, gave Kapoor his first leading role as an adult — a partition drama about a Hindu nationalist who discovers he was born Muslim — and failed commercially; Waqt in 1965, again directed by Yash, was the lost-and-found family epic that helped turn him into a star and effectively invented the Hindi multi-starrer. Born in 1914, B. R. Chopra built one of the most durable production houses in the industry on social-issue melodrama — Kanoon, Gumrah, Hamraaz, Nikaah — and later produced the television Mahabharat, which reached an audience beyond anything in his film career. He received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award for 1998 and the Padma Bhushan in 2001. His article does not discuss Kapoor.

name: B. R. Films
career_background: The production house founded by B. R. Chopra (PERSON-055). It has no Wikipedia article of its own; the source used here is the article on Chopra himself, which covers the company's output, and the entry is graded accordingly.
debut: Its films date from the 1950s; Dhool Ka Phool (1959) launched Yash Chopra as a director.
major_works: With Kapoor: Dharmputra (1961), Waqt (1965). Elsewhere: Dhool Ka Phool, Gumrah, Hamraaz, Ittefaq, The Burning Train, Nikaah, Baghban and the television Mahabharat.
recurring_themes: The social-issue film made on a commercial scale, and the large-cast family drama.
creative_style: Not applicable; a company, and in this period effectively an expression of its founder's own programme.
historical_importance: One of the principal family production houses of Hindi cinema, and the banner under which the multi-starrer form was established with Waqt.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, Dharmputra (1961) and Waqt (1965) — the same two on which B. R. Chopra takes the producer credit, so this row and PERSON-055 describe one relationship seen from two sides and should not be counted as separate collaborations. Both films were directed by Yash Chopra (PERSON-005) and gave Kapoor his adult debut and his first major success.
most_important_collaboration: Waqt (1965)
biography: B. R. Films is the banner on Shashi Kapoor's first two adult films, Dharmputra in 1961 and Waqt in 1965, both produced by its founder B. R. Chopra and directed by his brother Yash. Waqt matters beyond Kapoor's own career: its lost-and-found plot and large star cast established the multi-starrer as a commercial form, and Kapoor would spend much of the next two decades inside films built on that template. The company had launched Yash Chopra as a director with Dhool Ka Phool in 1959 and went on to make Gumrah, Hamraaz, Nikaah and, later, the television Mahabharat. It has no Wikipedia article of its own, so this entry is drawn from the article on B. R. Chopra, which covers the company's work; it is graded Medium for that reason and because the banner and producer credits describe a single relationship.

name: Chandivali Studio
career_background: A shooting facility in the Chandivali area of Mumbai. No Wikipedia article exists for the studio: the article at 'Chandivali' is about the Mumbai suburb itself and was rejected during research as a different subject. Everything here rests on the credits of the two films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Chor Machaye Shor (1974), Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974).
recurring_themes: Not applicable; a rental facility rather than a production house.
creative_style: Not applicable.
historical_importance: Not established from any available source.
relationship_with_actor: Two credits, both in 1974 and both on films that were among the top box-office releases of that year — Chor Machaye Shor and Roti Kapda Aur Makaan, the pair that made Kapoor one of the decade's most saleable stars. The credit is a facility credit, recording where the films were shot rather than any creative participation, and should be read as such.
most_important_collaboration: Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974)
biography: Chandivali Studio appears on two Shashi Kapoor films, both released in 1974 and both among the highest-grossing Hindi films of that year: Chor Machaye Shor and Roti Kapda Aur Makaan, which together transformed his commercial standing. The credit is a studio-facility credit — it records the stage on which the films were shot, not creative involvement — and is kept in this sheet only because the filmography data carries it as a production-banner credit. No Wikipedia article exists for the studio; the page at Chandivali describes the Mumbai suburb of that name and was rejected during research as the wrong subject. The entry is graded Low.

name: Filmalaya Studio
career_background: A Mumbai film studio. No Wikipedia article was found under this name or under Filmalaya, so everything here rests on the credits of the two films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Abhinetri (1970), Chor Machaye Shor (1974).
recurring_themes: Not applicable; a studio facility.
creative_style: Not applicable.
historical_importance: Not established from any available source, though Filmalaya was among the working Bombay studios of the period.
relationship_with_actor: Two facility credits four years apart: Abhinetri (1970), directed and produced by Subodh Mukherjee (PERSON-045), and Chor Machaye Shor (1974). As with the other studio credits in this sheet, these record where a film was shot rather than who made it.
most_important_collaboration: Chor Machaye Shor (1974)
biography: Filmalaya Studio carries a banner credit on two Shashi Kapoor films, Abhinetri in 1970 and Chor Machaye Shor in 1974. Both are facility credits rather than production ones — they name the stages where the films were made — and are retained here because the source data records them in the production-banner field. No Wikipedia article was located for the studio under this name or the shorter Filmalaya, so nothing can be said of its history, ownership or wider output. Chor Machaye Shor is the more consequential of the two films, one of the top-grossing Hindi releases of 1974 and a turning point in Kapoor's commercial standing. The entry is graded Low.

name: G. P. Sippy
career_background: Born Gopaldas Parmanand Sipahimalani on 14 September 1914; died 25 December 2007. A film producer and director, and the father of the director Ramesh Sippy (PERSON-038).
debut: Producing from the 1940s; the Sippy banner's greatest success was Sholay (1975).
major_works: With Kapoor: Trishna (1978), Shaan (1980). Elsewhere: Sholay (1975) and the other Sippy Films productions.
recurring_themes: Large-scale commercial entertainment, and the star-driven action ensemble of the 1970s.
creative_style: Not applicable; an industry figure and financier rather than a stylist.
major_awards: Filmfare Awards in 1968 and 1982. He was President of the Film Federation of India in 1972–73, 1985–86 and 1988–92, and chaired the Film and TV Producers Guild of India.
historical_importance: One of the most powerful producers of his era and, through Sholay, the financier of the film that reset the terms of Hindi commercial cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two producing credits, Trishna (1978) and Shaan (1980), both made through the Sippy organisation and the latter directed by his son Ramesh. Shaan is the important one: the large post-Sholay caper in which Kapoor and Amitabh Bachchan play brothers, and one of the defining multi-starrers of Kapoor's peak. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Shaan (1980)
biography: G. P. Sippy produced two Shashi Kapoor films: Trishna in 1978 and Shaan in 1980, the second directed by his son Ramesh Sippy. Shaan is the significant one — the enormous caper made in the wake of Sholay, with Kapoor and Amitabh Bachchan as brothers, and one of the most characteristic entries in the multi-starrer cycle that dominates Kapoor's late-1970s work. Born in 1914 as Gopaldas Sipahimalani, Sippy was among the most powerful figures in the industry's business life as well as one of its leading producers: he headed the Film Federation of India across three separate terms and chaired the Producers Guild, and his company had financed Sholay, the most commercially successful Hindi film ever made to that point. He won Filmfare Awards in 1968 and 1982. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Girish Karnad
industry: Kannada, Hindi and other Indian cinemas; Indian theatre
career_background: Born Girish Raghunath Karnad on 19 May 1938; died 10 June 2019. A playwright, actor, film director and writer who worked in Kannada, Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Marathi films. His emergence as a playwright in the 1960s is described as the coming of age of modern Indian playwriting in Kannada.
debut: Established first in the theatre; his plays include Tughlaq and Taledanda.
major_works: With Kapoor: Kalyug (1981) as writer, Utsav (1984) as director and writer. Elsewhere: the plays Tughlaq and Taledanda, and a long acting career.
recurring_themes: History and mythology used to argue contemporary questions; power, desire and social order.
creative_style: A dramatist's cinema, built on structure and argument, drawing openly on classical sources.
major_awards: The Jnanpith Award in 1998, the highest literary honour in India.
historical_importance: One of the most important Indian playwrights of the twentieth century and a central figure of the parallel cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both inside Kapoor's own producing programme. He wrote Kalyug (1981), Shyam Benegal's transposition of the Mahabharata to an industrial family, and wrote and directed Utsav (1984), an adaptation of the Sanskrit Mrichhakatika. Both were financed by Kapoor through Film-Valas, and Utsav — an expensive period piece about a courtesan — failed commercially and effectively ended his career as a producer. The romances in these two films are among the most unusual in the filmography, drawn from classical rather than contemporary models.
most_important_collaboration: Utsav (1984)
biography: Girish Karnad wrote one Shashi Kapoor film and wrote and directed another, and both belong to the parallel-cinema slate Kapoor financed himself. Kalyug in 1981, directed by Shyam Benegal from Karnad's script, restages the Mahabharata inside a warring industrial family, with Kapoor as one of its compromised heirs. Utsav in 1984, which Karnad directed, adapts the Sanskrit play Mrichhakatika into a lavish erotic comedy about a courtesan and a merchant; it cost a great deal, failed at the box office, and effectively ended Kapoor's career as a producer. The romances in the two films are drawn from classical rather than contemporary models, which makes their rows among the most unusual in this workbook's Romances sheet. Karnad, born in 1938, was among the most important Indian playwrights of his century — Tughlaq and Taledanda are staples of the modern Indian stage — and won the Jnanpith Award in 1998, the highest literary honour in India. He acted widely and directed in several languages, and died in 2019. His article does not discuss Kapoor directly.

name: Gulshan Rai
career_background: Born Gulshan Madhosh Rai on 2 March 1924 in Lahore; died 11 October 2004. He moved to Mumbai after partition in 1947 and began as a film distributor, founding the production company Trimurti Films (PERSON-085) in 1969.
debut: As producer, Johny Mera Naam (1970), directed by Vijay Anand.
major_works: With Kapoor: Deewaar (1975), Trishul (1978). Elsewhere: Johny Mera Naam (1970), Vidhaata (1982), Tridev, Vishwatma, Mohra and Gupt.
recurring_themes: Crime and revenge drama; the star vehicle built around a wronged protagonist.
creative_style: Not applicable; a producer and distributor with an unusually sure commercial instinct.
major_awards: His article places him in the category of Padma Shri recipients in the arts.
historical_importance: The producer of Deewaar and Trishul, two of the films that established the angry-young-man cycle, and the man who, his article says, made Amitabh Bachchan a superstar and launched Salim–Javed's careers.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, but two of the most important in the filmography: Deewaar (1975) and Trishul (1978), both directed by Yash Chopra (PERSON-005) and written by Salim–Javed (PERSON-010). In both, Kapoor plays the lawful brother against Amitabh Bachchan's transgressor, and Deewaar brought him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor. The Trimurti Films banner credit on the same two films is recorded at PERSON-085.
most_important_collaboration: Deewaar (1975)
biography: Gulshan Rai produced Deewaar and Trishul, two of the films on which Shashi Kapoor's reputation of the 1970s rests. Both were directed by Yash Chopra and written by Salim–Javed, and in both Kapoor is the lawful brother set against Amitabh Bachchan; Deewaar won him the Filmfare Award for Best Supporting Actor and gave him the most quoted line in Hindi cinema. Born in Lahore in 1924, Rai came to Bombay after partition, worked first as a distributor, and founded Trimurti Films in 1969, producing Johny Mera Naam the following year. His article credits the Yash Chopra films he financed with making Bachchan a superstar and with establishing Salim–Javed, and he continued producing into the 1990s through his son Rajiv Rai. He died in 2004. The article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Gyandev Agnihotri
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credits of the two films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ghar Ek Mandir (1984), Sindoor (1987).
recurring_themes: Family melodrama of the mid-1980s.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: Two writing credits, Ghar Ek Mandir (1984) and Sindoor (1987), the same pair produced by A. Krishnamurthy (PERSON-050) and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal (PERSON-001). Sindoor was the last commercial success of Kapoor's career, which makes this small unit the one that produced his final hit.
most_important_collaboration: Sindoor (1987)
biography: Gyandev Agnihotri wrote two Shashi Kapoor films, Ghar Ek Mandir in 1984 and Sindoor in 1987. The two go together: the same producer, A. Krishnamurthy, and the same composers, Laxmikant–Pyarelal, worked on both, so they represent one small production unit working twice in the family-melodrama register that suited Kapoor's senior roles of the mid-1980s. Sindoor was the last commercial success of his career. No Wikipedia article exists for Agnihotri under this name or any variant attempted in research, and no other biographical source was found, so nothing further can responsibly be said. The entry is graded Low and rests on the two films' credits.

name: Harmesh Malhotra
career_background: Born 14 June 1936; died 22 November 2005. An Indian film director, producer and screenplay writer. His article is brief and gives little beyond these facts.
debut: Directing from 1969.
major_works: With Kapoor: Amar Shakti (1978), Phaansi (1978).
recurring_themes: Commercial action and costume drama.
creative_style: Not assessed in the article.
historical_importance: Not established from the available source.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, both released in 1978 — Amar Shakti and Phaansi — at the height of Kapoor's output, when he was appearing in as many as six or seven releases a year. Amar Shakti was produced by A. K. Nadiadwala (PERSON-049). Both are scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal (PERSON-001). His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Amar Shakti (1978)
biography: Harmesh Malhotra directed two Shashi Kapoor films, Amar Shakti and Phaansi, both released in 1978 — a single year in which Kapoor appeared in a long string of films and was working at a pace that became notorious in the industry, and which accounts for more entries in this filmography than any other twelve months. Both are commercial vehicles of the period, scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, and Amar Shakti was produced by A. K. Nadiadwala, who had also produced Aa Gale Lag Jaa five years earlier. Malhotra, born on 14 June 1936, directed from 1969 until 2005 and also worked as a producer and screenplay writer across that period. His Wikipedia article is a few lines long: it records those three functions and his dates, offers no account of his style or standing and names none of his other films, and it does not mention Kapoor. This entry therefore rests mainly on the film credits, and is graded Medium.

name: J. V. Films
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for this banner under J. V. Films or JV Films. Everything here rests on the credits of the two films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Insaaniyat (1974), Oonch Neech Beech (1989).
recurring_themes: Commercial Hindi production across a fifteen-year span.
creative_style: Not applicable.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: Two banner credits fifteen years apart, Insaaniyat (1974) and Oonch Neech Beech (1989), and on both the producers are Jagdish Varma (PERSON-065) and Satpal Varma (PERSON-082). The initials and the constant producing team make it near certain that J. V. Films is the Varmas' own banner, though no source confirms this and it is recorded here as an inference rather than a fact.
most_important_collaboration: Insaaniyat (1974)
biography: J. V. Films is the banner on two Shashi Kapoor films fifteen years apart: Insaaniyat in 1974, directed by Prayag Raj, and Oonch Neech Beech in 1989. Both were produced by Jagdish Varma and Satpal Varma, who appear separately in this sheet, and the shared initials together with the identical producing team make it very likely that the banner was the Varmas' own company — an inference recorded as such, since no source was found to confirm it. No Wikipedia article exists under either spelling tried in research, so nothing can be said of the company's other output or its years of operation. The entry is graded Low and rests on the two films' credits.

name: Jagdish Varma
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credits of the two films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Insaaniyat (1974), Oonch Neech Beech (1989).
recurring_themes: Commercial Hindi production.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: Two producing credits fifteen years apart, Insaaniyat (1974) and Oonch Neech Beech (1989), on both of which he is paired with Satpal Varma (PERSON-082) under the J. V. Films banner (PERSON-064). The gap between the two films is unusual and suggests a family concern returning to the same star after a long interval rather than a continuous production business.
most_important_collaboration: Insaaniyat (1974)
biography: Jagdish Varma produced two Shashi Kapoor films, Insaaniyat in 1974 and Oonch Neech Beech in 1989, working on both with Satpal Varma under the J. V. Films banner. The fifteen-year gap between them is the striking feature: the same producing pair, the same banner and the same lead actor, with nothing in between recorded in this filmography, which suggests a family concern that returned to Kapoor long after their first film rather than a continuously active production house. No Wikipedia article exists for him under this name or any variant attempted in research, and no other biographical source was located. The entry is graded Low and rests entirely on the film credits.

name: Jainendra Jain
career_background: Born Jainendra Kumar Jain on 4 October 1939; died 23 December 2007. A Bollywood writer, director and film producer based in Mumbai. His article is short and offers little beyond these facts.
debut: Not recorded in the article.
major_works: With Kapoor: Satyam Shivam Sundaram (1978), Bhavani Junction (1985).
recurring_themes: Not established from the article; the two Kapoor films are very different in register.
creative_style: Not assessed in the article.
historical_importance: Not established from the available source.
relationship_with_actor: Two writing credits seven years apart. Satyam Shivam Sundaram (1978) is much the more significant — Raj Kapoor's production, directed by the actor's eldest brother, with Shashi as the adult lead opposite Zeenat Aman, and one of the most discussed films of his career. Bhavani Junction (1985) belongs to his later commercial period. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Satyam Shivam Sundaram (1978)
biography: Jainendra Jain has two writing credits in this filmography, and they sit at opposite ends of Shashi Kapoor's standing. Satyam Shivam Sundaram in 1978 is an R. K. production directed by Raj Kapoor, with his youngest brother as the adult male lead opposite Zeenat Aman in a film whose treatment of beauty and disfigurement drew large audiences and heavy criticism in equal measure; Bhavani Junction in 1985 is an ordinary commercial picture of his later career. Jain, born in 1939, worked as a writer, director and producer in Mumbai until his death in 2007. His Wikipedia article runs to a couple of sentences and records nothing of his style, training or wider output, so this entry rests largely on the two credits and is graded Medium.

name: K. Asif Studios
career_background: The studio bearing the name of the director K. Asif (born Asif Karim, 14 June 1922 – 9 March 1971). It has no Wikipedia article of its own; the source used here is the article on Asif himself, and the entry is graded accordingly. Both of its credits in this filmography fall after his death.
debut: Asif worked from 1945 to 1971; the studio credits here postdate him.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aa Gale Lag Jaa (1973), Chor Machaye Shor (1974). Asif's own defining work is Mughal-e-Azam (1960).
recurring_themes: Not applicable to the banner; Asif's own reputation rests on a single monumental historical epic.
creative_style: Not applicable.
major_awards: For Mughal-e-Azam: the Filmfare Award for Best Film in 1960, a Best Director nomination, and the President's award for Best Feature Film in Hindi.
historical_importance: Asif made Mughal-e-Azam, among the most celebrated films in Indian cinema; the studio carrying his name is a far smaller matter.
relationship_with_actor: Two banner credits, Aa Gale Lag Jaa (1973) and Chor Machaye Shor (1974), both after Asif's death in 1971 — so the credit records the facility and the name rather than any involvement by the director himself. Chor Machaye Shor was one of the top box-office films of 1974 and central to Kapoor's rise to full commercial stardom.
most_important_collaboration: Chor Machaye Shor (1974)
biography: K. Asif Studios appears on two Shashi Kapoor films, Aa Gale Lag Jaa in 1973 and Chor Machaye Shor in 1974, the second of them among the top-grossing Hindi releases of its year and a turning point in the actor's commercial standing. Both credits fall after the death in 1971 of K. Asif himself, so they record a facility operating under his name rather than any participation by the director. Asif, born Asif Karim in 1922, is remembered for one film above all others: Mughal-e-Azam in 1960, which won the Filmfare Award for Best Film and the President's award for Best Feature Film in Hindi and remains among the most celebrated productions in Indian cinema. The studio has no article of its own, so this entry is drawn from his, and is graded Low.

name: K. B. Pathak
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him under this name or the variant K.B. Pathak. Everything here rests on the credits of the two films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Aa Gale Lag Jaa (1973), Maa Beti (1986).
recurring_themes: Not established; the two credits are thirteen years apart and very different in kind.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: Two writing credits thirteen years apart: Aa Gale Lag Jaa (1973), the Manmohan Desai film that was among Kapoor's substantial successes of the early 1970s, and Maa Beti (1986), directed by Kalpataru near the end of his career as a regular lead.
most_important_collaboration: Aa Gale Lag Jaa (1973)
biography: K. B. Pathak has two writing credits in this filmography, thirteen years apart: Aa Gale Lag Jaa in 1973, directed by Manmohan Desai and among Shashi Kapoor's more successful films of the early 1970s, and Maa Beti in 1986, a late family melodrama directed by Kalpataru. No Wikipedia article exists for him under this spelling or the unspaced variant, and no other biographical source was found during research, so nothing can be said about his training, his wider output or even his dates. The two films share no director, producer or banner, and the pairing appears to be coincidence rather than an association. The entry is graded Low and rests on the film credits alone.

name: Kanak Mishra
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him under this name or the variant Kanak Mishra (director). Everything here rests on the credits of the two films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Dil Kisko Doon (1963), Naina (1973).
recurring_themes: Romantic drama, on the evidence of both credits.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
