biography: Bhushan Banmali wrote the screenplay of Bezubaan, released in 1982 — a Hindi remake of the Tamil film Mayangukiral Oru Maadhu, directed by the Telugu filmmaker Bapu with a story credit for the Dogri writer Ved Rahi. The division of writing labour on the film is unusually explicit for the period, with story and screenplay separately attributed. No Wikipedia article exists for Banmali under this name or any variant attempted during research, and no other biographical source was located, so nothing further can be said about his career. The entry is graded Low and rests on the single film credit.

name: Bimal Roy
career_background: Born 12 July 1909; died 7 January 1966. One of the most important directors of Hindi cinema, noted for realistic and socialistic films. He was inspired by Italian neo-realism and made Do Bigha Zamin after seeing De Sica's Bicycle Thieves.
debut: Working in film from 1934.
major_works: With Kapoor: Prem Patra (1962), which he directed and produced. Elsewhere: Do Bigha Zamin, Parineeta (1953), Biraj Bahu (1954), Devdas (1955), Madhumati (1958), Yahudi (1958), Sujata (1959), Parakh (1960) and Bandini (1963).
recurring_themes: Poverty, caste and social constraint treated without sentimentality; the dignity of ordinary lives.
creative_style: A realist celebrated for his mise en scène, using visual composition rather than dialogue to carry meaning.
major_awards: Eleven Filmfare Awards — four for Best Film and seven for Best Director — two National Film Awards, and the International Prize at the Cannes Film Festival. Madhumati won nine Filmfare Awards in 1958, a record that stood for thirty-seven years.
historical_importance: Among the greatest filmmakers in Indian cinema and the central figure in bringing neo-realist method to the Hindi mainstream.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Prem Patra (1962), which Roy directed and produced, with songs by Salil Chowdhury (PERSON-042), who also took a writing credit. It came early in Kapoor's adult career, in the uncertain years between the failure of Dharmputra and the stardom of 1965, and gave him the most distinguished director he would work with before the Merchant Ivory films. Roy died four years later. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Prem Patra (1962), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Bimal Roy directed and produced Prem Patra in 1962, the only film he made with Shashi Kapoor, and it arrived at a valuable moment: Dharmputra had failed the year before, Kapoor's standing as a leading man was unsettled, and Roy was by some distance the most distinguished filmmaker he would work with until the Merchant Ivory films. Salil Chowdhury wrote the songs and took a writing credit, alongside three other credited writers. Roy's company would produce one more Kapoor film, Benazir, two years later, though he did not direct it. Born in 1909, Roy came to Hindi cinema from Bengal and brought neo-realist method with him, making Do Bigha Zamin after seeing De Sica's Bicycle Thieves; Parineeta, Devdas, Madhumati, Sujata and Bandini followed, and his work is particularly admired for a mise en scène that carries meaning without dialogue. He won eleven Filmfare Awards, including four for Best Film and seven for Best Director, two National Film Awards and the International Prize at Cannes; Madhumati took nine Filmfare Awards in 1958, a record that stood for thirty-seven years. He died in January 1966.

name: Bimal Roy Productions
career_background: The production company of the director Bimal Roy (PERSON-124). No Wikipedia article exists for the company itself, and the entry rests on the credit of the single film together with what Roy's own article records.
major_works: With Kapoor: Benazir (1964).
recurring_themes: The socially engaged realist drama associated with Roy's own direction.
creative_style: Not applicable; a company.
historical_importance: The banner through which one of Hindi cinema's most important directors produced his own and others' films.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Benazir (1964), scored by S. D. Burman (PERSON-040) — a film made by Roy's company but not directed by him, two years after he had directed Kapoor himself in Prem Patra and two years before his death.
most_important_collaboration: Benazir (1964), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Bimal Roy Productions is the producing credit on Benazir, released in 1964 with a score by S. D. Burman. The company belonged to Bimal Roy, who had directed Shashi Kapoor himself in Prem Patra two years earlier and who died in January 1966; Benazir is a film made under his banner rather than by his hand. No Wikipedia article exists for the company as such, so this entry draws on Roy's own article for context and otherwise rests on the film credit. It is graded Low on that basis, though the association it records — Kapoor working twice within the orbit of one of Hindi cinema's most serious filmmakers, early in his adult career — is of real interest to this filmography.

name: Bindu Kala Mandir
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for this banner. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Dil Kisko Doon (1963).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not applicable.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Yeh Dil Kisko Doon (1963), written and directed by Kanak Mishra (PERSON-069) and produced by B. D. Kapoor (PERSON-110) — one of the modest successes that sustained Kapoor's career between the failure of his 1961 films and his stardom in 1965.
most_important_collaboration: Yeh Dil Kisko Doon (1963), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Bindu Kala Mandir is the banner on Yeh Dil Kisko Doon, released in 1963 — a film that matters to this filmography out of proportion to its obscurity, since it falls in the anxious stretch after Dharmputra and Char Diwari had failed and helped keep Shashi Kapoor working until Waqt and Jab Jab Phool Khile made him a star two years later. Kanak Mishra wrote and directed it and B. D. Kapoor produced, and neither of them, nor this banner, has any surviving biographical record: no Wikipedia article exists for the company, and no other source was located. The entry is graded Low.

name: Bishwanath Prasad Shahabadi
career_background: Also spelled Vishwanath Prasad Shahabadi and known as B. P. Shahabadi. A film producer and businessman who died on 13 July 2000. He is known as the father of Bhojpuri cinema, having produced the first Bhojpuri film, the black-and-white Ganga Maiyya Tohe Piyari Chadhaibo, in 1962.
debut: Ganga Maiyya Tohe Piyari Chadhaibo (1962), the first Bhojpuri film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rootha Na Karo (1970). Elsewhere: Ganga Maiyya Tohe Piyari Chadhaibo and Solaho Singar Kare Dulhaniya in Bhojpuri; Ganga Dham, Geet Ganga, Sasural, Tulsi and Ghar Jamai in Hindi.
recurring_themes: Regional-language production and devotional and family subjects.
creative_style: Not applicable; a producer and businessman.
historical_importance: The founder of Bhojpuri cinema as an industry — a claim his article makes directly and the single most consequential fact about him.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Rootha Na Karo (1970), scored by C. Ramchandra (PERSON-028). The film's dating is itself disputed in this workbook: its infobox gives 31 December 1969 against a 1970 year in the article text and the filmography table, and the row is noted accordingly.
most_important_collaboration: Rootha Na Karo (1970), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Bishwanath Prasad Shahabadi produced Rootha Na Karo, a Shashi Kapoor film whose release date is disputed between the last day of 1969 and 1970 and which this workbook notes on that ground. Shahabadi's significance lies elsewhere entirely: he is called the father of Bhojpuri cinema, having produced Ganga Maiyya Tohe Piyari Chadhaibo in 1962, the first film made in the language and the foundation of what became a substantial regional industry. He continued in both Bhojpuri and Hindi through to the early 1990s with Ganga Dham, Geet Ganga, Sasural and Tulsi, and died in July 2000. The Kapoor film, scored by C. Ramchandra, is a minor entry in that record, and his article does not mention the actor.

name: Bittu Anand
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him. He is identified in his father's article as a producer and the son of the writer Inder Raj Anand (PERSON-014) and brother of the director Tinnu Anand; the family detail comes from that article rather than from one of his own.
major_works: With Kapoor: Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979). Elsewhere: Shahenshah (1988), which he produced, his father wrote and his brother directed.
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit in this filmography.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biography of his own was located.
historical_importance: Not established independently of his family.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), written by his father Inder Raj Anand and scored by Rajesh Roshan (PERSON-017). The father-and-son pairing on the same film is the point of interest: Inder Raj Anand had written the first film Kapoor ever appeared in, Aag in 1948, and this is one of their last together.
most_important_collaboration: Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Bittu Anand produced Duniya Meri Jeb Mein in 1979, a film written by his father, Inder Raj Anand, and scored by Rajesh Roshan. The family connection is what makes the credit worth recording: Inder Raj Anand had written Aag in 1948, the film in which the nine-year-old Shashi Kapoor first appeared, and thirty-one years later father and son worked on a Kapoor picture together. The Anands went on to make Shahenshah in 1988, produced by Bittu, written by their father and directed by his brother Tinnu, released after Inder Raj Anand's death. No Wikipedia article exists for Bittu Anand himself; what is known comes from his father's article, and the entry is graded Low.

name: Bolu Khosla

recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.

most_important_collaboration: Prem Kahani (1975), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Bolu Khosla is credited as associate producer of Prem Kahani, released in 1975 and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, the only appearance of his name in this filmography. He shares the credit with Lekhraj Khosla, and the common surname points to a family production unit, though nothing found in research confirms the connection and it is recorded here as an inference. No Wikipedia article exists for him under this name or any variant attempted, and no other biographical source was located. The workbook normalises role qualifiers such as associate producer out of its name fields to keep the collaborator roster consistent; the qualifier is noted here instead. The entry is graded Low.

name: Bombay Talkies
career_background: A film studio founded in 1934 by Himanshu Rai, Niranjan Pal — son of Bipin Chandra Pal — and Devika Rani, which produced forty films at Malad, a suburb of Bombay. After Rai's death in 1940 Rani took over; following her retirement the studio passed to Ashok Kumar and Shashadhar Mukherjee. It went out of business in 1953, with a last film released in June 1954.
debut: Producing from 1934.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sangram (1950). Its wider output runs to forty films made in the 1930s and 1940s.
recurring_themes: The socially conscious studio picture of the 1930s and 1940s, made under a European-influenced production system.
creative_style: Not applicable; a studio, and one of the most organised production operations of its era.
historical_importance: One of the two or three most important studios of early Indian sound cinema, and the training ground for Ashok Kumar and for Shashadhar Mukherjee, who left in 1943 to found Filmistan (PERSON-013).
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Sangram (1950), one of Kapoor's child-actor films, made when he was twelve and billed as Shashiraj. The credit also explains a data problem corrected during this research: the film's wikitext gives the studio as 'The Bombay Talkies Limited Studios, Malad', which an automated extraction had split into a second banner named after the Bombay suburb.
most_important_collaboration: Sangram (1950), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Bombay Talkies produced Sangram in 1950, one of Shashi Kapoor's child-actor films, made when he was twelve and billed as Shashiraj. The studio was by then near its end — it closed in 1953 — but it had been among the most important in Indian cinema: founded in 1934 by Himanshu Rai, Niranjan Pal and Devika Rani, it made forty films at Malad under a production system consciously modelled on European practice, and gave Ashok Kumar his career. Kumar and Shashadhar Mukherjee took it over after Rani retired, having earlier left in 1943 to found Filmistan, which appears separately in this sheet and also produced a Kapoor child film. The credit also fixed an extraction error: the wikitext reads 'The Bombay Talkies Limited Studios, Malad', which had been split into a phantom banner named after the suburb.

name: Brij Katyal
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film — which is a notable absence, given what that film did for Kapoor's career.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit, though the film is a romance built entirely on class difference.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established, despite having written one of the defining romantic vehicles of 1960s Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, and it is the film that made Kapoor a star: Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965), directed by Suraj Prakash (PERSON-046) and scored by Kalyanji–Anandji (PERSON-002), in which he plays a Kashmiri boatman opposite Nanda's wealthy visitor. The role won him the BFJA Best Actor award and established the courteous romantic persona this workbook's scoring is built to measure.
most_important_collaboration: Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Brij Katyal wrote Jab Jab Phool Khile, and nothing else in this filmography — but that one film changed Shashi Kapoor's career. Released in 1965, it cast him as a Kashmiri boatman who falls in love with a wealthy visitor played by Nanda, won him the BFJA Best Actor award, and fixed the gentle, deferential romantic persona that the Romances sheet of this workbook exists to measure across the following three decades. The class-crossing premise is the template for a great deal that follows. Of its writer nothing could be found: no Wikipedia article exists under this name or any variant attempted in research, and no other biographical source was located. Together with the director Suraj Prakash and the banner Lime Light, both equally undocumented, the film's creative team has left almost no record.

name: Brij Sadanah

Narayan (PERSON-032), produced by Chander Sadanah (PERSON-138) and scored — as always with this director — by Kalyanji–Anandji. It is a characteristic Brij caper and one of the more enjoyable entries in Kapoor's crowded mid-1970s output. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Chori Mera Kaam (1975), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Brij Sadanah directed Chori Mera Kaam in 1975, his only film with Shashi Kapoor and a characteristic piece of his work: a caper written by K. A. Narayan, produced by Chander Sadanah — almost certainly a relative — and scored by Kalyanji–Anandji, the composers his article notes he chose consistently across his films. It belongs to the strongest year of Kapoor's career, alongside Deewaar and Prem Kahani, and is among the more purely enjoyable entries in a crowded period. Born Brijmohan Sadanah in 1933 and usually credited simply as Brij, he made a long run of commercially successful thrillers and capers from the 1960s to the 1980s — Do Bhai, Yeh Raat Phir Na Aaygi, Ustadon Ke Ustad, Night In London, Victoria No. 203, Ek Se Badhkar Ek, Yakeen and Professor Pyarelal — before a string of failures in the early 1980s damaged his standing, ended by the success of Mardon Wali Baat. He was married to the actress Sayeeda Khan, and their son Kamal Sadanah became an actor. He died in October 1990.

name: C. V. Sridhar

recurring_themes: Romantic comedy and serious melodrama in equal measure — his article calls him the Nava-rasa director for the range of moods he worked in.
creative_style: A writer-director with a particular gift for ensemble comedy, and for drawing strong work from comic performers.

It is an ensemble comedy rather than a romantic vehicle, and it comes immediately after the two 1965 hits that made him a star. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Pyar Kiye Jaa (1966), his only film with Kapoor
biography: C. V. Sridhar directed, produced and wrote Pyar Kiye Jaa in 1966, a Hindi ensemble comedy remade from his own Tamil hit Kaadhalikka Neramillai and his only film with Shashi Kapoor. It arrived immediately after the two 1965 successes that had made him a star, and it carries the first of Laxmikant–Pyarelal's twenty-seven scores for him — the largest single collaboration in this filmography. The film was made under the Chithralaya banner, the company Sridhar had founded in the early 1960s with the writer Gopu, the cinematographer A. Vincent and the still photographer Tiruchi Arunachalam, and Gopu shares the writing credit. Born Chithamur Vijayaraghavalu Sridhar on 22 July 1933, he directed nearly sixty films in Tamil, Hindi and Telugu and was known as the Nava-rasa director for his range, moving between comedy and serious melodrama; Dil Ek Mandir, his Hindi remake of Nenjil Or Aalayam, brought him two Filmfare nominations. He died on 20 October 2008.

name: Chithralaya

Both founders appear separately in this sheet. The film is an ensemble comedy and comes immediately after the two 1965 hits that made Kapoor a star.
most_important_collaboration: Pyar Kiye Jaa (1966), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Chithralaya produced Pyar Kiye Jaa in 1966, the Hindi version of its own Tamil hit Kadhalikka Neramillai and its only appearance in this filmography. The company had been founded in the early 1960s by four collaborators — the director C. V. Sridhar, the writer Gopu, the cinematographer A. Vincent and the still photographer Tiruchi Arunachalam — and functioned mainly as the production arm of Sridhar's own films. Kadhalikka Neramillai was the company's landmark: the first Tamil film shot in Eastmancolor with a contemporary setting, initially refused by distributors so that Chithralaya released it itself, and then a major success. Two of its founders appear separately in this sheet. The banner's article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Conrad Rooks
career_background: Born 15 December 1934 in Kansas City, Missouri; died 27 December 2011 in Massachusetts. An American writer, director and producer, best known for his 1972 adaptation of Hermann Hesse's novel Siddhartha.
debut: Working in film from 1966.
major_works: With Kapoor: Siddhartha (1972), which he directed, produced and wrote.
recurring_themes: Spiritual search and Eastern philosophy filtered through a Western counter-cultural sensibility.
creative_style: A director of very small output working outside the studio system on personal projects.
historical_importance: Chiefly as the filmmaker who brought Hesse's Siddhartha to the screen, at the height of the novel's Western counter-cultural popularity.
relationship_with_actor: One film, but a notable one in the English-language strand of Kapoor's career: Siddhartha (1972), which Rooks directed, produced and wrote, casting Kapoor in the title role of Hesse's seeker. It sits alongside the Merchant Ivory films as evidence that Kapoor was, through the 1960s and 1970s, the Indian actor international productions turned to — and it gave him a leading role in a Western art film at the same time as he was making masala pictures at home.
most_important_collaboration: Siddhartha (1972), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Conrad Rooks directed, produced and wrote Siddhartha in 1972, casting Shashi Kapoor in the title role of Hermann Hesse's novel about a young Brahmin's search for enlightenment, with music by Hemant Kumar and a writing credit shared with Paul Mayersberg and Natasha Ullman. The film belongs to the parallel English-language career that ran beside Kapoor's Hindi one, and it is the clearest instance outside Merchant Ivory of an international production building itself around him: at a moment when he was appearing in several commercial Hindi films a year, he was also carrying a Western art film adapted from one of the most widely read novels of the counter-culture. Rooks, born in Kansas City in 1934, made very few films and is remembered almost entirely for this one, which arrived at the height of Hesse's Western popularity and drew on the same fascination with Indian spiritual practice that ran through the period. He died in Massachusetts in 2011. His article does not discuss Kapoor's performance.

historical_importance: Not established; his article is unusually frank about a career of commercial disappointment.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Bhavani Junction (1985), directed by H. Dinesh (PERSON-175), written by Jainendra Jain (PERSON-066) and scored by Bappi Lahiri (PERSON-004). He shares a surname with Shyam Sunder Shivdasani (PERSON-043), who produced three Kapoor films in the 1970s, but no source confirms a relationship and none is asserted here.
most_important_collaboration: Bhavani Junction (1985), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Deepak Shivdasani produced Bhavani Junction in 1985, his only credit in this filmography, working with the director H. Dinesh, the writer Jainendra Jain and the composer Bappi Lahiri. He went on to direct Baaghi: A Rebel for Love with Salman Khan in 1990 and a run of pictures with Sunil Shetty in the 1990s, though his Wikipedia article is unusually blunt about the outcome, stating that his films were not successful and that many were termed box-office disasters; it quotes his own public acknowledgement, after Julie 2 in 2017, of money owed to technicians and vendors. He shares a surname with Shyam Sunder Shivdasani, who produced three Kapoor films in the 1970s, but no connection between them was established.

name: Desh Mukherjee
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film — a notable gap, given the standing of the film's other credits.
major_works: With Kapoor: Immaan Dharam (1977).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established, despite having directed a major Salim–Javed script.
relationship_with_actor: One directing credit, on Immaan Dharam (1977), written by Salim–Javed (PERSON-010), produced by Premji under the Suchitra Films banner and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal (PERSON-001). It is one of the six Salim–Javed films in this filmography and part of the multi-starrer cycle that defines Kapoor's peak, which makes the absence of any record of its director striking.
most_important_collaboration: Immaan Dharam (1977), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Desh Mukherjee directed Immaan Dharam in 1977, one of the six Salim–Javed films in this filmography and a substantial entry in the multi-starrer cycle that carried Shashi Kapoor's peak years; Laxmikant–Pyarelal scored it and Premji produced. For a director handed a script by the most celebrated writing team in Hindi cinema, the biographical record is remarkably thin: no Wikipedia article exists under this name or any variant attempted during research, and no other source was located. The pattern recurs across this sheet, where the writers and composers of major films are usually documented and their directors and producers frequently are not. The entry is graded Low.

name: Devar Films
career_background: The banner under which the producer Sandow M. M. A. Chinnappa Thevar (PERSON-081) launched all his films. It has no Wikipedia article of its own; the source here is Thevar's article, which covers the company, and the entry is graded accordingly.
debut: Producing from 1940.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Aur Do Paanch (1980). Elsewhere: Haathi Mere Saathi (1971), the Rajesh Khanna hit that brought the banner national attention, and sixteen films with M. G. Ramachandran.
recurring_themes: Films built around animals — the specialism for which Thevar and the banner are best known — and star vehicles in Tamil.
creative_style: Not applicable; a production company.
historical_importance: One of the major Tamil production houses of its era, and the banner that carried the animal picture into mainstream Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Do Aur Do Paanch (1980), the caper pairing Kapoor with Amitabh Bachchan. The credit is posthumous in effect: Thevar died in September 1978, two years before the film's release. The closely related Dhandayuthapani Films (PERSON-154) appears on the other Thevar production in this filmography.
most_important_collaboration: Do Aur Do Paanch (1980), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Devar Films is the banner on Do Aur Do Paanch, the 1980 caper in which Shashi Kapoor and Amitabh Bachchan play rivals, and the credit outlived its founder: Sandow M. M. A. Chinnappa Thevar, who launched all his films under this name, had died in September 1978. The company was among the significant Tamil production houses of its time, making sixteen films with M. G. Ramachandran and specialising in pictures built around animals — a formula it carried into Hindi with Haathi Mere Saathi in 1971, a major success for Rajesh Khanna. Devar Films has no Wikipedia article of its own, so this entry draws on Thevar's, and is graded Medium for that reason. The related banner Dhandayuthapani Films appears separately in this sheet.

name: Devendra Goel
career_background: Born 3 March 1919; died 26 February 1979. A film director and producer best known for his work in the 1950s and early 1960s. His son Ajay Goel was also a filmmaker.
debut: Aankhen, his first film as director.
major_works: With Kapoor: Do Musafir (1978). Elsewhere: Ek Saal (1957) with Madhubala, Dus Lakh, and the Marathi film Dost Asava Tar Asa.
recurring_themes: Mainstream romantic and family drama of the 1950s and 1960s.
creative_style: Not assessed in the article.
major_awards: A Silver Jubilee Award for Dus Lakh.
historical_importance: A commercially reliable director of the 1950s and early 1960s who also worked in Marathi.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Do Musafir (1978), scored by Kalyanji–Anandji (PERSON-002) — a late credit for Goel, made some two decades after the period of his greatest success and a year before his death. It falls in the most crowded stretch of Kapoor's filmography. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Do Musafir (1978), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Devendra Goel directed Do Musafir in 1978, his only film with Shashi Kapoor and one of his last: he died in February 1979, a year after its release, and his article dates his working life from 1950 to 1978. The credit comes well after his best period. Born on 3 March 1919, Goel made his name in the 1950s and early 1960s — he directed Aankhen on his debut, then the hit Ek Saal in 1957 with Madhubala, and Dus Lakh, which brought him a Silver Jubilee Award — and also worked in Marathi, directing Dost Asava Tar Asa with Ramesh Deo and Deven Varma. Do Musafir, produced by Rabindranath Kumar and scored by Kalyanji–Anandji, belongs to the year of Kapoor's heaviest output, when he appeared in a string of releases and the pace left little room for selection on either side. His son Ajay Goel also became a filmmaker. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Dhandayuthapani Films
career_background: A banner associated with the producer Sandow M. M. A. Chinnappa Thevar (PERSON-081). It has no Wikipedia article of its own; the source here is Thevar's article, which covers his production companies, and the entry is graded accordingly.
debut: Not separately recorded; Thevar produced from 1940.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jaanwar Aur Insaan (1972).
recurring_themes: The animal picture, Thevar's identifying specialism.
creative_style: Not applicable; a production company.
historical_importance: Not established independently of its founder.
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Jaanwar Aur Insaan (1972), directed by Tapi Chanakya (PERSON-137), produced and co-written by Thevar himself, written also by Inder Raj Anand (PERSON-014) and scored by Kalyanji–Anandji (PERSON-002). The subject matches the banner's animal specialism exactly.
most_important_collaboration: Jaanwar Aur Insaan (1972), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Dhandayuthapani Films is the banner on Jaanwar Aur Insaan, released in 1972 — a Shashi Kapoor film directed by Tapi Chanakya, produced and co-written by Sandow M. M. A. Chinnappa Thevar, and scored by Kalyanji–Anandji. Its title alone signals the specialism that made Thevar's name: films built around animals, a formula he had carried into Hindi the previous year with Haathi Mere Saathi. The banner has no Wikipedia article of its own and is documented here from Thevar's, alongside the related Devar Films, which appears separately in this sheet on his other Kapoor production. The entry is graded Medium on that basis.

name: Dilip Chitre
industry: Marathi and English literature; Indian parallel cinema
career_background: Born Dilip Purushottam Chitre on 17 September 1938; died 10 December 2009. One of the foremost Indian poets and critics to emerge after independence, a bilingual writer in Marathi and English who was also a teacher, painter, filmmaker and magazine columnist.
debut: Established first as a poet; his film work is occasional.
major_works: With Kapoor: Vijeta (1982). Elsewhere: his own film Godam, and a large body of Marathi and English poetry, translation and criticism.
recurring_themes: The interior life of the modern Indian city; translation between languages and traditions.
creative_style: A poet and translator whose screen work carries the same concern with precise language.
major_awards: Several Maharashtra State Awards; the Prix Special du Jury for his film Godam at the Festival des Trois Continents in 1984; fellowships including the University of Iowa's International Writing Program, the Indira Gandhi Fellowship and the Villa Waldberta Fellowship from the City of Munich.
historical_importance: A major figure in post-independence Marathi and Indian English poetry.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Vijeta (1982), directed by Govind Nihalani (PERSON-170) and produced by Kapoor through Film-Valas, with Kapoor's son Kunal in the lead. It belongs to the parallel-cinema slate Kapoor financed between 1979 and 1984, and is another instance of that programme drawing serious literary figures — Chitre, Girish Karnad, Satyadev Dubey, Ismat Chughtai — into his films.
most_important_collaboration: Vijeta (1982), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Dilip Chitre wrote Vijeta, released in 1982, directed by Govind Nihalani and produced by Shashi Kapoor through Film-Valas, with Kapoor's son Kunal in the leading role and Kapoor himself in support. It is a characteristic product of the programme he financed between 1979 and 1984, which repeatedly drew writers of serious literary standing into his films — Chitre here, alongside Girish Karnad, Satyadev Dubey and Ismat Chughtai elsewhere in this sheet. Chitre, born in 1938, was among the foremost poets and critics to emerge in post-independence India, writing in both Marathi and English, and also worked as painter, translator and filmmaker; his own film Godam won the Prix Special du Jury at the Festival des Trois Continents in 1984. He died in 2009.

name: Donald Rosenfeld
career_background: An American film producer who was president of Merchant Ivory Productions (PERSON-073) from 1986 to 1998 and lead producer on the company's major films of what is now considered its golden decade, working alongside Ismail Merchant (PERSON-006), James Ivory (PERSON-015) and Ruth Prawer Jhabvala (PERSON-019). He is now publisher of County Highway, a magazine in the form of a nineteenth-century newspaper.
debut: Producing for Merchant Ivory from 1986.
major_works: With Kapoor: In Custody (1993). Elsewhere: Mr. and Mrs. Bridge, Howards End, which received eight Academy Award nominations, and The Remains of the Day, which received nine.
recurring_themes: Literary adaptation and period drama.
creative_style: Not applicable; a producer and studio executive.
major_awards: In 1992 he became the youngest producer ever admitted to membership of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.
historical_importance: The producer who ran Merchant Ivory through its most commercially and critically successful period.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on In Custody (1993), Ismail Merchant's directorial debut, in which Kapoor plays the failing Urdu poet Nur — among the most admired performances of his late career and the source of National Film Award recognition. Rosenfeld was president of Merchant Ivory at the time, so the credit places Kapoor's last major role inside the company's strongest years.
most_important_collaboration: In Custody (1993), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Donald Rosenfeld produced In Custody, the 1993 film in which Shashi Kapoor gave one of the finest performances of his late career as a dissipated Urdu poet, and which brought him National Film Award recognition. Rosenfeld was then president of Merchant Ivory Productions, a post he held from 1986 to 1998, and was lead producer on the films of the company's strongest decade — Mr. and Mrs. Bridge, Howards End with its eight Academy Award nominations, and The Remains of the Day with nine. In 1992 he became the youngest producer ever elected to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. He now publishes County Highway, a magazine designed as a nineteenth-century newspaper. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Essel Studios
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for this studio. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mukti (1977).
recurring_themes: Not applicable; a facility credit.
creative_style: Not applicable.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Mukti (1977), which also carries credits for Famous Cine Studios (PERSON-160), Natraj Studios (PERSON-240), R. K. Studios (PERSON-034) and Rajkamal Kalamandir (PERSON-079) — five studio credits on a single film, which confirms that these are facility records rather than production ones. The film was directed and produced by Raj Tilak (PERSON-269).
most_important_collaboration: Mukti (1977), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Essel Studios appears on Mukti, released in 1977, and the film makes the nature of such credits unmistakable: it carries five separate studio names — Essel, Famous Cine Studios, Natraj Studios, R. K. Studios and Rajkamal Kalamandir — none of which produced it, since Raj Tilak both directed and produced. These are records of where the picture was shot, spread across several rented facilities as was common practice, and this workbook keeps them distinct from production credits so that the collaboration counts are not inflated. No Wikipedia article exists for Essel Studios, and no other source was located, so nothing further can be said about it. The entry is graded Low.

name: Evan Lurie
career_background: Born in 1954 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. An American composer and musician who plays piano and occasionally organ, and was a founding member of the band the Lounge Lizards with his saxophonist brother John Lurie. He began studying composition with Julius Eastman in the early 1980s and in 1985 formed a quintet to perform his compositions for bandoneon.
debut: Active from 1978 with the Lounge Lizards.
major_works: With Kapoor: Side Streets (1998). Elsewhere: the recordings Pieces for Bandoneon (1987) and Selling Water by the Side of the River (1990), and music for the Nickelodeon series Oswald from 2001.
recurring_themes: Tango and bandoneon writing, downtown New York jazz, and later children's television scoring.
creative_style: A composer moving between avant-garde jazz, tango and film and television scoring.
historical_importance: A founding member of the Lounge Lizards, a significant band in the downtown New York scene of the late 1970s and 1980s.
relationship_with_actor: One song-composing credit, on Side Streets (1998), the American independent film directed by Tony Gerber that is among the last three of Kapoor's career, produced by Bruce Weiss (PERSON-133) with Ismail Merchant (PERSON-006) as executive producer.
most_important_collaboration: Side Streets (1998), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Evan Lurie wrote the songs for Side Streets, released in 1998 — an American independent film directed by Tony Gerber and written with Lynn Nottage, and one of the last three credits of Shashi Kapoor's acting life, with Ismail Merchant among its executive producers. Lurie's own work lies almost entirely outside cinema. Born in Minneapolis in 1954, he was a founding member of the Lounge Lizards alongside his saxophonist brother John, one of the defining bands of the downtown New York scene of the late 1970s and 1980s, playing piano and occasionally organ. He began studying composition with Julius Eastman in the early 1980s — Eastman having approached him, his article records, with the words 'Don't you play with the Lounge Lizards? I want to meet their keyboard player' — and in 1985 formed a quintet to perform his own bandoneon compositions, recording Pieces for Bandoneon in 1987 and Selling Water by the Side of the River in 1990. From 2001 he composed for Nickelodeon, including the series Oswald.

name: Faiz Saleem
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ilzaam (1986).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Ilzaam (1986), directed by Shibu Mitra (PERSON-024), written also by Ram Kelkar (PERSON-037) and Rahi Masoom Reza (PERSON-035), and scored by Bappi Lahiri (PERSON-004). The film launched Govinda; Kapoor's role is the senior supporting one.
most_important_collaboration: Ilzaam (1986), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Faiz Saleem shares a writing credit on Ilzaam, released in 1986 — the Shibu Mitra picture that launched Govinda's career, scored by Bappi Lahiri, with Ram Kelkar and the distinguished Urdu novelist Rahi Masoom Reza also credited on the script. Shashi Kapoor appears as the established senior figure in a film built around a newcomer, a pattern typical of his mid-1980s work. No Wikipedia article exists for Saleem under this name or any variant attempted during research, and no other biographical source was located. The entry is graded Low and rests on the single film credit.

name: Famous Cine Studios
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for this studio. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mukti (1977).
recurring_themes: Not applicable; a facility credit.
creative_style: Not applicable.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Mukti (1977), one of five studio credits carried by that film alongside Essel Studios (PERSON-157), Natraj Studios (PERSON-240), R. K. Studios (PERSON-034) and Rajkamal Kalamandir (PERSON-079).
most_important_collaboration: Mukti (1977), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Famous Cine Studios appears on Mukti, released in 1977, as one of five studio credits on a single film — with Essel Studios, Natraj Studios, R. K. Studios and Rajkamal Kalamandir also named. The cluster is the clearest illustration in this filmography of what such credits mean: a production moving between several rented facilities, each recorded in the production-company field, none of them the film's producer, which was Raj Tilak. This workbook keeps facility credits separate from production ones so that collaboration counts reflect creative involvement. No Wikipedia article exists for Famous Cine Studios and no other source was located; the entry is graded Low.

name: Film Group
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for this banner, whose name as credited is generic enough to make searching unreliable. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Zameen Aasmaan (1984).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not applicable.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Zameen Aasmaan (1984), directed by Bharat Rangachary (PERSON-122), written by Sachin Bhowmick (PERSON-012) and Rahi Masoom Reza (PERSON-035), and scored by R. D. Burman (PERSON-003).
most_important_collaboration: Zameen Aasmaan (1984), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Film Group is the banner on Zameen Aasmaan, released in 1984 — a film with a stronger creative line-up than its reputation suggests, directed by Bharat Rangachary, written by Sachin Bhowmick and Rahi Masoom Reza, and scored by R. D. Burman. No Wikipedia article exists for the company, and the credited name is generic enough that searching for it returns nothing usable, so its ownership and other productions remain unknown. The entry is recorded because this workbook lists every credited banner, and it is graded Low on the strength of the single film credit.

name: Film-Valas
career_background: The production banner Shashi Kapoor established to finance serious films from the earnings of his commercial work. No Wikipedia article exists for the company itself; what is recorded here comes from the film credits and from the account of Kapoor's producing career in his own article.
debut: Junoon (1979) was the first film produced under the banner.
major_works: With Kapoor: Utsav (1984) carries the banner credit. The banner also produced Junoon (1979), Kalyug (1981), Vijeta (1982) and 36 Chowringhee Lane (1981), the last of which Kapoor produced without acting in and which therefore falls outside this filmography.
recurring_themes: Literary and historical adaptation, the Mahabharata, the 1857 rebellion, and Sanskrit drama — subjects with no obvious commercial constituency.
creative_style: Not applicable; a production banner, and an instrument of deliberate patronage rather than a commercial business.
historical_importance: One of the few instances in Hindi cinema of a major star systematically converting commercial earnings into art-cinema production, and the banner behind Junoon, Kalyug, Vijeta and 36 Chowringhee Lane.
relationship_with_actor: The banner credit appears on only one film in the source data, Utsav (1984), which understates its importance: four of Kapoor's productions came through Film-Valas, and the others are recorded in this workbook under their directors and under his own producer entry (PERSON-023). Utsav, an expensive adaptation of the Sanskrit Mrichhakatika directed by Girish Karnad (PERSON-060), failed commercially and effectively ended the programme.
most_important_collaboration: Utsav (1984), the banner's last film and the one that closed his producing career
biography: Film-Valas was Shashi Kapoor's own production banner, and its short life is among the most consequential facts in this filmography. Between 1979 and 1984 he used it to finance Junoon, Kalyug, Vijeta and 36 Chowringhee Lane — films by Shyam Benegal, Govind Nihalani and Aparna Sen that the mainstream would not have funded — paying for them out of the multi-starrer work that made him bankable. The banner credit survives in the source data on only one of them, Utsav in 1984, which understates its reach; the others are recorded here under their directors and under Kapoor's own producer entry. Utsav, Girish Karnad's costly adaptation of a Sanskrit play, lost money and closed the programme. No article exists for the company, so the entry is graded Low.

name: FilmFour International
career_background: The feature film division of Channel 4 Television Corporation, founded in 1982 and now known as Film4 Productions, which develops and co-finances films from British and international filmmakers. The company is documented here under its current name, since no separate article exists for the FilmFour International label as credited.
debut: Producing from 1982.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987). The company's wider output has collectively won forty-three Academy Awards and ninety-seven BAFTAs.
recurring_themes: Socially engaged British filmmaking, often on race, class and sexuality, and support for first-time and international directors.
creative_style: Not applicable; a broadcaster's film division.
major_awards: Multiple Academy Awards and British Academy Film Awards, including Outstanding British Film and Film Not in the English Language in 2024.
historical_importance: The single most important institution in British independent film since 1982, and the financier of the 1980s British cinema of which Sammy and Rosie Get Laid is a characteristic product.
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987), directed by Stephen Frears and written by Hanif Kureishi (PERSON-176), in which Kapoor plays Rafi, a former minister of an unnamed Asian government visiting his son in a riot-torn London. It is the most politically pointed English-language role of his career and quite unlike anything his Hindi work offered him.
most_important_collaboration: Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987), its only film with Kapoor
biography: FilmFour International financed Sammy and Rosie Get Laid, Stephen Frears's 1987 film from a Hanif Kureishi screenplay, in which Shashi Kapoor plays Rafi — a former government minister with blood on his hands, visiting his son in a London torn by riots. It is the most politically uncomfortable role of his career and belongs to a strand of English-language work that had no counterpart in his Hindi filmography. The company, founded in 1982 as Channel 4's film division and now called Film4 Productions, was the central institution of British independent cinema in that decade, and its output has collectively won forty-three Oscars and ninety-seven BAFTAs. Its article does not mention Kapoor; this entry rests on it together with the film credit.

name: Frank Granat
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film and on the name of the production company, George-Granat Productions (PERSON-169), which he evidently formed with George W. George (PERSON-168).
major_works: With Kapoor: Pretty Polly (1967).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Pretty Polly (1967), directed by Guy Green (PERSON-173) and produced with George W. George under their joint banner. The film, shot in Singapore with Hayley Mills, is an early entry in Kapoor's English-language career, made two years after Shakespeare Wallah.
most_important_collaboration: Pretty Polly (1967), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Frank Granat produced Pretty Polly in 1967 with George W. George, under the joint banner George-Granat Productions — an early credit in Shashi Kapoor's English-language career, directed by the Oscar-winning cinematographer Guy Green and made two years after Shakespeare Wallah had established him internationally. The film gave Kapoor a leading role opposite Hayley Mills in a British production, evidence that his appeal beyond India extended past the Merchant Ivory circle. Of Granat himself nothing could be found: no Wikipedia article exists under this name or any variant attempted in research, and the only trace is the company name he shared with his partner. The entry is graded Low.

name: Friends Films International
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for this banner. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Gehri Chot - Urf: Durdesh (1983).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not applicable.
historical_importance: Not established.

Every credit on the film except the composer's is undocumented.
most_important_collaboration: Gehri Chot - Urf: Durdesh (1983), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Friends Films International is the banner on Gehri Chot - Urf: Durdesh, released in 1983, and the film is a compact illustration of how thin the record becomes at the margins of this filmography: its director Ambrish Sangal, both its producers Ashok 'Charlie' Mehra and Jagdish Bahroos, and this banner all lack any biographical source, and only the composer Usha Khanna is documented. No Wikipedia article exists for the company and no other source was located. The film itself comes from the transitional years when Shashi Kapoor's run as a commercial lead was ending. The entry is graded Low.

name: G. R. Kamat
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Baseraa (1981).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Baseraa (1981), directed by Ramesh Talwar (PERSON-039), written also by Gulzar (PERSON-031) and scored by R. D. Burman (PERSON-003) — a Yash Chopra production and one of the more romantically substantial films of Kapoor's later career, turning on a wife's illness and her sister's place in the household.
most_important_collaboration: Baseraa (1981), his only film with Kapoor
biography: G. R. Kamat shares a writing credit on Baseraa, released in 1981 — a Yash Chopra production directed by Ramesh Talwar, with Gulzar also on the script and R. D. Burman composing. It is among the more interesting romantic films of Shashi Kapoor's later career, built on a wife's mental illness and the sister who takes her place in the household, and it supplies one of the more ambivalent rows in this workbook's Romances sheet. No Wikipedia article exists for Kamat under this name or any variant attempted during research, and no other biographical source was located, so nothing can be said of his wider output. The entry is graded Low.

name: G. V. Iyer
career_background: Born Ganapathi Venkataramana Iyer on 3 September 1917; died 21 December 2003. A film director and actor nicknamed Kannada Chitra Bheeshma, known for philosophical and devotional films, including the only feature ever made in Sanskrit.
debut: Acting and directing from the mid-twentieth century; his most celebrated period began with Adi Shankaracharya in 1983.
major_works: With Kapoor: Swami Vivekananda (1998), which he directed and wrote. Elsewhere: Adi Shankaracharya (1983), Madhvacharya (1987) and Bhagavad Gita (1993).
recurring_themes: The lives of Indian philosophers and saints; religious and philosophical texts treated as narrative cinema.
creative_style: A director of austere devotional films made far outside commercial practice, including work in Sanskrit.
major_awards: Adi Shankaracharya won four National Film Awards, for Best Film, Best Screenplay, Best Cinematography and Best Audiography. Swami Vivekananda was nominated in the Best Film category at the Bogotá Film Festival and brought Mithun Chakraborty the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actor.
historical_importance: The maker of the only Sanskrit feature film and one of the most singular figures in Indian cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Swami Vivekananda (1998), which Iyer directed and wrote and which is among the last three of Kapoor's career. Its production is unusual in several respects recorded elsewhere in this workbook: songs credited to Salil Chowdhury (PERSON-042) three years after his death, and separate background scores for the Hindi and English versions by Vijaya Bhaskar and B. V. Karanth (PERSON-115).
most_important_collaboration: Swami Vivekananda (1998), his only film with Kapoor
biography: G. V. Iyer directed and wrote Swami Vivekananda, released in 1998 and one of the last three films of Shashi Kapoor's acting career, alongside Jinnah and Side Streets. Iyer was among the most singular filmmakers India has produced. Born Ganapathi Venkataramana Iyer in 1917 and nicknamed Kannada Chitra Bheeshma, he devoted his later career to the lives of philosophers and saints, making Adi Shankaracharya in 1983 — the only feature film ever shot in Sanskrit, which won four National Film Awards including Best Film, Best Screenplay, Best Cinematography and Best Audiography — followed by Madhvacharya in 1987 and a Bhagavad Gita in 1993. Swami Vivekananda was nominated in the Best Film category at the Bogotá Film Festival and won Mithun Chakraborty the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actor. Its production carries several oddities noted elsewhere in this workbook: a posthumous song credit for Salil Chowdhury, and separate background scores for the Hindi and English versions. Iyer died in 2003.

name: George W. George
career_background: Born George Warren Goldberg on 8 February 1920 in New York City; died there on 7 November 2007. An American theatre, Broadway and film producer, educated at Williams College, and the son of the cartoonist Rube Goldberg.
debut: His Broadway debut as producer came in 1964 with Dylan, starring Alec Guinness.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pretty Polly (1967). Elsewhere: the film My Dinner with Andre (1981) and the Broadway productions Dylan and Any Wednesday, the latter running more than two years and leading to a film version.
recurring_themes: Character-driven theatre and film rather than spectacle.
creative_style: Not applicable; a producer working across Broadway and film.
historical_importance: A successful Broadway producer of the 1960s and the producer of My Dinner with Andre, a landmark of American independent cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Pretty Polly (1967), made with Frank Granat (PERSON-164) under their joint banner George-Granat Productions (PERSON-169) and directed by Guy Green (PERSON-173). The film cast Kapoor opposite Hayley Mills and is an early sign that his international appeal extended beyond the Merchant Ivory circle.
most_important_collaboration: Pretty Polly (1967), his only film with Kapoor
biography: George W. George produced Pretty Polly in 1967, with Frank Granat and under their joint banner, giving Shashi Kapoor a leading role opposite Hayley Mills in a British production directed by Guy Green. It is a significant credit in the English-language strand of his career, coming two years after Shakespeare Wallah and showing that his appeal to international producers was not confined to Merchant Ivory. George, born George Warren Goldberg in New York in 1920 and the son of the cartoonist Rube Goldberg, was principally a man of the theatre: he produced Dylan with Alec Guinness in 1964 and Any Wednesday, which ran on Broadway for more than two years. His best-known film credit is My Dinner with Andre. He died in 2007.

name: George-Granat Productions
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for this banner. Its name identifies it as the joint company of the producers George W. George (PERSON-168) and Frank Granat (PERSON-164), both credited on the same film. Everything else rests on that credit.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pretty Polly (1967).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not applicable.
historical_importance: Not established independently of its two principals.
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Pretty Polly (1967), directed by Guy Green (PERSON-173), in which Kapoor plays opposite Hayley Mills. The banner, its two producers and the director are all credited on this single film and nowhere else in the filmography.
most_important_collaboration: Pretty Polly (1967), its only film with Kapoor
biography: George-Granat Productions made Pretty Polly in 1967, the British film in which Shashi Kapoor appeared opposite Hayley Mills under the direction of Guy Green. The banner was plainly the joint venture of George W. George and Frank Granat, who take the producer credits on the same picture and both appear separately in this sheet; no Wikipedia article exists for the company itself, so the inference rests on the name and the credits rather than on a source. The film matters to this filmography as evidence that Kapoor's international work in the 1960s reached beyond Merchant Ivory into mainstream British production. The entry is graded Low.

name: Govind Nihlani
career_background: Born 19 December 1940. A film director, cinematographer, screenwriter and producer known for his work in Hindi cinema and particularly in the parallel-cinema movement. The name is spelt Govind Nihalani in his own article; the film credit in this workbook uses the variant Nihlani.
debut: Working from 1962, first as a cinematographer, notably for Shyam Benegal (PERSON-083).
major_works: With Kapoor: Vijeta (1982). Elsewhere: Aakrosh (1980), Ardh Satya (1983), Party, Tamas and Drohkaal, whose script Kamal Haasan adapted for the Tamil remake Kuruthipunal in 1996.
recurring_themes: State violence, caste oppression, police and army institutions, and the individual crushed by systems.
creative_style: A cinematographer-turned-director whose films are visually exact and politically unsparing.
major_awards: Six National Film Awards and five Filmfare Awards.
historical_importance: With Shyam Benegal, one of the two central directors of the Indian parallel cinema of the 1970s and 1980s.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Vijeta (1982), which Kapoor produced through Film-Valas (PERSON-162) and in which his son Kunal took the lead while he played the father. Written by Dilip Chitre (PERSON-155) and scored by Ajit Varman (PERSON-091), it belongs to the parallel-cinema slate Kapoor financed between 1979 and 1984 and is the only one of those films not directed by Benegal or Karnad.
most_important_collaboration: Vijeta (1982), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Govind Nihalani directed Vijeta in 1982, a film Shashi Kapoor produced through Film-Valas and in which he cast his son Kunal as the young man entering the air force while he himself played the father. Written by the poet Dilip Chitre and scored by Ajit Varman, it belongs to the run of serious films Kapoor financed from his commercial earnings between 1979 and 1984, and it is the only one of those not made by Shyam Benegal or Girish Karnad. Nihalani, born in 1940, came to directing from cinematography, having shot Benegal's early films, and made an unsparing body of work on caste, state violence and institutional cruelty — Aakrosh in 1980, Ardh Satya in 1983, Party, the television Tamas and Drohkaal, whose script Kamal Haasan later adapted for the Tamil remake Kuruthipunal. He has received six National Film Awards and five Filmfare Awards. His name is spelt Nihalani in his own article, while the film credit in this workbook uses the variant Nihlani. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Gregory Cascante
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. The source data records his credit as executive producer; role qualifiers have been normalised out of the name fields across this workbook.
major_works: With Kapoor: Side Streets (1998).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Side Streets (1998), the last of the American independent films in which Kapoor appeared, produced by Bruce Weiss (PERSON-133) with Ismail Merchant (PERSON-006) and Tom Borders also credited as executive producers.
most_important_collaboration: Side Streets (1998), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Gregory Cascante is credited as an executive producer of Side Streets, released in 1998 — the American independent film directed by Tony Gerber that stands among the last three credits of Shashi Kapoor's acting life, alongside Jinnah and Swami Vivekananda. Bruce Weiss produced, with Ismail Merchant and Tom Borders also credited as executive producers, so the film closes the long Merchant Ivory association on a project outside that company. No Wikipedia article exists for Cascante under this name or any variant attempted in research, and no other biographical source was located. This workbook normalises role qualifiers such as executive producer out of its name fields; the qualifier is recorded here instead. The entry is graded Low.

name: Gulshan Nanda
industry: Hindi cinema and Hindi popular fiction
career_background: Born in Rawalpindi, British India, in 1919; died 16 November 1985. A novelist and screenwriter, many of whose novels were adapted into Hindi films in the 1960s and 1970s, including more than a dozen major hits of the period. His sons Rahul and Himanshu Nanda became publicity designers for the industry.
debut: His novels began reaching the screen in the 1960s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sharmeelee (1971). Elsewhere: Kaajal (1965), Khilona (1970), Daag (1973), Mehbooba and Nazrana — he worked frequently with Rajesh Khanna.
recurring_themes: Romance, social issues and the action thriller; plots built on concealed identity, substitution and reversal.
creative_style: A popular novelist whose screen stories carry the construction of serialised fiction — strong hooks, reversals and a firm moral shape.
major_awards: Six nominations for the Filmfare Award for Best Story, for Kaajal (1965), Neel Kamal (1968), Khilona (1970), Naya Zamana (1971) and others.
historical_importance: The most commercially adapted Hindi novelist of his generation, and the source of more than a dozen major film hits.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Sharmeelee (1971), directed by Samir Ganguly (PERSON-021), produced by Subodh Mukherjee (PERSON-045) and scored by S. D. Burman (PERSON-040) — the double-role romance with Raakhee as twin sisters of opposite temperament, and one of the defining romantic vehicles of Kapoor's star period. The twin-substitution premise is characteristic of Nanda's fiction. His article names Sharmeelee among the hits adapted from his work.
most_important_collaboration: Sharmeelee (1971), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Gulshan Nanda wrote Sharmeelee, the 1971 romance in which Raakhee plays twin sisters of opposite temperament opposite Shashi Kapoor — one of the defining vehicles of his star period and a film whose doubling premise is characteristic of Nanda's fiction. Born in Rawalpindi in 1919, Nanda was the most heavily adapted Hindi novelist of his generation: more than a dozen major hits of the 1960s and 1970s came from his books, among them Kaajal, Khilona and Daag, and he was nominated six times for the Filmfare Award for Best Story. He worked repeatedly with Rajesh Khanna. His article names Sharmeelee among his successes, though it does not mention Kapoor. He died in 1985.

name: Guy Green
career_background: Born Guy Mervin Charles Green on 5 November 1913; died 15 September 2005. An English film director, producer, screenwriter and cinematographer, who began in the industry in 1929.
debut: Working in film from 1929, first as a cinematographer; he turned to directing in the 1950s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pretty Polly (1967). Elsewhere: Great Expectations (1946), as cinematographer.
recurring_themes: Character drama and literary adaptation.
creative_style: A director formed as a cinematographer, with a corresponding attention to image.
major_awards: The Academy Award for Best Cinematography, Black-and-White, for Great Expectations in 1948; a BAFTA Lifetime Achievement Award in 2002; and appointment as an Officer of the Order of the British Empire in 2004 for his contributions to British cinema.
historical_importance: An Oscar-winning cinematographer of the British post-war cinema who became a working director on both sides of the Atlantic.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Pretty Polly (1967), produced by George W. George (PERSON-168) and Frank Granat (PERSON-164), in which Kapoor appears opposite Hayley Mills. It gave him a leading role in a mainstream British picture directed by an Academy Award winner, two years after Shakespeare Wallah — a striking position for a Hindi film actor of the period. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Pretty Polly (1967), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Guy Green directed Pretty Polly in 1967, casting Shashi Kapoor opposite Hayley Mills in a British production shot partly in Singapore, from a screenplay by Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall with music by Michel Legrand. The credit is worth more than its obscurity suggests: two years after Shakespeare Wallah, Kapoor was taking a leading role in a mainstream British film under a director who had won an Academy Award, alongside a composer about to win his first and the most prolific writing partnership in British television — a position almost no Hindi film actor of his generation occupied. Green, born in 1913, had won his Oscar as cinematographer of David Lean's Great Expectations in 1948 before moving into directing, and worked in Britain and America until the mid-1980s across a career running from 1929. BAFTA gave him a Lifetime Achievement Award in 2002 and he was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire in 2004 for his contributions to British cinema. He died in 2005. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Gyan Mukherjee
career_background: Born 30 September 1909; died 13 November 1956. A film director and screenwriter in Hindi cinema, associated with Bombay Talkies (PERSON-130) and best known for two of the biggest successes of the 1940s.
debut: Directing from the late 1930s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sangram (1950), which he directed and co-wrote. Elsewhere: Jhoola (1941) and Kismet (1943).
recurring_themes: The anti-hero and the socially transgressive protagonist — Kismet is generally credited with introducing that figure to Hindi cinema.
creative_style: A studio-system director working within the disciplined production methods of Bombay Talkies.
historical_importance: The director of Kismet, one of the longest-running and most influential Hindi films of the 1940s.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Sangram (1950), which he directed and co-wrote with Vrajendra Gaur, made at Bombay Talkies with a C. Ramchandra (PERSON-028) score. It is one of Kapoor's child-actor films, made when he was twelve and billed as Shashiraj, and it places the beginning of his screen life inside one of the major studios of the era. Mukherjee died six years later, long before Kapoor's adult career began. His article does not mention him.
most_important_collaboration: Sangram (1950), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Gyan Mukherjee directed and co-wrote Sangram in 1950, one of Shashi Kapoor's child-actor films, made when he was twelve and billed as Shashiraj. The credit places the very beginning of his screen life in serious company. Mukherjee was among the leading directors of the Bombay Talkies studio, one of the most organised production operations in Indian cinema, and had made Jhoola in 1941 and, in 1943, Kismet — a film that ran for years, became one of the greatest commercial successes of the decade, and is generally credited with introducing the anti-hero to Hindi cinema. Sangram was written with Vrajendra Gaur, who took the dialogue while Mukherjee kept story and screenplay, produced by Sargam Pictures' Unit and scored by C. Ramchandra. Born on 30 September 1909, Mukherjee died on 13 November 1956 at forty-seven, long before Kapoor's adult career began, so the two never worked together again. His article does not mention him.

career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Bhavani Junction (1985).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One directing credit, on Bhavani Junction (1985), produced by Deepak Shivdasani (PERSON-150), written by Jainendra Jain (PERSON-066) and scored by Bappi Lahiri (PERSON-004).
most_important_collaboration: Bhavani Junction (1985), his only film with Kapoor
biography: H. Dinesh directed Bhavani Junction in 1985, his only credit in this filmography — a commercial picture produced by Deepak Shivdasani, written by Jainendra Jain and scored by Bappi Lahiri, from the phase in which Shashi Kapoor was moving into senior and supporting roles. No Wikipedia article exists for the director under this name or any variant attempted during research, and no other biographical source was located, so nothing can be said about his other films or his dates. The entry is included because this workbook records every credited director, and it is graded Low.

name: Hanif Kureishi
career_background: Born 5 December 1954. A British playwright, screenwriter and novelist. Following a spinal injury in 2022 he wrote Shattered (2024), which was a finalist for the 2025 National Book Critics Circle Award for Autobiography.
debut: His breakthrough screenplay was My Beautiful Laundrette (1985) for Stephen Frears.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987). Elsewhere: My Beautiful Laundrette (1985) and the novel The Buddha of Suburbia (1990), adapted as a four-part BBC drama.
recurring_themes: Race, class and sexuality in Thatcher-era Britain; the second-generation British Asian experience; the collision of private desire with public politics.
creative_style: A writer of abrasive, comic and politically direct dialogue, unsentimental about both British racism and his characters' own evasions.
major_awards: Academy Award and BAFTA Award nominations for Best Original Screenplay for My Beautiful Laundrette.
historical_importance: The defining writer of British Asian experience on screen in the 1980s, and one of the central voices of that decade's British cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987), directed by Stephen Frears and financed by FilmFour International (PERSON-163), in which Kapoor plays Rafi — a former minister of an unnamed Asian government, implicated in torture, who visits his son in a London convulsed by riots. It is the least comfortable role of Kapoor's career and the furthest from the romantic persona this workbook measures: a charming man the film refuses to forgive.
most_important_collaboration: Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Hanif Kureishi wrote Sammy and Rosie Get Laid, the 1987 film directed by Stephen Frears in which Shashi Kapoor plays Rafi, a former government minister with a record of torture behind him, arriving in a riot-torn London to see his son. It is the hardest role of Kapoor's career and the one furthest from the courteous romantic persona this workbook tracks — Kureishi uses his charm against him, and the film declines to absolve the character. Born in 1954, Kureishi had already written My Beautiful Laundrette for Frears, earning Academy Award and BAFTA nominations, and would publish The Buddha of Suburbia in 1990; after a spinal injury in 2022 he wrote the memoir Shattered. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Hans Choudhary
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.

recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.

relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Neend Hamari Khwab Tumhare (1966), scored by Madan Mohan (PERSON-218) — a film from the year after Kapoor's rise to stardom, when he was consolidating his position as a romantic lead.
most_important_collaboration: Neend Hamari Khwab Tumhare (1966), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Hans Choudhary produced Neend Hamari Khwab Tumhare in 1966, his only credit in this filmography. The film comes from the year after Waqt and Jab Jab Phool Khile had made Shashi Kapoor a star, when he was taking a run of romantic leads to consolidate that position, and it carries a score by Madan Mohan, one of the most admired melodists of the period and the composer of only this one film in the filmography. No Wikipedia article exists for Choudhary under this name or any variant attempted in research, and no other biographical source was located. The entry is graded Low and rests on the single film credit.

name: Hemant Bhonsle
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.

recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
