most_important_collaboration: Bandhan Kuchchey Dhaagon Ka (1983), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Hemant Bhonsle composed the songs for Bandhan Kuchchey Dhaagon Ka, released in 1983, his only credit in this filmography. The film was written and directed by Anil Sharma three years into a career that would later produce Gadar: Ek Prem Katha, and it belongs to the transitional stretch in which Shashi Kapoor's commercial standing was falling away. No Wikipedia article exists for Bhonsle under this name or any variant attempted during research, and no other biographical source was located, so nothing further can be established about his output. The entry is graded Low.

name: Hemant Kumar
career_background: Born Hemanta Mukhopadhyay on 16 June 1920; died 26 September 1989. Known professionally as Hemanta Mukherjee and Hemant Kumar, he was a music director and playback singer who sang chiefly in Bengali and Hindi but also in Marathi, Gujarati, Odia, Assamese, Tamil, Punjabi, Bhojpuri, Konkani, Sanskrit and Urdu, and was an important interpreter of Rabindra Sangeet.
debut: Recording from 1935.
major_works: With Kapoor: Siddhartha (1972). Elsewhere, a very large body of Bengali and Hindi film music and Rabindra Sangeet recordings.
recurring_themes: Rabindra Sangeet and Bengali melody carried into Hindi film scoring.
creative_style: A composer-singer of exceptional vocal warmth, popularly called the Voice of God.
major_awards: Two National Film Awards for Best Male Playback Singer.
historical_importance: One of the defining voices of Bengali music in the twentieth century and a significant Hindi film composer.
relationship_with_actor: One film, and an unexpected one: Siddhartha (1972), the American adaptation of Hermann Hesse directed by Conrad Rooks (PERSON-144), in which Kapoor plays the title role. Commissioning one of Bengal's great composer-singers for a Western art film about Indian spiritual search is a characteristic piece of that production's ambition. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Siddhartha (1972), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Hemant Kumar wrote the music for Siddhartha, Conrad Rooks's 1972 adaptation of Hermann Hesse's novel, in which Shashi Kapoor plays the young Brahmin of the title. It is the only meeting between them, and an unusual commission on both sides: an American production about Indian spiritual search turning to one of the greatest of Bengali composer-singers rather than to a Hindi film composer, and Kapoor carrying a Western art film at the height of his commercial Hindi output. Born Hemanta Mukhopadhyay in 1920 and known professionally as both Hemanta Mukherjee and Hemant Kumar, he was a music director and playback singer who sang chiefly in Bengali and Hindi but recorded in more than a dozen Indian languages, and was among the foremost interpreters of Rabindra Sangeet. He won two National Film Awards for Best Male Playback Singer, and his voice — unusually deep and unornamented — was popularly called the Voice of God. He worked from 1935 until his death in 1989. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Indeevar
career_background: Born Shyamalal Babu Rai on 1 January 1924; died 27 February 1997. Also credited as Indiwar and Indeewar, he was one of the leading Hindi film lyricists from the 1960s to the mid-1990s. His article's own occupation field gives him solely as a lyricist, which sits oddly beside the writing credit recorded here.
debut: Writing lyrics from the 1960s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Neeyat (1980) carries his writing credit; he also wrote lyrics for several other films in this filmography, which the workbook records in the Films sheet rather than here.
recurring_themes: Devotional and philosophical lyrics alongside romantic ones; a plain, direct diction.
creative_style: A lyricist of great facility working across four decades of changing musical fashion.
major_awards: The Filmfare Best Lyricist Award, which his article records among his honours.
historical_importance: One of the most prolific and durable Hindi film lyricists of the second half of the twentieth century.
relationship_with_actor: One credit in the writing field, on Neeyat (1980), directed by Anil Ganguly (PERSON-052). The credit should be read with care: Indeevar was a lyricist by trade, and his article describes him as nothing else, so this may reflect the film's own credit block rather than screenplay work. His lyric contributions to other Kapoor films are recorded in the Films sheet.
most_important_collaboration: Neeyat (1980), his only credit in this sheet
biography: Indeevar appears in this sheet on the strength of a writing credit on Neeyat in 1980, though his trade was lyric-writing and his article describes him as a lyricist and nothing more — the credit may well reflect how the film's titles were arranged rather than screenplay work, and it is recorded here with that caution. Born Shyamalal Babu Rai in 1924, he was among the leading Hindi film lyricists from the 1960s to the mid-1990s, working across four decades of changing musical fashion in a plain, direct idiom that served devotional and philosophical songs as readily as romantic ones, and won the Filmfare Best Lyricist Award. He wrote lyrics for several other films in this filmography, which the workbook records in the Films sheet. He died in 1997.
collaboration_film_ids: FILM-005; FILM-022; FILM-040; FILM-042; FILM-047; FILM-071; FILM-082; FILM-093; FILM-110; FILM-115; FILM-128; FILM-142

name: Inder Kapoor
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. He is not known to be related to the Kapoor film family. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Anari (1975).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.

most_important_collaboration: Anari (1975), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Inder Kapoor produced Anari in 1975, his only credit in this filmography. The film was directed by Asit Sen, whose reputation had been made in Bengali art melodrama, and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal, and it sits at the quieter end of Shashi Kapoor's output in a year otherwise dominated by Deewaar and Prem Kahani. No Wikipedia article exists for the producer under this name or any variant attempted during research, and despite the surname he is not known to be connected to the Kapoor film family. The entry is graded Low and rests on the single film credit.

name: Iqbal Qureshi
career_background: Born 12 May 1930; died 21 March 1998. A music composer and director credited with scores for several Hindi films between 1958 and 1986. His interest in music began in childhood, singing at private gatherings and for All India Radio; after moving to Mumbai he became involved with the Indian People's Theatre Association and began directing music for dramas.
debut: Panchayat (1958).
major_works: With Kapoor: Yeh Dil Kisko Doon (1963). Elsewhere: Bindiya (1960), Love in Simla (1960), Banarsi Thug (1962) and Cha Cha Cha (1964), whose song 'Ek Chameli Ke Mandve Tale' is his best-known composition.
recurring_themes: Melodic film songs written for the leading playback voices of the period, including Mohammed Rafi, Mukesh, Mahendra Kapoor and the three Mangeshkar sisters.
creative_style: A composer formed partly in the left cultural theatre of the IPTA, working in the mainstream melodic idiom of the early 1960s.
historical_importance: Composer for Cha Cha Cha, described in his article as the first Indian film to feature Western dance.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Yeh Dil Kisko Doon (1963), written and directed by Kanak Mishra (PERSON-069) and produced by B. D. Kapoor (PERSON-110). It falls in the uncertain years after Dharmputra and Char Diwari had failed, and was among the modest successes that kept Kapoor working until 1965. His article names the film among his credits but does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Yeh Dil Kisko Doon (1963), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Iqbal Qureshi composed the songs for Yeh Dil Kisko Doon in 1963, a film that matters in this filmography chiefly for its timing: it came after Dharmputra and Char Diwari had both failed, when Shashi Kapoor's standing as a leading man was genuinely unsettled, and it was among the modest successes that sustained him until Waqt and Jab Jab Phool Khile made him a star two years later. Kanak Mishra wrote and directed it and B. D. Kapoor produced, under the Bindu Kala Mandir banner. Born on 12 May 1930, Qureshi sang at private gatherings and for All India Radio as a boy, became involved with the Indian People's Theatre Association after moving to Bombay and directed music for its dramas before scoring his first film, Panchayat, in 1958; Bindiya, Love in Simla and Banarsi Thug followed. His best-known composition is 'Ek Chameli Ke Mandve Tale' from Cha Cha Cha in 1964, which his article calls the first Indian film to feature Western dance. He died on 21 March 1998.

name: Ismat Chugtai
career_background: Born Ismat Chughtai on 21 August 1911 in Budaun, United Provinces; died 24 October 1991 in Bombay. An Urdu novelist, short-story writer, liberal humanist and filmmaker, educated at Aligarh Muslim University and married to the filmmaker Shaheed Latif. The workbook credits her under the spelling used on the film.
debut: Writing from the 1930s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Junoon (1979). Elsewhere, a large body of Urdu fiction, most famously the story Lihaaf.
recurring_themes: Female sexuality and femininity, middle-class gentility and class conflict, frequently treated from a Marxist perspective.
creative_style: A literary realist whose fiction was direct about subjects Urdu letters had avoided, and who was prosecuted for obscenity over Lihaaf.
historical_importance: One of the most important Urdu writers of the twentieth century and a foundational figure in Indian feminist literature.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Junoon (1979), the Shyam Benegal (PERSON-083) film of the 1857 rebellion that Kapoor produced through Film-Valas and in which he plays the obsessive Javed Khan. Her involvement is another instance of the Film-Valas programme drawing major literary figures into Kapoor's films, alongside Girish Karnad, Satyadev Dubey and Dilip Chitre.
most_important_collaboration: Junoon (1979), her only film with Kapoor
biography: Ismat Chughtai has a writing credit on Junoon, the 1979 film of the 1857 rebellion that Shashi Kapoor produced through Film-Valas and in which he plays a Pathan destroyed by his obsession with an English girl. Her presence on it is characteristic of that programme, which repeatedly brought serious literary figures into his films. Chughtai, born in 1911, was among the most important Urdu writers of her century: she wrote from the 1930s on female sexuality, middle-class respectability and class conflict, often from a Marxist standpoint, and was prosecuted for obscenity over her story Lihaaf. She was married to the filmmaker Shaheed Latif and worked in cinema herself. She died in 1991. Her article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Jamil Dehlavi
career_background: Born in 1944. A London-based independent film director and producer of Pakistani-French origin, making films since the 1970s and widely screened internationally.
debut: Filmmaking from the 1970s; The Blood of Hussain (1980) is among his early works.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jinnah (1998), which he directed, produced and wrote. Elsewhere: The Blood of Hussain (1980), Born of Fire (1987), Immaculate Conception (1992), Infinite Justice (2006) and Godforsaken (2010).
recurring_themes: Religion, political violence and Muslim identity; the unresolved consequences of partition.
creative_style: An independent filmmaker working outside both the British mainstream and commercial Pakistani cinema, with a taste for allegory and political provocation.
major_awards: For Jinnah: the Grand Prize at the Festival of the Dhow Countries, Best International Film at the World Film Awards in Indonesia, the Gold Award at Worldfest Flagstaff, Best Foreign Film at Worldfest Houston, and a Golden Pyramid nomination at the Cairo International Film Festival.
historical_importance: The director of the most substantial film ever made about Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the partition of India from a Pakistani perspective.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Jinnah (1998), which Dehlavi directed, produced and wrote with Akbar S. Ahmed (PERSON-092), and in which Kapoor is the narrator — a role this workbook records as narration rather than a conventional part. It is one of the last three credits of his career, made in the year he stopped acting, and gives the filmography an unexpected final association with an internationally awarded political film.
most_important_collaboration: Jinnah (1998), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Jamil Dehlavi directed, produced and co-wrote Jinnah, released in 1998, in which Shashi Kapoor serves as the film's narrator — one of the last three credits of an acting career that ended that year. The film is a defence of Muhammad Ali Jinnah and an account of partition from the Pakistani side, written with the academic and former diplomat Akbar S. Ahmed, mounted through a British company formed for the purpose and scored by Nigel Clarke and Michael Csányi-Wills. It travelled widely on the festival circuit, taking the Grand Prize at the Festival of the Dhow Countries, Best International Film at the World Film Awards in Indonesia, the Gold Award at Worldfest Flagstaff and Best Foreign Film at Worldfest Houston, and a Golden Pyramid nomination at Cairo. Dehlavi, born in 1944, is a London-based independent filmmaker of Pakistani-French origin who has worked since the 1970s on films preoccupied with religion and political violence — The Blood of Hussain, Born of Fire, Immaculate Conception, Infinite Justice and Godforsaken. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: John Scott
career_background: Born Patrick John O'Hara Scott on 1 November 1930, and also credited as Johnny Scott and Patrick John Scott. An English composer, conductor and jazz musician who began as a pop and jazz arranger and session musician before becoming known for film and television scores. He also composes contemporary classical music.
debut: Working from the 1960s, first as an arranger and session player.
major_works: With Kapoor: The Deceivers (1988). Elsewhere, scores for directors including Richard Donner, Mike Hodges, Hugh Hudson, Norman Jewison, Irvin Kershner, Ilaiyaraaja and Norman J. Warren.
recurring_themes: Orchestral film scoring across adventure, historical and horror subjects.
creative_style: A jazz-trained arranger turned orchestral composer, at home with large symphonic scores.
major_awards: A BASCA Gold Badge Award, presented on 16 October 2013 in recognition of his contribution to music.
historical_importance: A prolific and versatile British film composer who has worked with a wide range of international directors.
relationship_with_actor: One film, The Deceivers (1988), the Merchant Ivory production directed by Nicholas Meyer in which Kapoor appears — one of the seven films he made with Ismail Merchant (PERSON-006). Scott's score is characteristic of the orchestral treatment Merchant Ivory brought to its period subjects.
most_important_collaboration: The Deceivers (1988), his only film with Kapoor
biography: John Scott scored The Deceivers, the 1988 Merchant Ivory production about the Thuggee cult directed by Nicholas Meyer and written by Michael Hirst, one of the seven films Shashi Kapoor made under Ismail Merchant's production across thirty-five years. The orchestral treatment is characteristic of what the company brought to its period subjects by that stage of its work. Born Patrick John O'Hara Scott on 1 November 1930, and also credited as Johnny Scott and Patrick John Scott, he came to film music from jazz and pop arranging and session playing, and became one of the most prolific and versatile British composers of his generation, writing for Richard Donner, Mike Hodges, Hugh Hudson, Norman Jewison, Irvin Kershner, Ilaiyaraaja and Norman J. Warren — a list that spans Hollywood spectacle, British social drama, Indian cinema and horror. He also composes contemporary classical music. He received a BASCA Gold Badge Award on 16 October 2013 in recognition of his contribution to music. His article does not mention Kapoor.

biography: K. Bapaiah directed Ghar Ek Mandir in 1984, his only film with Shashi Kapoor. It sits inside a small recurring unit in this filmography: A. Krishnamurthy produced it under the Tina Films International banner and would produce Sindoor three years later with much the same team, Kader Khan and Gyandev Agnihotri wrote both, and Laxmikant–Pyarelal scored both — a southern family concern that used Kapoor twice in the family-melodrama register suited to his senior roles. Born Kovelamudi Bapayya in Hyderabad, he has directed about eighty films in Telugu and Hindi, and belongs to a notable filmmaking family: orphaned young, he was raised by his paternal uncle, the director and producer K. S. Prakash Rao, and is a first cousin of the director K. Raghavendra Rao. He studied in Vijayawada and Chennai and has two daughters. Born Krishnamoorthy Ravi Shankar, he directed mostly for the home banner Tina Films International and has a particular record of casting performers before they were established: Govinda in Dariya Dil in 1988 and Shilpa Shetty in Aag in 1994. name: Kaifi Azmi
career_background: Born Athar Husain Rizvi on 14 January 1919; died 10 May 2002. An Urdu poet remembered as the figure who brought Urdu literature into Indian motion pictures, and a lifelong communist who hoped to see India become a socialist state. He took part in many of the century's notable mushaira gatherings. His wife was the theatre and film actress Shaukat Kaifi.
debut: Established as a poet before entering cinema.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naina (1973). Elsewhere: the National Film Award-winning lyric 'Aandhi Aaye Ki Toofan', and the screenplay, story and dialogue for Garm Hava, written with Ismat Chughtai (PERSON-183), which was India's official submission to the Academy Awards.
recurring_themes: Social justice and political commitment expressed in classical Urdu forms; the Muslim experience of partition.
creative_style: A poet of the progressive movement who wrote for cinema without lowering his literary register.
major_awards: The National Film Award for Best Lyrics in 1970; the Padma Shri in 1974; the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1975 and a Sahitya Akademi Fellowship in 2002. For Garm Hava he won a National Film Award for Best Story with Ismat Chughtai and Filmfare Awards for Best Dialogue, Best Story and Best Screenplay.
historical_importance: One of the major Urdu poets of the twentieth century and the writer most credited with carrying Urdu literary seriousness into Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Naina (1973), directed by Kanak Mishra (PERSON-069) — a modest commercial film carrying the work of a major poet, which was a common pattern in his screen career. He also wrote lyrics used in other films in this filmography, recorded in the Films sheet rather than here. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Naina (1973), his only credit in this sheet
biography: Kaifi Azmi has a writing credit on Naina, a modest 1973 film directed by Kanak Mishra — a small entry in the career of one of the twentieth century's major Urdu poets. Born Athar Husain Rizvi in 1919, Azmi is remembered as the writer who brought Urdu literature into Indian cinema, and he did it without diluting his register: a committed communist and a fixture of the great mushaira gatherings, he won the National Film Award for Best Lyrics in 1970, the Padma Shri in 1974 and the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1975. With Ismat Chughtai, who also appears in this sheet, he wrote Garm Hava, India's official Academy Award submission, taking a National Film Award and three Filmfare Awards for it. He died in 2002.

name: Kalpataru
career_background: Born K Parvez in 1937; died at a hospital in Santacruz West, Mumbai, on 17 May 2015, aged 78. An Indian film director known for melodramatic family dramas. He was survived by his wife and two daughters.

The title and subject fit Kalpataru's specialism exactly, and Kapoor's role belongs to his senior phase. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Maa Beti (1986), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Kalpataru directed Maa Beti in 1986, his only film with Shashi Kapoor and an entirely characteristic piece of his work. He was known for melodramatic family dramas, and his best-remembered titles — Ghar Dwaar, Ghar Ghar Ki Kahani, Bade Ghar Ki Beti, Khoon Ka Badla Khoon — almost all name a household or a daughter, as this one names a mother and daughter. The film carries an early score by Anand–Milind, two years before Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak made them famous, and Kapoor appears in the senior family register that defined most of his mid-1980s work. It is among the more thinly documented pictures in this filmography: its three credited writers and both its producers lack any biographical record, leaving only the director and the composers traceable. Born K Parvez in 1937, Kalpataru worked under that single name throughout his career and died at a hospital in Santacruz West, Mumbai, on 17 May 2015, aged seventy-eight, survived by his wife and two daughters. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Keith Waterhouse
industry: British literature, journalism, theatre and cinema
career_background: Born Keith Spencer Waterhouse on 6 February 1929; died 4 September 2009. A British novelist, newspaper columnist and writer of many television series, appointed CBE, and a noted arbiter of newspaper style and journalistic writing.
debut: Established as a novelist before his screen work; Billy Liar is his best-known book.

George (PERSON-168) and Frank Granat (PERSON-164), in which Kapoor appears opposite Hayley Mills. The film placed him in a mainstream British production written by a leading English novelist, two years after Shakespeare Wallah.
most_important_collaboration: Pretty Polly (1967), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Keith Waterhouse wrote Pretty Polly, the 1967 British film in which Shashi Kapoor appeared opposite Hayley Mills under Guy Green's direction. The credit is a good measure of how far Kapoor's international standing had reached by then: two years after Shakespeare Wallah he was taking a leading role in a mainstream British picture written by one of the country's best-known novelists. Waterhouse, born in 1929 and appointed CBE, wrote Billy Liar, the television series Worzel Gummidge and a celebrated newspaper column, and was regarded as an authority on English journalistic style. He died in 2009. His article does not mention Kapoor or this film specifically; the entry rests on it together with the credit.

The three Khosla credits on one film make this plainly a family concern, though no source confirms the relationships.
most_important_collaboration: Prem Kahani (1975), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Khosla Enterprises is the banner on Prem Kahani, released in 1975 and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal. Two producers named Khosla are credited on the same film — Lekhraj Khosla and Bolu Khosla, the latter as associate producer — so the banner is plainly a family concern, an inference drawn from the credits since no source confirms the relationships and no Wikipedia article exists for the company or either man. Prem Kahani belongs to the strongest stretch of Shashi Kapoor's commercial career, the year of Deewaar. The entry is graded Low.

name: Khwaja Ahmad Abbas
industry: Hindi cinema and Urdu, Hindi and English journalism
career_background: Born in Panipat on 7 June 1914; died 1 June 1987. A film director, screenwriter, novelist and journalist working in Urdu, Hindi and English, and one of the pioneers of Indian parallel or neo-realist cinema.
debut: Working from 1935; Dharti Ke Lal (1946), about the Bengal famine of 1943, was among Indian cinema's first social-realist films and opened the Soviet market to Indian films.
major_works: With Kapoor: Awaara (1951). Elsewhere, as director: Dharti Ke Lal (1946), Pardesi (1957), Shehar Aur Sapna (1963), Saat Hindustani (1969) and Do Boond Pani (1972).
recurring_themes: Poverty, social justice and the promise and failure of the new nation; the city as both opportunity and trap.
creative_style: A neo-realist by conviction who also wrote some of the most popular commercial films of his era, and a working journalist throughout.
major_awards: Four National Film Awards; internationally, the Grand Prize at the Cannes Film Festival from three nominations, and the Crystal Globe at Karlovy Vary. Shehar Aur Sapna won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film, and Saat Hindustani and Do Boond Pani also won National Film Awards.
historical_importance: One of the founders of socially committed Indian cinema, and the writer of Raj Kapoor's most internationally successful films.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Awaara (1951), in which the thirteen-year-old Shashi plays the child version of Raj Kapoor's tramp hero. Abbas wrote the film that took Indian cinema to audiences across the Soviet Union and beyond, and it is the second of the two child appearances that begin this filmography.
most_important_collaboration: Awaara (1951), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Khwaja Ahmad Abbas wrote Awaara, the 1951 film in which the young Shashi Kapoor plays the child version of his brother Raj's tramp — one of two child roles that open this filmography and one of the most widely seen Indian films ever made, especially in the Soviet Union. Abbas, born in Panipat in 1914, was among the founders of socially committed Indian cinema: he directed Dharti Ke Lal about the Bengal famine, Shehar Aur Sapna, Saat Hindustani and Do Boond Pani, winning four National Film Awards, and took the Grand Prize at Cannes and the Crystal Globe at Karlovy Vary. He wrote for Raj Kapoor across the films that made him internationally famous while working as a journalist in three languages until his death in 1987.

name: Kranthi Kumar
career_background: Born Talasila Kranthi Kumar on 5 April 1942; died 9 May 2003. A producer, director and screenwriter known for his work in Telugu cinema, who over nearly three decades produced twenty-one films and directed nineteen.
debut: Producing and directing from the mid-1970s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Swati (1986), which he directed and wrote. Elsewhere: Sravanthi (1985), which won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Telugu, and 9 Nelalu (2000), screened in a retrospective at the Toronto International Film Festival.
recurring_themes: Domestic and social drama centred on women's lives, treated seriously within a commercial frame.
creative_style: A Telugu filmmaker whose work was regularly selected for national and international showcases while remaining commercially viable.
major_awards: A National Film Award, five Nandi Awards and two Filmfare Awards South. One of his films was featured in the Indian Panorama section of the International Film Festival of India.
historical_importance: A significant figure in Telugu cinema of the 1980s and 1990s, respected both commercially and critically.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Swati (1986), which he directed and wrote and which was produced by L. V. Prasad (PERSON-208), with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal (PERSON-001) score. It is a Hindi film made by a southern creative team of unusual standing, and it belongs to the phase in which Kapoor was working increasingly with directors from outside Bombay. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Swati (1986), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Kranthi Kumar directed and wrote Swati in 1986, his only film with Shashi Kapoor, produced by the veteran L. V. Prasad with music by Laxmikant–Pyarelal — a Hindi film made by a southern creative team of unusual standing, from the phase in which Kapoor was working increasingly with filmmakers from outside Bombay. Born Talasila Kranthi Kumar on 5 April 1942, he was a substantial figure in Telugu cinema, producing twenty-one films and directing nineteen across nearly three decades, and his work was taken seriously well beyond commercial circles: Sravanthi won the National Film Award for Best Feature Film in Telugu in 1985, another of his films was chosen for the Indian Panorama section of the International Film Festival of India, and 9 Nelalu was shown in a retrospective at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2000. He received a National Film Award, five Nandi Awards and two Filmfare Awards South. He died on 9 May 2003. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: L. V. Prasad
career_background: Born Akkineni Laxmi Vara Prasada Rao on 17 January 1907; died 22 June 1994. A director, producer, actor and businessman, and one of the pioneers of Telugu cinema. He founded the Prasads Group in 1956, which came to include Prasad Art Pictures, Prasad Studios, Prasad's IMAX and the L. V. Prasad Eye Institute, and was elected president of the South Indian Film Chamber of Commerce for 1982–83.
debut: Working in film from 1930; he has the distinction of appearing in the first talkies of three different Indian languages — Alam Ara in Hindi, Bhakta Prahlada in Telugu and Kalidas in Tamil.
major_works: With Kapoor: Swati (1986). Elsewhere, a very large body of production and direction across three languages.
recurring_themes: Family and social drama made for a mass audience across several language industries.
creative_style: Not applicable; a producer, studio-builder and institution-founder as much as a filmmaker.
major_awards: The Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1982, the highest film honour in India, and the Raghupathi Venkaiah Award in 1980 for his contribution to Telugu cinema. The Government of India issued a commemorative postage stamp in his memory in 2006.
historical_importance: One of the founding figures of Telugu cinema, present at the very beginning of Indian sound film, and the builder of a studio and philanthropic group that outlived him.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Swati (1986), directed and written by Kranthi Kumar (PERSON-205) and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal (PERSON-001). Prasad was seventy-nine when it was made, near the end of a sixty-year career; for Kapoor it is one of several mid-1980s films made with southern production units. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Swati (1986), his only film with Kapoor
biography: L. V. Prasad produced Swati in 1986, his only film with Shashi Kapoor and a late entry in one of the longest careers in Indian cinema. Born in 1907, Prasad had appeared in the first talkies made in three different Indian languages — Alam Ara, Bhakta Prahlada and Kalidas — and went on to become a pioneer of Telugu cinema as director and producer, founding the Prasads Group in 1956, which grew to include studios, an IMAX theatre and the L. V. Prasad Eye Institute. He received the Raghupathi Venkaiah Award in 1980 and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1982, and a commemorative stamp was issued in his memory in 2006. He died in 1994. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Lekh Tandon
career_background: Born 13 February 1929; died 15 October 2017. A filmmaker and actor who directed numerous Hindi films and television serials, beginning as an assistant director in the 1950s. He was the brother of the Urdu playwright Yograj Tandon.
debut: Professor (1962) was his first film as director.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jahan Pyar Mile (1970), which he directed and produced. Elsewhere: Professor (1962), Amrapali, Prince (1969), Jhuk Gaya Aasman, Ek Baar Kaho and Agar Tum Na Hote; later he acted in Swades, Rang De Basanti and Chennai Express.
recurring_themes: Romantic comedy and historical romance; in his later career, television and character acting.
creative_style: A commercial director of the 1960s whose films, including the unsuccessful Jhuk Gaya Aasman, have since been reassessed as classics.
historical_importance: The director of Professor and Amrapali, and a working presence in Indian film and television across seven decades.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Jahan Pyar Mile (1970), which he directed and produced, scored by Shankar–Jaikishan (PERSON-008). The workbook notes a title and dating question on this film: the article gives it as Jahan Pyar Miley, released 30 October 1970, against the filmography table's own rendering. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Jahan Pyar Mile (1970), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Lekh Tandon directed and produced Jahan Pyar Mile in 1970, his only film with Shashi Kapoor, with a Shankar–Jaikishan score — one of the credits issued under the joint name around the time of Jaikishan's death. This workbook notes a title and dating question on the film: the article gives it as Jahan Pyar Miley, released 30 October 1970, against the filmography table's own rendering, and the row records the discrepancy. Tandon had made his name eight years earlier with Professor and went on to Amrapali, Prince, Ek Baar Kaho and Agar Tum Na Hote; Jhuk Gaya Aasman, with Rajendra Kumar and Saira Banu, failed commercially but is now considered a classic, as is Amrapali. Born in 1929, he began as an assistant director in the 1950s and worked for nearly seventy years, directing television serials as well as films and, after 2000, appearing as a character actor in Swades, Rang De Basanti, Chennai Express and Chaarfutiya Chhokare. He was the brother of the Urdu playwright Yograj Tandon, and died in 2017.

name: Louis Banks
industry: Indian jazz, advertising and film music
career_background: Born Dambar Bahadur Budaprithi on 11 February 1941. A composer, record producer, keyboardist and singer, frequently described as the godfather of Indian jazz.
debut: Composing for film and recording from the early 1980s.
major_works: With Kapoor: New Delhi Times (1986). Elsewhere: the 2008 album Miles from India, a tribute to Miles Davis, on which he was co-producer, arranger and keyboardist.
recurring_themes: Jazz, world music and Indian pop; the fusion of Indian idioms with jazz harmony.
creative_style: A jazz pianist and arranger bringing a jazz sensibility to Indian film and commercial music.
major_awards: Miles from India was nominated for a Grammy Award in 2008 in the Best Contemporary Jazz Album category.
historical_importance: The central figure in the development of Indian jazz and a defining presence in Indian commercial and film music from the 1980s.
relationship_with_actor: One film, New Delhi Times (1986), directed by Ramesh Sharma (PERSON-080) and written by Gulzar (PERSON-031), for which Kapoor won the National Film Award for Best Actor. Banks's spare jazz-inflected scoring suits the film's political register and is quite unlike the songs of Kapoor's commercial work. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: New Delhi Times (1986), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Louis Banks wrote the music for New Delhi Times, the 1986 political drama directed by Ramesh Sharma and written by Gulzar in which Shashi Kapoor plays a newspaper editor pursuing a political murder through a system that gradually closes around him — the performance that won him the National Film Award for Best Actor and the high point of his late career. Banks's contribution matters to the film's tone: his spare, jazz-inflected scoring is entirely unlike the song-driven music of Kapoor's commercial pictures, and it suits the film's restrained political register. Born Dambar Bahadur Budaprithi on 11 February 1941, he is widely called the godfather of Indian jazz, and has worked as composer, record producer, keyboardist and singer across jazz, world music and Indian pop since the early 1980s. His 2008 collaboration on Miles from India, a tribute album to Miles Davis on which he was co-producer, arranger and pianist, was nominated for a Grammy Award. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Lynn Nottage
career_background: Born 2 November 1964. An American playwright whose work focuses on the experience of working-class people, particularly those who are Black. She is a professor of playwriting at Columbia University and an artist-in-residence at the Park Avenue Armory.
debut: Her plays date from the 1990s; Crumbs from the Table of Joy (1995) is among the earliest.
major_works: With Kapoor: Side Streets (1998). Elsewhere: Intimate Apparel (2003), Fabulation (2004), Ruined (2008), By the Way, Meet Vera Stark (2011), Sweat (2015) and Clyde's.
recurring_themes: Work and its loss; race and class in America; women's labour, both waged and unwaged.
creative_style: A dramatist of documentary attentiveness, building plays from extensive interview and research.
major_awards: The Pulitzer Prize for Drama twice — in 2009 for Ruined and in 2017 for Sweat — making her the first and still the only woman to win it twice; a MacArthur Fellowship in 2007; the Susan Smith Blackburn Prize; three Obie Awards; and inclusion in Time magazine's 2019 list of the 100 most influential people.
historical_importance: One of the most decorated American playwrights of her generation.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Side Streets (1998), the American independent film directed by Tony Gerber in which Kapoor appears — one of the last three credits of his career. The film is an ensemble piece about immigrant lives in New York, a subject entirely consistent with Nottage's later work, and it came a decade before her first Pulitzer.
most_important_collaboration: Side Streets (1998), her only film with Kapoor
biography: Lynn Nottage wrote Side Streets, the 1998 New York ensemble film directed by Tony Gerber that is among the last three credits of Shashi Kapoor's acting career. The subject — immigrant lives across a single city — fits squarely with the work that would make her reputation, though the film came a decade before it: Nottage went on to win the Pulitzer Prize for Drama twice, for Ruined in 2009 and Sweat in 2017, the first and only woman to do so, alongside a MacArthur Fellowship and three Obie Awards. Born in 1964, she teaches playwriting at Columbia. That Kapoor's filmography ends with a credit from a writer of this standing is one of its stranger symmetries. Her article does not mention him.

name: M. G. Hashmat
career_background: A lyricist and script writer in Indian films, working mostly as a songwriter. His article gives no dates. He wrote 202 film songs across fifty-one Hindi films and also worked as a dialogue writer, in a style his article describes as using simple words close to daily life.
debut: Not recorded in the article; his best-known work dates from the mid-1970s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Trishna (1978). Elsewhere: Kora Kagaz (1974), for whose song 'Mera Jeevan Kora Kagaz' he won a BFJA Award, and whose dialogue he also wrote.
recurring_themes: Plain-spoken lyrics and dialogue built from everyday language.
creative_style: A lyricist who wrote in deliberately simple diction, and who moved between songwriting and dialogue.
major_awards: The BFJA Award for Best Lyricist in 1975, and a Filmfare Award nomination for Best Lyricist the same year, both for 'Mera Jeevan Kora Kagaz' from Kora Kagaz.
historical_importance: The author of one of the best-known Hindi film songs of the 1970s.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Trishna (1978), directed by Anil Ganguly (PERSON-052) and written with Sachin Bhowmick (PERSON-012) and Amarjeet (PERSON-095). The connection is neat: Hashmat's award-winning song came from Kora Kagaz, also an Anil Ganguly film, so the director brought him along to this one. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Trishna (1978), his only film with Kapoor
biography: M. G. Hashmat shares a writing credit on Trishna, the 1978 Anil Ganguly melodrama pairing Shashi Kapoor with Raakhee. The association runs through the director: Hashmat had written the lyrics for Ganguly's Kora Kagaz in 1974, including 'Mera Jeevan Kora Kagaz', which won him the BFJA Award for Best Lyricist and a Filmfare nomination, and he wrote that film's dialogue too. Across his career he produced 202 songs for fifty-one Hindi films in a deliberately plain idiom, close, as his article puts it, to daily speech. It gives no dates for him and does not mention Kapoor, so this entry rests on it together with the single credit.

name: Madan Mohan
career_background: Born Madan Mohan Kohli on 25 June 1924; died 14 July 1975. A music director of the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, considered one of the most melodious and skilled composers of the Hindi film industry and particularly remembered for the ghazals he wrote for films. He worked most often with Lata Mangeshkar, Mohammed Rafi and Talat Mahmood.
debut: Composing from 1950.
major_works: With Kapoor: Neend Hamari Khwab Tumhare (1966). Elsewhere: Adalat, Anpadh, Dulhan Ek Raat Ki, Mera Saya, Dastak, Hanste Zakhm, Heer Raanjha, Maharaja and Mausam.
recurring_themes: The film ghazal, raised to a level of refinement that has kept his reputation growing since his death.
creative_style: A composer of unusual melodic subtlety, whose settings of Urdu verse are generally regarded as the finest in Hindi cinema.
major_awards: The National Film Award for Best Music Direction in 1971 for Dastak.
historical_importance: Widely regarded as the greatest composer of film ghazals in Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Neend Hamari Khwab Tumhare (1966), produced by Hans Choudhary (PERSON-177), from the year after Kapoor's rise to stardom. It is the only meeting between them, which is itself striking given that Madan Mohan was at the height of his powers through exactly the decade in which Kapoor established his romantic persona. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Neend Hamari Khwab Tumhare (1966), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Madan Mohan scored one Shashi Kapoor film, Neend Hamari Khwab Tumhare, in 1966 — a single meeting that is worth noting precisely because it is single. Madan Mohan was at the peak of his powers through the 1960s, the decade in which Kapoor's romantic persona was formed, and he is generally regarded as the finest composer of ghazals Hindi cinema has produced; that the two crossed only once, on a film whose director, producer, writer and banner are all otherwise undocumented, is one of the odder gaps in this filmography. Born Madan Mohan Kohli in 1924, he composed from 1950 until his death in 1975, writing for Adalat, Anpadh, Dulhan Ek Raat Ki, Mera Saya, Dastak, Hanste Zakhm, Heer Raanjha, Maharaja and Mausam, and working most often with Lata Mangeshkar, Mohammed Rafi and Talat Mahmood. He won the National Film Award for Best Music Direction for Dastak in 1971. He died at fifty-one, and his reputation has risen steadily since.

name: Michael Hirst
career_background: Born 21 September 1952 and educated at the University of Nottingham. An English screenwriter and producer working in historical fiction, principally on the history of England. He launched his production company, Green Pavilion Entertainment, in December 2017.
debut: Screenwriting from the 1980s; The Deceivers (1988) is an early credit.

recurring_themes: Historical fiction; power, dynasty and religious conflict.
creative_style: A writer of large-canvas historical drama, increasingly for long-form television.
historical_importance: One of the most successful writers of historical drama in British film and television, and the creator of The Tudors and Vikings.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on The Deceivers (1988), the Merchant Ivory production directed by Nicholas Meyer and scored by John Scott (PERSON-188), in which Kapoor appears. It is an early credit for Hirst, a decade before Elizabeth established him, and one of the seven Ismail Merchant (PERSON-006) productions in this filmography.
most_important_collaboration: The Deceivers (1988), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Michael Hirst wrote The Deceivers, the 1988 Merchant Ivory production directed by Nicholas Meyer in which Shashi Kapoor appeared — one of seven films he made under Ismail Merchant's production across thirty-five years. The credit is an early one for Hirst: born in 1952, he would not reach prominence until Elizabeth in 1998, followed by Elizabeth: The Golden Age and then the television series that made his name, The Tudors and Vikings, which between them ran for more than a decade. He founded his own production company in 2017. His article, which concentrates on that later work, does not mention The Deceivers or Kapoor; the entry rests on it together with the film credit.

name: Michel Legrand
career_background: Born Michel Jean Legrand on 24 February 1932; died 26 January 2019. A French composer, arranger, conductor, jazz pianist and singer who wrote more than two hundred film and television scores as well as many songs.
debut: Working from 1946; his international reputation was made with the Jacques Demy films of the 1960s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pretty Polly (1967). Elsewhere: The Umbrellas of Cherbourg (1964) and The Young Girls of Rochefort (1967) for Jacques Demy, The Thomas Crown Affair (1968), Summer of '42 (1971) and Yentl (1983).
recurring_themes: Jazz harmony inside popular song; the through-sung film musical.
creative_style: A jazz pianist's harmonic sophistication applied to film melody, with an unusual gift for the memorable tune.
major_awards: Three Academy Awards — for the song 'The Windmills of Your Mind' from The Thomas Crown Affair (1968), and for the scores of Summer of '42 (1971) and Yentl (1983) — following his first nominations for the Demy films.
historical_importance: One of the most celebrated film composers of the twentieth century, and a central figure of the French New Wave's musical side.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Pretty Polly (1967), directed by Guy Green (PERSON-173) and written by Keith Waterhouse (PERSON-198), in which Kapoor appears opposite Hayley Mills. Legrand scored it in the same year as The Young Girls of Rochefort and a year before his first Oscar — so Kapoor's British film carries music by a composer then at the height of his international standing.
most_important_collaboration: Pretty Polly (1967), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Michel Legrand wrote the music for Pretty Polly, the 1967 British film in which Shashi Kapoor appeared opposite Hayley Mills under Guy Green's direction, from a screenplay by Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall. The timing is worth dwelling on: Legrand scored it in the same year as The Young Girls of Rochefort and a year before 'The Windmills of Your Mind' won him his first Academy Award, so Kapoor's English-language work of this period placed him alongside a composer then at the height of international reputation — as it also did with an Oscar-winning director and Britain's most prolific writing partnership. Born in 1932, Legrand was a composer, arranger, conductor, jazz pianist and singer who wrote more than two hundred film and television scores; his work for Jacques Demy on The Umbrellas of Cherbourg brought his first nominations, and he went on to win three Oscars, for The Thomas Crown Affair, Summer of '42 and Yentl. He worked until his death in 2019. His article does not mention Kapoor or this film.

biography: Mohan Segal directed Kanyadaan in 1968, his only film with Shashi Kapoor and one of the more substantial successes of the actor's early years as a star, when he was consolidating the position that Jab Jab Phool Khile had won him three years earlier. Rajendra Bhatia produced under the Kiron Productions banner, R. A. Baqueri wrote it and Shankar–Jaikishan scored it — the composers whose association with Kapoor reached back to his child role in Awaara. Segal, born on 1 December 1921, worked primarily in Hindi cinema and was active mainly through the 1950s and 1960s, a period in which his article says he directed several commercially successful films. It also credits him with introducing or mentoring actors who later became prominent in the industry, which was the aspect of his career most often remarked on. He received a Certificate of Merit at the 6th National Film Awards. He died on 19 October 2005. His article does not mention Kapoor.

name: N. Dutta
career_background: Born Datta Naik on 12 December 1927; died 30 December 1987. Also credited as N. Datta, he was a music director in Hindi films across three decades.

Chopra (PERSON-055) and written by Akhtar-ul-Iman (PERSON-051). The film was a commercial failure but is historically significant as a partition drama and as the start of Kapoor's adult career; its songs are Dutta's only contribution to this filmography. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Dharmputra (1961), his only film with Kapoor
biography: N. Dutta composed the songs for Dharmputra, released in 1961 and the film in which Shashi Kapoor took his first adult leading role — a B. R. Chopra production directed by Yash Chopra, from a script by Akhtar-ul-Iman that won a Filmfare Award for its dialogue and a story credited to the B. R. Films Story Department. The film failed commercially, and Kapoor's career as a leading man took four more years and two 1965 hits to establish; but it remains historically significant as one of the few Hindi films to address communal identity and partition directly, its protagonist a Hindu nationalist who discovers he was born Muslim. Born Datta Naik on 12 December 1927 and also credited as N. Datta, the composer worked in Hindi films from 1955 until his death on 30 December 1987. His Wikipedia article runs to two lines, gives no account of his style or his other films, and does not mention Kapoor, so this entry is graded Medium.

name: Nabendu Ghosh
career_background: Born 27 March 1917; died 15 December 2007. An author in Bengali literature and a screenwriter, who also acted briefly and directed four films late in his career. His daughter Ratnottama Sengupta is a film festival curator, author and former film journalist; his autobiography, Eka Naukar Jatri, was published in March 2008.
debut: Screenwriting from the 1950s, in the circle around Bimal Roy (PERSON-124).
major_works: With Kapoor: Krodhi (1981). Elsewhere, screenplays for Sujata, Bandini, Devdas, Majhli Didi, Abhimaan and Teesri Kasam, and stories for Baap Beti, Shatranj and Raja Jani. He acted briefly in Do Bigha Zameen, Teesri Kasam and Lukochuri.
recurring_themes: Caste, social constraint and interior suffering; the Bengali literary sensibility carried into Hindi screenwriting.
creative_style: A novelist who wrote screenplays of unusual psychological density, and the principal writer of the Bimal Roy school.
historical_importance: One of the most important screenwriters of Hindi cinema's golden age, responsible for the scripts of several of its defining films.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Krodhi (1981), directed by Subhash Ghai (PERSON-084) and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal (PERSON-001) — a late and incongruous assignment for the writer of Sujata and Bandini. Kapoor had worked with Ghosh's own milieu two decades earlier in Bimal Roy's Prem Patra, which Ghosh did not write. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Krodhi (1981), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Nabendu Ghosh wrote Krodhi, a 1981 Subhash Ghai commercial picture — a strange late credit for the man who had written Sujata, Bandini, Devdas, Majhli Didi and Teesri Kasam, and who was the principal screenwriter of the Bimal Roy school. Born in 1917, Ghosh was a significant Bengali novelist as well as a screenwriter, brought his literary sensibility to Hindi cinema's most serious films of the 1950s and 1960s, acted briefly in Do Bigha Zameen and Teesri Kasam, and directed four films himself. He died in 2007, and his autobiography appeared the following year; his daughter Ratnottama Sengupta became a film journalist and curator. Shashi Kapoor had worked within the same circle in 1962 on Bimal Roy's Prem Patra, though Ghosh did not write that film.

name: Nasir Hussain
career_background: Born Mohammad Nasir Hussain Khan on 16 November 1926; died 13 March 2002. A producer, director and screenwriter with a career spanning decades, credited as a major trendsetter in Hindi cinema. He began as a writer at Filmistan (PERSON-013) in 1948.
debut: Writing from 1948 for Filmistan, on films including Anarkali, Munimji and Paying Guest; he turned to directing with Tumsa Nahin Dekha.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pyar Ka Mausam (1969), which he directed, produced and wrote. Elsewhere: Yaadon Ki Baraat (1973) and Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak (1988), which he wrote and produced.
recurring_themes: The musical romance; lost-and-found families; youth, music and modernity.
creative_style: A filmmaker who built pictures around music and youthful energy, and whose structures were widely copied.
major_awards: A special Filmfare Award in 1996 for his contribution to Hindi cinema, and Filmfare Awards for Best Movie and Best Screenplay for Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak.
historical_importance: His article credits him with creating the masala film genre through Yaadon Ki Baraat and, fifteen years later, the musical-romance template of the 1990s through Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak. Javed Akhtar rates him the most underrated producer-director of his generation and credits him with changing the career trajectories of Shammi Kapoor and Dev Anand.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Pyar Ka Mausam (1969), which he directed, produced and wrote, with an R. D. Burman (PERSON-003) score. It is a single meeting with a filmmaker who shaped the two commercial forms Kapoor worked inside for the rest of his career — the masala multi-starrer of the 1970s, which Yaadon Ki Baraat helped define, and whose logic governs most of his peak-period films. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Pyar Ka Mausam (1969), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Nasir Hussain directed, produced and wrote Pyar Ka Mausam in 1969, the only film he made with Shashi Kapoor, with an early R. D. Burman score. The single credit understates his importance to this filmography, because Hussain shaped the form Kapoor spent his peak years working inside: Yaadon Ki Baraat in 1973 is generally credited with creating the masala film, the genre that dominated the decade in which Kapoor became one of its most saleable stars, and whose lost-and-found logic governs a great many of the films recorded here. Born Mohammad Nasir Hussain Khan in 1926, he began as a writer at Filmistan in 1948 on Anarkali, Munimji and Paying Guest, turned to directing with Tumsa Nahin Dekha, and fifteen years after Yaadon Ki Baraat wrote and produced Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak, which reset the Hindi musical romance for the 1990s. Javed Akhtar rates him the most underrated producer-director of his generation and credits him with changing the careers of Shammi Kapoor and Dev Anand. He received a special Filmfare Award in 1996 and died in 2002.

name: Nicholas Meyer
career_background: Born 24 December 1945. An American screenwriter, director, producer and novelist, known for his best-selling novel The Seven-Per-Cent Solution and for a varied directing career across film and television.
debut: Writing from the 1970s; his first major success was the novel and screenplay of The Seven-Per-Cent Solution.
major_works: With Kapoor: The Deceivers (1988). Elsewhere: Time After Time, two of the Star Trek feature films, the 1983 television film The Day After, and the 1999 HBO film Vendetta.
recurring_themes: Historical and literary pastiche; moral consequence played out on a large canvas.
creative_style: A novelist-director with a taste for period reconstruction and for genre material treated seriously.
major_awards: An Academy Award nomination for Best Adapted Screenplay for The Seven-Per-Cent Solution (1976), adapting his own novel; nominations for a Satellite Award and three Emmy Awards; four Saturn Awards.
historical_importance: The director of The Day After, among the most widely watched and politically consequential American television films ever made, and of two of the most admired Star Trek features.
relationship_with_actor: One film, The Deceivers (1988), a Merchant Ivory production written by Michael Hirst (PERSON-223) and scored by John Scott (PERSON-188), in which Kapoor appears — one of the seven Ismail Merchant (PERSON-006) productions in this filmography. It is an unusual assignment for Meyer, whose work otherwise lies well outside that company's orbit. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: The Deceivers (1988), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Nicholas Meyer directed The Deceivers in 1988, the Merchant Ivory production about the Thuggee cult in which Shashi Kapoor appeared — one of seven films he made under Ismail Merchant's production across thirty-five years, and an unusual assignment for a director whose work otherwise lay far from that company's orbit. Michael Hirst wrote it, a decade before Elizabeth made his name, and John Scott scored it. Born in New York in 1945, Meyer is a novelist as much as a filmmaker: he was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay for The Seven-Per-Cent Solution in 1976, adapting his own best-selling Sherlock Holmes novel, and went on to direct Time After Time and two of the Star Trek features, generally reckoned the best of them. His most widely seen work was for television: The Day After in 1983, about nuclear war, drew an enormous American audience and is credited with shifting public debate. He has won four Saturn Awards and been nominated for three Emmys.

name: Nigel Clarke
career_background: Born in 1960. A British composer and musician and a former head of composition and contemporary music at the London College of Music and Media. He began his career as a military bandsman, then studied composition at the Royal Academy of Music with Paul Patterson, where he was awarded the Queen's Commendation for Excellence. He has been Young Composer in Residence at the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts and Associate Composer to the Black Dyke Mills Band, the Band of the Grenadier Guards and the Marine Band of the Royal Netherlands Navy.
debut: Composing from the 1980s, principally in the concert and wind-band repertoire.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jinnah (1998). Elsewhere: The Thief Lord, and the concert works Mysteries of the Horizon and A Richer Dust.
recurring_themes: Wind-band and brass writing alongside film and concert composition.
creative_style: A concert composer of the British band tradition who also writes for film.
major_awards: Co-nominee for Discovery of the Year at the 2006 World Soundtrack Awards for The Thief Lord; winner of a BASCA British Composer Award in 2013 for Mysteries of the Horizon — a prize his article records that he asked to have withdrawn — and a nominee again in 2016 for A Richer Dust.
historical_importance: A significant figure in British wind-band and brass composition, and a teacher of composition at several conservatoires.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Jinnah (1998), directed, produced and written by Jamil Dehlavi (PERSON-186) with Akbar S. Ahmed (PERSON-092), on which he shares the music credit with Michael Csányi-Wills (PERSON-222). Kapoor is the film's narrator, and it is among the last three credits of his career.
most_important_collaboration: Jinnah (1998), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Nigel Clarke wrote the music for Jinnah, Jamil Dehlavi's 1998 film about the founder of Pakistan, sharing the credit with Michael Csányi-Wills; Shashi Kapoor provided the narration, in one of the last three credits of his acting career. Clarke's own career lies mainly in the concert hall and the band tradition. Born in 1960, he began as a military bandsman, then studied composition at the Royal Academy of Music under Paul Patterson, where he was awarded the Queen's Commendation for Excellence, and went on to head composition and contemporary music at the London College of Music and Media. He has been Young Composer in Residence at the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts and associate composer to the Black Dyke Mills Band, the Band of the Grenadier Guards and the Marine Band of the Royal Netherlands Navy. He was co-nominated for Discovery of the Year at the 2006 World Soundtrack Awards for The Thief Lord, and won a BASCA British Composer Award in 2013 for Mysteries of the Horizon — a prize his article records that he asked to have withdrawn.

It is one of the most emotionally serious films of Shashi Kapoor's later career. historical_importance: A significant figure in British film criticism of the 1960s and subsequently a screenwriter associated with Nicolas Roeg's most distinctive work.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Siddhartha (1972), Conrad Rooks's (PERSON-144) adaptation of Hermann Hesse in which Kapoor plays the title role, written with Natasha Ullman (PERSON-239) and scored by Hemant Kumar (PERSON-179). The film is among the most distinctive entries in the English-language half of his career. His article does not mention Kapoor.

biography: Paul Mayersberg shares the writing credit on Siddhartha, Conrad Rooks's 1972 adaptation of Hermann Hesse, in which Shashi Kapoor plays the young Brahmin of the title — a leading role in a Western art film taken at the height of his Hindi commercial output. Mayersberg, born in 1941, had come to screenwriting from criticism: he wrote for Movie magazine in the early 1960s and published Hollywood, The Haunted House in 1968, before writing several films for Nicolas Roeg and eventually directing his own, beginning with Captive. Croupier brought him an Edgar Award nomination in 2001. His article does not mention Kapoor or Siddhartha specifically; the entry rests on it together with the film credit.

Roy, born in 1934 in what is now Bangladesh, was a substantial Bengali novelist whose subject was displacement and the lives of the dispossessed; he received the Bankim Puraskar and, in 2003, the Sahitya Akademi Award for his novel Krantikal, and his Keya Patar Nouko is among his best-known books. name: Raamlaxman
career_background: Originally a duo of Vijay Patil (16 September 1942 – 22 May 2021), who performed as Laxman, and Surendra, who died in 1976; Patil continued alone under the joint name. A composer, pianist, musician and accordionist, he worked on about 150 films across four decades in Hindi, Marathi and Bhojpuri.
debut: Pandu Havaldar (1975).
major_works: With Kapoor: Bezubaan (1982). Elsewhere: Maine Pyar Kiya (1989), Hum Aapke Hain Koun..! (1994), Hum Saath Saath Hain (1999), Police Public (1990) and 100 Days (1991).
recurring_themes: The wedding and family musical, above all for Rajshri Productions; melodic, unfashionably sweet songwriting.
creative_style: A melodist whose deliberately traditional idiom became, through the Rajshri films, the dominant sound of the Hindi family musical in the 1990s.
major_awards: The Filmfare Award for Best Music Director for Maine Pyar Kiya (1989); the film set a record for the most Filmfare Awards won by a single film, with seven from thirteen nominations, and was the first to take all three major music categories.
historical_importance: The composer of Maine Pyar Kiya and Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!, two of the most commercially successful Hindi soundtracks ever made.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Bezubaan (1982), directed by Bapu (PERSON-118) and produced by Pranlal Mehta (PERSON-255). The credit catches the composer seven years before Maine Pyar Kiya transformed his standing; he had worked with directors including Manmohan Desai (PERSON-072), G. P. Sippy (PERSON-059) and Anil Ganguly (PERSON-052), all of whom appear in this sheet.
most_important_collaboration: Bezubaan (1982), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Raamlaxman scored Bezubaan in 1982, his only film with Shashi Kapoor and a credit that catches him well before the work that made him famous. The name was originally a duo — Vijay Patil, who performed as Laxman, and Surendra, who died in 1976 — after which Patil carried on alone under it, working on some 150 films in Hindi, Marathi and Bhojpuri from his debut on Pandu Havaldar in 1975. His article records collaborations with Manmohan Desai, G. P. Sippy and Anil Ganguly, all of whom appear elsewhere in this sheet. The association that transformed his standing was with Rajshri Productions and Sooraj Barjatya: Maine Pyar Kiya in 1989 won him the Filmfare Award for Best Music Director and took seven Filmfare Awards in all from thirteen nominations, a record for a single film at the time and the first to sweep the three major music categories; Hum Aapke Hain Koun..! followed in 1994. Born on 16 September 1942, he died on 22 May 2021.

name: Raj Khosla
career_background: Born Desraj Khosla on 31 May 1925; died 9 June 1991. One of the leading directors, producers and screenwriters in Hindi cinema from the 1950s to the 1980s. He began his career under Guru Dutt, and his early training in classical music is credited with the musical strength of his films.
debut: Working from 1949; C.I.D. (1956) established him.
major_works: With Kapoor: Prem Kahani (1975), which he directed and co-wrote. Elsewhere: C.I.D. (1956), Woh Kaun Thi? (1964), Mera Saaya (1966), Mera Gaon Mera Desh (1971), Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki (1978), which won the Filmfare Award for Best Film, and Dostana (1980).
recurring_themes: Mystery and suspense in a neo-noir register; women at the centre of the narrative.
creative_style: Known for bringing neo-noir style into Indian cinema and as a women's director who showcased actresses at their best; he, Guru Dutt and Vijay Anand were all drawn to the Hitchcock school of suspense.
historical_importance: One of the defining stylists of Hindi cinema across four decades, and among its finest directors of actresses.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Prem Kahani (1975), which he directed and co-wrote, produced by the Khosla family concern (PERSON-201, PERSON-212, PERSON-129) and scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal (PERSON-001). It comes in the strongest year of Kapoor's career, alongside Deewaar, and pairs him with Mumtaz in a romantic drama set against the independence movement. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Prem Kahani (1975), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Raj Khosla directed and co-wrote Prem Kahani in 1975, his only film with Shashi Kapoor, made in the strongest year of the actor's career alongside Deewaar and produced by the Khosla family concern with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score. It pairs Kapoor with Mumtaz in a romantic drama set against the independence movement, and belongs to the run of substantial leading roles he was taking in the mid-1970s between the multi-starrers. Khosla was among the most distinctive directors of his era. Born Desraj Khosla in 1925, he trained under Guru Dutt and brought a neo-noir sensibility into Hindi cinema with C.I.D., Woh Kaun Thi? and Mera Saaya, films his article groups with Guru Dutt's and Vijay Anand's as inspired by the Hitchcock school of suspense. He was also widely described as a women's director, for the roles he built around actresses; Main Tulsi Tere Aangan Ki won the Filmfare Award for Best Film in 1978. His early classical training is credited with the musical strength of his films. He died in 1991.

name: Rajesh Khanna
career_background: Born Jatin Khanna on 29 December 1942; died 18 July 2012. An actor, film producer and politician regarded as one of the greatest and most successful actors in Indian cinema and considered its first superstar.
debut: Acting from 1966 with Aakhri Khat, which was India's official Academy Awards entry in 1967; his stardom dates from Aradhana and Do Raaste in 1969.
major_works: With Kapoor: Alag Alag (1985), which he produced and in which he also starred. Elsewhere: Aradhana, Do Raaste and the long run of films that made him the first Hindi superstar.
recurring_themes: The romantic melodrama of the late 1960s and early 1970s, in which he was the dominant male star.
creative_style: Not applicable here; this row records him as a producer rather than an actor.
major_awards: Five Filmfare Awards, and the Padma Bhushan posthumously in 2013.
historical_importance: The first superstar of Hindi cinema, whose run of successes from 1969 onward defined the industry until the rise of Amitabh Bachchan.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Alag Alag (1985), made with Kusum Nirula (PERSON-207) under the Aashirwad Films banner (PERSON-089), written by Sachin Bhowmick (PERSON-012) and Ehsan Rizvi (PERSON-030) and scored by R. D. Burman (PERSON-003). The meeting is worth noting: two stars whose peak periods bracketed each other — Khanna's ending roughly where Kapoor's multi-starrer decade began — working together as the commercial standing of both had declined.
most_important_collaboration: Alag Alag (1985), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Rajesh Khanna produced Alag Alag in 1985, the one film in this filmography on which he and Shashi Kapoor worked together. The pairing has a certain poignancy: Khanna had been the first superstar of Hindi cinema, carrying the industry from Aradhana in 1969 until Amitabh Bachchan displaced him, while Kapoor's own peak ran through the multi-starrer decade that followed; by 1985 both were past their commercial height. Born Jatin Khanna in 1942, Khanna made his debut in Aakhri Khat, India's official Academy Award entry for 1967, won five Filmfare Awards, later served in Parliament, and was awarded the Padma Bhushan posthumously in 2013. R. D. Burman, who had scored many of his greatest successes, wrote the music here too.

name: Rajendra Krishan
career_background: Born Rajinder Krishan Duggal on 6 June 1919; died 23 September 1987. Also credited as Rajendra Krishan, he was a poet, lyricist and screenwriter, working as a film songs lyricist and as a dialogue and screenplay writer.
debut: Working in films from 1948.
major_works: With Kapoor: Samadhi (1950), Prem Patra (1962), Pyar Kiye Jaa (1966), Neend Hamari Khwab Tumhare (1966) and Silsila (1981). Elsewhere: the Filmfare-winning lyric 'Tumhi mere mandir, tumhi meri pooja' from Khandan (1965).
recurring_themes: Devotional and romantic lyrics; dialogue for mainstream drama.
creative_style: A lyricist-screenwriter of the studio era, equally at home in song and dialogue.
major_awards: The Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist in 1966, for Khandan (1965).
historical_importance: One of the most prolific lyricists and screen writers of Hindi cinema's golden age.
relationship_with_actor: Five films across thirty years, the spelling of his name differing between them: the Films sheet credits him as Rajinder Krishan on Samadhi (1950) and Prem Patra (1962) and as Rajendra Krishan on Pyar Kiye Jaa (1966), Neend Hamari Khwab Tumhare (1966) and Silsila (1981). His Wikipedia article gives both forms for one man, so the two are reconciled here onto this entry rather than split. Prem Patra remains the most distinguished of the five, a Bimal Roy (PERSON-124) film made when Kapoor's future as a leading man was uncertain; Pyar Kiye Jaa (1966) is the commercial high point, a hit carried by Mehmood's comedy.
most_important_collaboration: Pyar Kiye Jaa (1966)
biography: Rajinder Krishan is one of four credited writers on Prem Patra, released in 1962 — the Bimal Roy film that gave Shashi Kapoor his most distinguished director of the years before stardom, at a point when Dharmputra had failed and his future as a leading man was uncertain. Born Rajinder Krishan Duggal in 1919 and also credited as Rajendra Krishan, he was principally a lyricist, and one of the most prolific of the studio era: he won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist in 1966 for 'Tumhi mere mandir, tumhi meri pooja' from Khandan, and wrote dialogue and screenplays alongside his songs. He also supplied lyrics to other films in this filmography, recorded in the Films sheet. He died in 1987.

biography: Ramesh Behl produced Baseraa in 1981, the Ramesh Talwar film written by Gulzar that turns on a wife's mental illness and the sister who takes her place in the household — one of the more emotionally complicated romantic films of Shashi Kapoor's later career. He produced The Train and Kasme Vaade and directed Pukar, Jawaani and Apne Apne before his death in January 1990. His son Goldie Behl and daughter Srishti Arya both became producers, the latter a vice president of the Producers Guild of India. His article does not mention Kapoor.

Saigal worked as director, producer, screenwriter and actor in Hindi films from 1942 to 1975, but his Wikipedia article runs to a single sentence, gives no dates of birth or death and names no other titles. name: Ravi
career_background: Born Ravi Shankar Sharma on 3 March 1926; died 7 March 2012. Known mononymously as Ravi, he composed for Hindi and Malayalam films. After a successful Hindi career he took a hiatus in the 1970s and returned in 1982 in Malayalam cinema under the name Bombay Ravi.
debut: Composing from 1955.
major_works: With Kapoor: Waqt (1965). Elsewhere: Chaudhvin Ka Chand (1960), Gharana (1961), Khandan (1965), Do Badan (1966), Hamraaz (1967), Ankhen (1968), Neel Kamal, Gumraah and Nikaah (1982).
recurring_themes: Melodic film songs of the 1960s, several of which — 'Aaj mere yaar ki shaadi hai', 'Babul ki duyaen leti ja' — became standards for weddings and departures.
creative_style: A melodist of the mainstream 1960s idiom whose songs entered popular ritual use.
major_awards: Filmfare Awards for Gharana (1961) and Khandan (1965), with further nominations for Chaudhvin Ka Chand, Do Badan, Hamraaz, Ankhen and Nikaah.
historical_importance: One of the leading Hindi composers of the 1960s, and later a significant figure in Malayalam film music under a second name.
relationship_with_actor: One film, but a consequential one: Waqt (1965), the B. R. Chopra (PERSON-055) production directed by Yash Chopra (PERSON-005) that established the multi-star family melodrama and helped make Kapoor a star. Ravi's songs are central to the film's standing. His article names Waqt among his successes but does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Waqt (1965), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Ravi composed the songs for Waqt, released in 1965 — the lost-and-found family epic that effectively invented the Hindi multi-starrer, and one of the two films that made Shashi Kapoor a star that year. It is his only credit in this filmography, but a central one: the film's songs are a large part of its standing, and his own article names it among his successes. Born Ravi Shankar Sharma in 1926, he was among the leading Hindi composers of the 1960s, winning Filmfare Awards for Gharana in 1961 and Khandan in 1965 and taking further nominations for Chaudhvin Ka Chand, Do Badan, Hamraaz, Ankhen and Nikaah. Several of his songs — 'Aaj mere yaar ki shaadi hai', 'Babul ki duyaen leti ja', 'Doli chadh ke dulhan' — passed into ritual use at weddings and farewells, an afterlife few film composers achieve. After a hiatus in the 1970s he returned in 1982 in Malayalam cinema under the name Bombay Ravi, building a second career there. He died in 2012.

name: Ravi Tandon
career_background: Born 17 February 1935 into a Punjabi family in Agra; died of respiratory failure in Mumbai on 11 February 2022, aged 86, after several years with pulmonary fibrosis. A film director and producer who also worked as an assistant director and story writer. He was the father of the actress Raveena Tandon; his son Rajeev produced and directed the television series Heena.
debut: Working from 1960.
major_works: With Kapoor: Ek Main Aur Ek Tu (1986). Elsewhere: Khel Khel Mein, Anhonee, Majboor, Khud-daar, Zindagi and Nazrana (1987), which was the fifth highest-grossing film of its year.
recurring_themes: Light romantic comedy and family drama.
creative_style: A commercial director with a light touch, working chiefly in comedy and melodrama.
historical_importance: A dependable commercial director across three decades, and the head of a continuing film family.
relationship_with_actor: One film, Ek Main Aur Ek Tu (1986), scored by R. D. Burman (PERSON-003) — a late credit for both men, in the phase when Kapoor's leading roles were becoming scarce and Tandon's own directing career was closing; his last film, Nazrana, followed in 1987. His article does not mention Kapoor.
most_important_collaboration: Ek Main Aur Ek Tu (1986), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Ravi Tandon directed Ek Main Aur Ek Tu in 1986, his only film with Shashi Kapoor and one of the last of his own career — Nazrana, with Rajesh Khanna, followed in 1987 and was the fifth highest-grossing release of its year, after which he stopped directing. R. D. Burman scored the Kapoor film, in the eleventh and last of their collaborations. Born into a Punjabi family in Agra on 17 February 1935, Tandon worked from 1960 as assistant director, story writer and then director, making Khel Khel Mein, Anhonee, Majboor, Khud-daar and Zindagi, mostly in a light comic and melodramatic register that his article treats as his strength. He was the father of the actress Raveena Tandon and of Rajeev Tandon, a producer and director who made the television series Heena. He died of respiratory failure at his Mumbai home on 11 February 2022, aged eighty-six, having had pulmonary fibrosis in his final years. His article does not mention Kapoor.
