biography: Wasi Khan directed and co-wrote Oonch Neech Beech, released in 1989 — the second film the Varma family made with Shashi Kapoor under the J. V. Films banner, fifteen years after Insaaniyat, with a Laxmikant–Pyarelal score that was among the last of that duo's twenty-seven for the actor. No Wikipedia article exists for Khan under this name or any variant attempted during research, and no other biographical source was located; nor is there one for his co-writer. The entry is graded Low and rests on the single film credit.

name: Willis Hall
career_background: Born Willis Edward Hall on 6 April 1929; died 7 March 2005. An English playwright and radio, television and film writer who drew on his working-class roots in Leeds. His military service inspired his first play, The Disciplines of War, which premiered on the Edinburgh fringe in 1957 and, renamed The Long and the Short and the Tall, was professionally produced at the Nottingham Playhouse. He formed an extremely prolific partnership with his lifelong friend Keith Waterhouse (PERSON-198), producing more than two hundred and fifty works together.
debut: The Disciplines of War (1957), later The Long and the Short and the Tall.
major_works: With Kapoor: Pretty Polly (1967). Elsewhere: the plays Billy Liar and Celebration; the screenplays for Whistle Down the Wind, A Kind of Loving and Hitchcock's Torn Curtain; and the television series Budgie, Worzel Gummidge and Minder. His musical theatre work includes Wind in the Willows and Peter Pan: A Musical Adventure.
recurring_themes: Working-class English life, fantasy and self-invention, and comic social observation.
creative_style: A prolific writer across every medium, at his best in collaboration and in comic dialogue.
historical_importance: With Waterhouse, one of the most productive writing partnerships in British postwar theatre and television.
relationship_with_actor: One writing credit, on Pretty Polly (1967), written with Keith Waterhouse, directed by Guy Green (PERSON-173) and scored by Michel Legrand (PERSON-224), in which Kapoor appears opposite Hayley Mills. The film placed him in a British production written by the country's most prolific writing partnership and scored by a composer about to win his first Oscar.
most_important_collaboration: Pretty Polly (1967), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Willis Hall co-wrote Pretty Polly, the 1967 British film in which Shashi Kapoor appeared opposite Hayley Mills, with his lifelong collaborator Keith Waterhouse — a partnership that produced more than two hundred and fifty works across theatre, television and film. The picture is a good measure of Kapoor's international standing two years after Shakespeare Wallah: a mainstream British production directed by an Oscar-winning cinematographer, scored by Michel Legrand and written by that partnership. Born in Leeds in 1929, Hall wrote Billy Liar with Waterhouse, the screenplays of Whistle Down the Wind, A Kind of Loving and Torn Curtain, and the television series Worzel Gummidge and Minder. He died in 2005.

name: Working Title Films
career_background: A British film and television production company, formerly Visionensure Limited and Working Title Limited, founded by Tim Bevan (PERSON-339) and Sarah Radclyffe (PERSON-298) in 1983. It was owned by PolyGram Filmed Entertainment from 1992 to 1998 and by Universal Pictures thereafter, and is now a subsidiary of NBCUniversal. Bevan and Eric Fellner are its co-chairmen.
debut: My Beautiful Laundrette (1985) was its first significant production.
major_works: With Kapoor: Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987). Elsewhere: My Beautiful Laundrette (1985), The Hudsucker Proxy (1994), Dead Man Walking and Four Weddings and a Funeral (1994), which became the highest-grossing British film of all time with a worldwide gross of $245 million.
recurring_themes: In the 1980s, socially engaged British filmmaking on race, class and sexuality; from the 1990s, mainstream international comedy and drama.
creative_style: Not applicable; a company, whose early identity was formed by the Frears–Kureishi films.
major_awards: Dead Man Walking was the company's first film to win an Academy Award; its productions have since won many more.
historical_importance: The most commercially successful British production company of the past forty years, and in its first years the home of the decade's most politically pointed British cinema.
relationship_with_actor: One banner credit, on Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987), directed by Stephen Frears (PERSON-320), written by Hanif Kureishi (PERSON-176), produced by Bevan and Radclyffe and scored by Stanley Myers (PERSON-319), in which Kapoor plays a former minister implicated in torture. The film belongs to the company's earliest phase, two years after My Beautiful Laundrette and well before Four Weddings and a Funeral changed its direction.
most_important_collaboration: Sammy and Rosie Get Laid (1987), its only film with Kapoor
biography: Working Title Films produced Sammy and Rosie Get Laid in 1987, Stephen Frears's film from a Hanif Kureishi script in which Shashi Kapoor plays Rafi, a former government minister with a record of torture, visiting his son in a rioting London. It is the hardest role of his career and it came from the company at its most politically abrasive: founded by Tim Bevan and Sarah Radclyffe in 1983, Working Title had made My Beautiful Laundrette two years earlier and would not become a mainstream international studio until Four Weddings and a Funeral in 1994, then the highest-grossing British film ever made. The company is now a subsidiary of NBCUniversal. Its article does not mention Kapoor.

name: Yakub Hasan Rizvi
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Naach Uthe Sansaar (1976).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not established; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One directing credit, on Naach Uthe Sansaar (1976), scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal (PERSON-001). The film is the one remaining open question in this workbook's validation: its Films row records a central romance, but no Romances row has been written for it, so the pairing has still to be researched.
most_important_collaboration: Naach Uthe Sansaar (1976), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Yakub Hasan Rizvi directed Naach Uthe Sansaar in 1976, his only credit in this filmography — a commercial picture from the middle of Shashi Kapoor's busiest years, scored by Laxmikant–Pyarelal. The film carries a small outstanding question in this research: its Films row records romance as central to the story, but no corresponding row has yet been written in the Romances sheet, and the validation flags it. No Wikipedia article exists for the director under this name or any variant attempted during research, and no other biographical source was located, which is part of why the film's romantic content has been harder to establish than most. The entry is graded Low.

name: Ziaul Hasan
career_background: No Wikipedia article exists for him, and none was found under any variant spelling. Everything here rests on the credit of the single film.
major_works: With Kapoor: Farishta Ya Qatil (1977).
recurring_themes: Not established from a single credit.
creative_style: Not applicable; no biographical source was located.
historical_importance: Not established.
relationship_with_actor: One producing credit, on Farishta Ya Qatil (1977), made with Mohd Ilyas (PERSON-230) — the one film in this filmography that S. M. Abbas (PERSON-011) both wrote and directed, scored by Kalyanji–Anandji (PERSON-002).
most_important_collaboration: Farishta Ya Qatil (1977), his only film with Kapoor
biography: Ziaul Hasan produced Farishta Ya Qatil in 1977 with Mohd Ilyas, his only credit in this filmography and the last entry in this sheet by person id. The film has a small distinction: of the five S. M. Abbas films in the filmography it is the only one he both wrote and directed, the other four being writing credits alone. Kalyanji–Anandji scored it, in one of the nineteen films they made with Shashi Kapoor. No Wikipedia article exists for Hasan under this name or any variant attempted during research, and no other biographical source was located. The entry is graded Low.

name: Anand Bakshi
career_background: Born Bakshi Anand Prakash Vaid in Rawalpindi on 21 July 1930; died in Mumbai on 30 March 2002. He wrote film lyrics from 1945 until his death, becoming one of the most prolific lyricists in Hindi cinema.
debut: Writing film lyrics from 1945.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965), Mukti (1977), Amar Shakti (1978), Shaan (1980), Ghar Ek Mandir (1984), Alag Alag (1985) and seven more. Elsewhere: a catalogue of several thousand songs across six decades.
recurring_themes: Plain-spoken romantic and devotional lyrics in colloquial Hindi rather than literary Urdu.
creative_style: A lyricist of directness, writing for the ear and the situation rather than for the page, which made him unusually adaptable across composers and decades.
major_awards: Four Filmfare Awards for Best Lyricist, in 1978, 1981, 1995 and 1999.
historical_importance: Among the most prolific and commercially successful lyricists in the history of Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Thirteen films, the largest lyric-writing presence in this filmography and more than any single director. The run opens with Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965), the blockbuster that made Kapoor a star and whose songs carried it, and continues through the multi-starrer years to the supporting roles of the mid-1980s. No Filmfare citation attaches to any of the thirteen.
most_important_collaboration: Jab Jab Phool Khile (1965)
biography: Anand Bakshi has thirteen credits in this filmography, more than any other lyricist and more than any director. The first is the most consequential: Jab Jab Phool Khile, released in 1965, the year Shashi Kapoor became a star, a blockbuster that ranked second for its year and whose songs were the engine of its success. Born Bakshi Anand Prakash Vaid in Rawalpindi in 1930, he wrote from 1945 until his death in 2002 and became the most prolific lyricist of the industry, winning the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist four times, in 1978, 1981, 1995 and 1999 — none of them for a Kapoor film. His presence here spans the whole adult career, from the 1965 breakthrough through Mukti, Amar Shakti and Shaan to the character roles of the mid-1980s.
collaboration_film_ids: FILM-018; FILM-034; FILM-057; FILM-058; FILM-068; FILM-074; FILM-090; FILM-091; FILM-094; FILM-098; FILM-112; FILM-118; FILM-124

name: Sahir Ludhianvi
career_background: Born Abdul Hayee in Ludhiana on 8 March 1921; died in Bombay on 25 October 1980. An Urdu poet of standing before and alongside his film work, he was among the few lyricists whose published poetry carried independent literary weight.
debut: Film lyrics from the late 1940s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Dharmputra (1961), Waqt (1965), Aa Gale Lag Jaa (1973), Deewaar (1975), Kabhi Kabhie (1976), Trishul (1978) and Kaala Patthar (1979). Elsewhere: Pyaasa and Kabhi Kabhie are the films most associated with him.
recurring_themes: Social protest, the cost of poverty and the futility of war, set beside an unusually unsentimental romantic register.
creative_style: A poet first, writing lyrics that read as verse and frequently argue a position rather than merely serve a scene.
major_awards: The Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist, including the 1977 award for Kabhi Kabhie, and a 2013 commemorative stamp from India Post.
historical_importance: One of the two or three most important poets to work in Hindi cinema, and the one whose film lyrics are most often read as literature.
relationship_with_actor: Seven films, and the densest concentration of them in the Yash Chopra (PERSON-005) multi-starrers that define Kapoor's peak decade: Waqt, Deewaar, Kabhi Kabhie, Trishul and Kaala Patthar. He won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist for Kabhi Kabhie (AWARD-043), whose title song is the most quoted lyric attached to any film in this workbook.
most_important_collaboration: Kabhi Kabhie (1976)
biography: Sahir Ludhianvi wrote the lyrics for seven films here, and they cluster where the filmography is strongest: Waqt (1965), Deewaar (1975), Kabhi Kabhie (1976), Trishul (1978) and Kaala Patthar (1979), five of the Yash Chopra and multi-starrer titles that define Kapoor's peak. Born Abdul Hayee in Ludhiana in 1921, he was an Urdu poet of independent reputation before he was a film lyricist, and he remained one: his songs argue about poverty, war and social arrangement in a way few film lyrics attempt. He won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist for Kabhi Kabhie, recorded here as AWARD-043, and its title song is the most quoted lyric attached to any film in this workbook. He died in 1980, before the last of these films reached the screen in revival.
collaboration_film_ids: FILM-007; FILM-017; FILM-043; FILM-052; FILM-060; FILM-078; FILM-085

name: Anjaan
career_background: Born Lalji Pandey in Benares on 28 October 1930; died in Mumbai on 3 September 1997. His son Sameer followed him into the trade and became one of the most prolific lyricists of the 1990s.
debut: Film lyrics from the 1950s, with the major run from the 1970s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Muqaddar (1978), Namak Halaal (1982), Zameen Aasmaan (1984), Aandhi-Toofan (1985), Ilzaam (1986), Commando (1988) and Oonch Neech Beech (1989). Elsewhere: the Bachchan-era masala songbook, including Laawaris and Namak Halaal.
recurring_themes: Street-level romance and comic swagger written for the masala film.
creative_style: A writer of hooks built for performance, pitched to the star rather than to the page.
major_awards: A Filmfare nomination for Best Lyricist for Namak Halaal (1982), shared with Prakash Mehra.
historical_importance: One of the defining lyricists of the masala decade, and the father of Sameer, who extended the line into the 1990s.
relationship_with_actor: Seven films, all from Kapoor's later career and most of them the supporting and co-lead roles of the 1980s rather than the lead years. The important one is Namak Halaal (1982), for which Anjaan was nominated for the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist (AWARD-112); it is also one of the highest-grossing films in this filmography, third for its year.
most_important_collaboration: Namak Halaal (1982)
biography: Anjaan has seven credits here, and unlike Sahir Ludhianvi or Anand Bakshi they fall almost entirely in the later career: Muqaddar (1978), Namak Halaal (1982), and then the run of supporting parts through Ilzaam, Commando and Oonch Neech Beech. Born Lalji Pandey in Benares in 1930, he was the lyricist of the masala decade, writing for swagger and performance rather than for literary effect. His Namak Halaal lyrics brought a Filmfare nomination for Best Lyricist, recorded here as AWARD-112, on a film that was the third highest grosser of its year and one of the commercial peaks of this filmography. He died in 1997; his son Sameer became one of the most prolific lyricists of the following decade.
collaboration_film_ids: FILM-073; FILM-105; FILM-113; FILM-116; FILM-123; FILM-134; FILM-144

name: Majrooh Sultanpuri
career_background: Born on 1 October 1919; died on 24 May 2000. An Urdu poet active in the Progressive Writers' Movement and regarded as one of the finest avant-garde Urdu poets of the twentieth century, he wrote film lyrics from 1946 for more than fifty years.
debut: Film lyrics from 1946.
major_works: With Kapoor: Mohabbat Isko Kahete Hain (1965), Pyar Ka Mausam (1969), Doosra Aadmi (1977) and Sawaal (1982). Elsewhere: a career spanning the 1950s through the 1990s, and a 2013 commemorative stamp.
recurring_themes: The classical ghazal tradition adapted to film, with romantic longing handled in literary Urdu.
creative_style: A ghazal writer who kept the form's discipline inside the film song, which made his lyrics unusually durable.
major_awards: The Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist, won once, and recognition as a leading figure of the Progressive Writers' Movement; a 2013 stamp of India.
historical_importance: Considered one of the finest Urdu poets of the twentieth century and, with Faiz Ahmed Faiz and Khumar Barabankvi, among the most notable ghazal writers of his era.
relationship_with_actor: Four films across twenty years, bracketing the career rather than clustering in it: the article-less Mohabbat Isko Kahete Hain (1965) from the Nanda years, Pyar Ka Mausam (1969), the Doosra Aadmi cameo of 1977 and Sawaal in 1982.
most_important_collaboration: Pyar Ka Mausam (1969)
biography: Majrooh Sultanpuri wrote for four films here across twenty years, from Mohabbat Isko Kahete Hain in 1965 through Pyar Ka Mausam (1969) and Doosra Aadmi (1977) to Sawaal in 1982. Born in 1919, he was a figure of the Progressive Writers' Movement and is regarded as one of the finest avant-garde Urdu poets of the twentieth century, ranked with Faiz Ahmed Faiz among the notable ghazal writers of his generation, and honoured with a commemorative stamp in 2013. He wrote film lyrics from 1946 for more than fifty years while keeping the ghazal's discipline inside the film song. His presence in this filmography is slight against that stature — four credits, none of them on the films Kapoor is remembered for — and he won his single Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist elsewhere. He died in 2000.

name: Hasrat Jaipuri
career_background: Born Iqbal Hussain in Jaipur on 15 April 1922; died in Mumbai on 17 September 1999. A film song lyricist for fifty years, he was the brother-in-law of the composer Sardar Malik and the uncle of Anu Malik (PERSON-053).
debut: Film lyrics from 1949.
major_works: With Kapoor: Rootha Na Karo (1970), Naina (1973), Insaaniyat (1974) and Deewaangee (1976). Elsewhere: the Shankar–Jaikishan (PERSON-008) and Raj Kapoor (PERSON-036) songbook, including the Filmfare-winning 'Baharo Phool Barsao' and 'Zindagi Ek Safar Hai Suhana'.
recurring_themes: Courtship as courtesy; romantic address in a formal, unhurried register.
creative_style: A lyricist of restraint and politeness, writing songs that approach rather than declare.
major_awards: Two Filmfare Awards for Best Lyricist, in 1967 for 'Baharo Phool Barsao' from Suraj and in 1972 for 'Zindagi Ek Safar Hai Suhana' from Andaz, plus the Josh Malihabadi and Dr. Ambedkar awards.
historical_importance: One of the central lyricists of the Shankar–Jaikishan era and of Raj Kapoor's films, and the author of some of the most enduring courtship songs in Hindi cinema.
relationship_with_actor: Four films in the early 1970s, all of them lead roles and none of them documented successes: Rootha Na Karo, Naina, Insaaniyat and Deewaangee. His registered style, courtship conducted as courtesy, is a close match for the romantic persona this workbook measures, which makes the thinness of the four films' documentation a particular loss.
most_important_collaboration: Naina (1973)
biography: Hasrat Jaipuri has four credits here, all lead roles of the early 1970s — Rootha Na Karo (1970), Naina (1973), Insaaniyat (1974) and Deewaangee (1976) — and not one of them is a documented success or carries a plot detailed enough to score. Born Iqbal Hussain in Jaipur in 1922, he wrote film lyrics for fifty years and won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist twice, in 1967 for 'Baharo Phool Barsao' and in 1972 for 'Zindagi Ek Safar Hai Suhana', both elsewhere. He was the brother-in-law of Sardar Malik and the uncle of Anu Malik, who appears in this sheet as PERSON-053. His characteristic manner, courtship written as courtesy and address rather than declaration, is unusually close to the romantic persona this filmography exists to measure.

name: Gulshan Bawra
career_background: Born Gulshan Kumar Mehta in Sheikhupura on 12 April 1937; died in Mumbai on 7 August 2009. He wrote under the pen name Gulshan Bawra and also acted in small parts.
debut: Film lyrics from 1961.
major_works: With Kapoor: Jaanwar Aur Insaan (1972) and Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979). Elsewhere: 'Mere Desh Ki Dharti' from Upkar and 'Yaari Hai Imaan Mera' from Zanjeer, both Filmfare winners.
recurring_themes: Patriotic address and male friendship, written for the chorus rather than the couple.
creative_style: A lyricist of the collective sentiment, strongest where a song has to speak for a crowd or a bond between men.
major_awards: Two Filmfare Awards for Best Lyricist, in 1968 for 'Mere Desh Ki Dharti' from Upkar and in 1974 for 'Yaari Hai Imaan Mera' from Zanjeer.
historical_importance: The author of two of the best known non-romantic songs in Hindi cinema, one patriotic and one about friendship.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, Jaanwar Aur Insaan (1972) and Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), neither a success and neither carrying a romance that belongs to Kapoor's character. His two famous lyrics, on patriotism and on male friendship, were both written elsewhere, though the second theme is the one this filmography is full of.
most_important_collaboration: Jaanwar Aur Insaan (1972)
biography: Gulshan Bawra has two credits here, Jaanwar Aur Insaan (1972) and Duniya Meri Jeb Mein (1979), neither of them successful and neither giving Kapoor's character the film's romance. Born Gulshan Kumar Mehta in Sheikhupura in 1937, he wrote under the pen name Bawra from 1961, acted in small parts, and won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist twice — in 1968 for 'Mere Desh Ki Dharti' from Upkar and in 1974 for 'Yaari Hai Imaan Mera' from Zanjeer. Both are songs for a collective rather than a couple, one patriotic and one about male friendship, and the second is precisely the register that the multi-starrers at the centre of this filmography run on, even though he did not write their songs. He died in 2009.

name: Santosh Anand
career_background: Born on 5 March 1929 in Sikandrabad, Bulandshahr, and educated at Aligarh Muslim University. He attained success in the 1970s and won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist twice.
debut: Film lyrics from the early 1970s.
major_works: With Kapoor: Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974) and Kranti (1981). Elsewhere: 'Ek Pyaar Ka Nagma Hai' from Shor.
recurring_themes: Moral argument and romantic idealism in plain Hindi, often addressed to a condition rather than a person.
creative_style: A writer of declarative, almost editorial lyrics, suited to films that argue a case.
major_awards: Two Filmfare Awards for Best Lyricist, in 1975 for Roti Kapda Aur Makaan and in 1983, with further nominations including Shor (1973).
historical_importance: The lyricist of the Manoj Kumar message film at its commercial height.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, and both are among the biggest commercial successes in this filmography: Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974) and Kranti (1981), each the top-ranked Hindi release of its year on the trade figures. He won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist for the first (AWARD-022, for 'Main Na Bhoolunga') and took a second nomination in the same category at the same ceremony (AWARD-026, for 'Aur Nahin Bus Aur Nahin').
most_important_collaboration: Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974)
biography: Santosh Anand has only two credits in this filmography, but they are the two biggest commercial successes in it: Roti Kapda Aur Makaan (1974) and Kranti (1981), each the top-ranked Hindi release of its year on Box Office India's figures. He won the Filmfare Award for Best Lyricist for the first, recorded here as AWARD-022 for 'Main Na Bhoolunga', and was nominated a second time in the same category at the same ceremony for 'Aur Nahin Bus Aur Nahin' (AWARD-026) — one of eleven nominations the film took. Born in 1929 at Sikandrabad and educated at Aligarh Muslim University, he came to prominence in the 1970s writing for the Manoj Kumar (PERSON-033) message film, and won the award a second time in 1983.

name: Nida Fazli
career_background: Born Muqtida Hasan Nida Fazli in Delhi on 12 October 1938; died in Mumbai on 8 February 2016. An Urdu and Hindi poet, lyricist and dialogue writer.
debut: Published poetry from the 1960s; film lyrics alongside it.
major_works: With Kapoor: Silsila (1981) and Bepanaah (1985). Elsewhere: the poetry collection Khoya Hua Sa Kuchh, and lyrics for Sur.
recurring_themes: The short, plain-spoken Hindi doha and the unresolved emotional situation.
creative_style: A poet who wrote with deliberate simplicity, compressing feeling into very short forms.
major_awards: The Sahitya Akademi Award in Urdu (1998) for Khoya Hua Sa Kuchh, the Star Screen and Bollywood Movie awards for Best Lyricist (2003) for Sur, and the Padma Shri (2013).
historical_importance: A major modern Urdu poet who kept a parallel career in film without subordinating the poetry to it.
relationship_with_actor: Two films, Silsila (1981) and Bepanaah (1985). Silsila is the more significant: a Yash Chopra (PERSON-005) film on marriage and an affair, in which Kapoor's part is supporting, and one of the few titles here where the lyric writing is credited across several poets including Javed Akhtar and Rajendra Krishan (PERSON-274).
most_important_collaboration: Silsila (1981)
biography: Nida Fazli has two credits here, Silsila (1981) and Bepanaah (1985). The first matters more: Yash Chopra's film about a marriage and an affair, on which Kapoor plays a supporting part and the lyrics are divided among several poets. Born Muqtida Hasan Nida Fazli in Delhi in 1938, he was a significant modern Urdu poet who kept film work beside the poetry rather than beneath it, winning the Sahitya Akademi Award in Urdu in 1998 for the collection Khoya Hua Sa Kuchh and the Padma Shri in 2013, with Best Lyricist awards from Star Screen and the Bollywood Movie Awards in 2003 for Sur. His manner — very short forms, plain Hindi, feeling left unresolved — suits Silsila's subject more than it suits the multi-starrers that surround it. He died in 2016.
